content: Elon Musk has regained his title as the world's only trillionaire. The Tesla CEO made history earlier this year by becoming the first person worth 13 figures after SpaceX's blockbuster initial public offering in June. Musk's wealth came back down a little closer to Earth after SpaceX's stock price fell following an initial surge. The rocket and AI company's stock price has been creeping back up since early August, reaching $171.09 as of Monday's market close. The nearly 8% boost on Monday brought Musk's net worth back over the trillion-dollar threshold, according to Forbes, which estimated his wealth at $1.046 trillion. Musk's wealth previously peaked on June 16 at $1.32 trillion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. While Musk had long been counted among the richest people in the world, the SpaceX IPO put him in another stratosphere. The second- and third-wealthiest people in the world as of Monday were Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Google cofounder Larry Page, worth $371 billion and $284 billion, respectively, according to Forbes. Much of Musk's net worth comes from stakes in SpaceX and Tesla, so it is typically tied to the success of those companies. SpaceX's stock reached its highest level since June on Monday. Besi makes the machines that bond chip surfaces directly together, a market Bernstein expects it to dominate in 2028, and the Dutch company was the worst performer in the Stoxx 600 last quarter before Bank of America halved its price target ASML air freight containers in Tainan, May 2025 Bank of America cut BE Semiconductor Industries to neutral and nearly halved its price target, saying the share price does not reflect the threat of ASML entering hybrid bonding, the market Besi depends on for growth. Besi has also been approached by two American rivals, one of which has owned 9% of it since last year. Bank of America has cut BE Semiconductor Industries to neutral and nearly halved its price target, because another Dutch company might enter its market. Besi makes the machines that bond chip surfaces directly to each other. ASML has said in public that it is looking at the same technology. The threat is “not reflected in the stock and could remain an overhang” until ASML’s plans are clearer, analysts led by Didier Scemama wrote, as Bloomberg reported. Besi fell as much as 6.4% on Tuesday. Neither company responded immediately to requests for comment. Hybrid bonding joins two chip surfaces directly, with no metal bumps in between, which moves heat out better. For Besi it is the whole investment case. The company told investors in August it could ship more than 2,000 of the tools by 2030 in an optimistic scenario. Its 2025 annual report put cumulative orders above 150. Bernstein expects three of every four hybrid bonders shipped in 2028 to be Besi’s. The shares were the worst performer in the Stoxx 600 last quarter. They have fallen about 40% from a June peak and are still up 45% this year. ASML shipped its first advanced packaging product last year, and its chief executive Christophe Fouquet said in April that it continues to look at supporting customers in hybrid bonding. ASML is $300B from a trillion. Yields are the reason there is an opening at all. Manufacturers struggle to produce working chips consistently at the accuracy needed to stack logic or memory, Bank of America said, which is the kind of precision ASML sells. The analysts are not assuming it takes significant market share. Besi is also a target rather than only a competitor. Reuters reported in March that Lam Research and Applied Materials had approached it and that it had hired Morgan Stanley, with talks starting in mid-2025, pausing over tensions between Washington and Brussels and then resuming. Applied Materials has held 9% since April 2025. Any bid would need clearance in The Hague, where semiconductors have sat inside the investment screening law since 2023. Besi said in March that it was committed to remaining independent. The government blocked an American buyer of a Dutch cloud provider in May, which established that the regime applies whoever the money belongs to, and six more technologies come inside the law in January. GameStopPlayStationPrice IncreasePS5 Pro  It’s getting more expensive and annoying to play and enjoy video games in 2026. Case in point, GameStop is now selling used PlayStation 5 Pro consoles for $1400 as the sought-after machines become harder and harder to find in the lead-up to Grand Theft Auto 6‘s launch. On Monday, someone leaked on Reddit what appears to be an internal message that GameStop sent to stores, alerting employees that the company was increasing the price of several pre-owned variants of Sony’s more powerful PlayStation 5 Pro console. Currently, the PS5 Pro has a suggested retail price of $900, though good luck finding a store that actually has them in stock for that. GameStop’s memo suggested it would instead start charging anywhere from $1,400 to $1,500 for various versions of the PS5 Pro. Yes, that’s way more than the cost of a new PS5 Pro, something the alleged memo claims is “intentional.” On October 6, GameStop updated the price of a standard edition pre-owned PS5 Pro on its website to $1,400, seemingly confirming the validity of the leaked memo. Currently, as of 9:30 a.m. ET, the pre-owned PS5 Pro on GameStop’s site is out of stock. A new PS5 Pro is still listed at $900 on GameStop’s site. It is also out of stock. Kotaku has contacted GameStop for more information about this change and what’s behind it. Some former GameStop employees have suggested the reason for the massive price increase on used consoles is because GameStop, like everyone else in the world, is struggling to get their hands on new PS5 Pros. And those consoles are pricey to stock and have to allegedly be sold at $900 or bundled with other items to increase the price. Don’t worry, Sony says it has all the RAM it needs to make more PS5 consoles. However, used consoles can be sold for any price GameStop decides on, and are much cheaper for it to acquire. The chain can offer people trade-in credit far below the hardware’s actual value to take advantage of people who might not realize just how hard a PS5 Pro is to get right now. So these former employees believe GameStop is prioritizing used PS5 Pros, which are being sold online for $1,400 or more, over trying to stock new consoles in order to make more money as people rush out to upgrade their consoles before Grand Theft Auto 6′s launch in November. GameStop isn’t the only retailer that’s charging more than $900 for a PS5 Pro. Walmart, Best Buy, and Amazon, among others, also have PS5 Pro consoles, some used, listed for $1,400 or more. However, these are being sold through third-party resellers and partners and not directly from the retailers. Anyway, remember when the PS5 Pro was announced at $700, and people thought that price was wild? I mean, it was, but now it looks so quaint. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. The pay figures, from Anthropic's IPO prospectus, put him above Alphabet's and Amazon's chiefs but behind Oracle's. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei arrives near the White House for a meeting with President Donald Trump, Washington, DC, 29 September 2026 Dario Amodei earned $18M last year as chief executive of Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, according to the company’s IPO prospectus. Reuters reported the figure on Tuesday after seeing the filing, which has not been made public. Most of the package came as stock and options rather than salary. Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s president, each had their annual salary doubled to $1.4M in July. Daniela Amodei received a total of $16.4M for 2025. The board of Anthropic has also committed to giving the two of them more shares this year in the form of restricted stock units, some of which are conditional on them remaining with the company and some of which are tied to the listing. The document states that Krishna Rao’s salary for 2025 will be $720,250. Rao, who joined the company in 2024 and was granted options to 1.4 million shares, exercised options valued at $385,285 the previous year. Anthropic did not provide any comment on the figures when Reuters inquired. Anthropic is set to go public as early as this autumn at a valuation that could exceed $2 trillion, as stated in the prospectus, and it submitted its application for the listing confidentially in June. Amodei’s salary is typical of what top executives at big technology companies receive, since Oracle’s co-CEO Clayton Magouyrk earned $627.5 million in 2025. Also, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet made $10.9 million, most of which was paid for his personal security, and Andy Jassy of Amazon made $2.1 million. The annual figures fail to take into account most of the wealth which these founders and executives possess in the form of shares. If, instead, the SEC measure of compensation actually paid is applied, one that includes changes in the value of unvested stock, Pichai received $213.9 million and Jassy $13.2 million. Founders rarely need large annual pay, said Courtney Yu, director of research at pay data firm Equilar. “They can just live off the wealth of the equity they already own,” Yu told Reuters. The prospectus fails to state the founders’ ownership percentages, whereas Amodei and Anthropic’s other six co-founders committed in the filing to donating 80% of their personal shares in Anthropic to charity. This week, AI researcher Yann LeCun also described Amodei as “deluded”. Tech > Services & Software > AI Mistral Large 4 is a state-of-the-art model for cyberdefense, manufacturing, finance-related tasks and multimodal use. Reporter II Reporter II October 6, 2026, 3:35 pm ET New AI models are coming, and they don’t stop coming.  On the heels of the recent rollout of Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, Mistral AI is launching a new flagship model, Mistral Large 4, with a public preview available on Tuesday. A French company known for its open-source and open-weight LLMs, Mistral AI reports that the Large 4 model “ranks among the best open-weight models of the world” on aggregated metrics and also outperforms European and US models, while also catching up to Chinese competitors, who have been dominating the open-weight sector.  More from CNET I talked with Mistral Chief Scientist Guillaume Lample and VP of Science Pierre Stock about the new model – affectionately known as “le Chonk” – its specialized capabilities and extreme compute efficiency. Here’s what to know.  Lample and Stock said that Mistral Large 4 was built to process both text and images, closing performance gaps from previous Mistral models. Specifically, Large 4 touts more advanced cybersecurity and agentic capabilities, as well as a better ability to handle manufacturing- and finance-related tasks. Mistral Large 4 was designed to excel at defensive cybersecurity tasks, including log inspection, code auditing and checking for newly published exploits or vulnerabilities. Beyond defensive measures, Mistral says the new model offers offensive cybersecurity measures to identify and address weaknesses.  “Really, the core competency we’re looking at for ML4 is agentic capabilities,” said Stock.  Mistral Large 4 was built with a focus on agentic performance for planning, research or handling complex enterprise tasks that would take human experts hours or days to complete. The Mistral AI team said the model reaches “state-of-the-art” performance on critical agentic benchmarks like SWE-bench and Terminal Bench – evaluation frameworks for testing how well agents handle complex tasks – for tasks like coding, analyzing and pulling requests.  The Mistral team says the model outperforms competitors in aerial and satellite imagery analysis, with the capacity to identify visual patterns and objects on maps, such as forest fires.  “On grounding capabilities, it outperforms all existing models, including the closed ones,” the press release for the model says. “These are critical as cyberattacks get faster and cheaper, companies write more code than ever and the world needs more chips to keep up with AI demand.” Grounding is a technique used in AI development to try to eliminate hallucinations – when the LLM generates inaccurate information – by anchoring the AI’s outputs in external resources, like documents and databases, rather than just the materials it was trained on internally. Grounding also helps keep data and information fresh while providing context for the AI’s responses.  Mistral says the new model was also trained on more than 160 languages, including every official language of the European Union, as well as Latin and non-Latin languages, to answer prompts natively.  Mistral will roll out ML4 on Oct. 27. Until then, the model is available for a public preview period, allowing the Mistral team to further assess it with feedback from developers, cybersecurity experts and state officials. The team will also use this period for additional reinforcement learning and fine-tuning. You can try the preview API here.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Santé says it serves nearly 1,000 retailers handling $2 billion in annual merchandise sales. FINTOP led the round, and the next challenge is using that data to make each liquor store more profitable. Every bottle sitting unsold on a liquor store shelf ties up cash. Deciding when to discount it, which customers might buy it and whether to order another case requires information and time. An independent retailer may struggle to pull that together. Santé sees a business opportunity in those everyday decisions. This week, the company announced $15 million in Series A funding led by FINTOP. Returning investors Bonfire Ventures, Operator Collective, Y Combinator and Veridical Ventures participated. Its pitch is that artificial intelligence, connected to the software merchants already use to run their stores, can help them make better decisions about inventory, marketing and staffing. Santé says it serves nearly 1,000 retailers representing $2 billion in annual gross merchandise volume. That measures merchandise sales across its retail footprint, rather than Santé’s revenue. Still, it gives the company a substantial base of commercial activity around which to build its next generation of products. The funding follows a $7.6 million seed round announced earlier this year. It signals an increasingly ambitious agenda for CEO Darren Fike: moving from software that reduces administrative work to software that helps generate business. “When we started Santé, our mission was to eliminate the operational headaches that plague independent wine and liquor retailers,” Fike said in the announcement. Now, he said, the company wants to “build a growth engine that proactively drives sales, re-engages lapsed customers, and actively boosts the bottom line of our customers.” That is a compelling proposition in a market where growth has become harder to find. U.S. spirits supplier revenue declined 2.2% to $36.4 billion in 2025, according to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States. That was even as sales volume increased 1.9%. Premixed cocktails, including spirits-based ready-to-drink products, were a bright spot, while other major categories declined. Those are supplier figures, rather than store-level results. But they illustrate an industry in which moving more product does not automatically produce more revenue. For retailers, that puts greater weight on the assortment they carry, the prices they charge and the customers they can persuade to return. Santé’s strategy starts with bringing those parts of the business into one system. Its platform spans checkout, inventory, e-commerce, delivery orders, marketing and subscriptions. It also incorporates details specific to alcohol retail. These include wine vintages, bottle and keg tracking, and mix-and-match case discounts. Those features may sound mundane alongside the promise of autonomous AI. But they help explain the company’s investment thesis: useful automation depends on understanding how the merchant’s business actually works. A system recommending a promotion needs accurate costs and stock levels. A campaign advertising a particular wine needs to distinguish the right vintage. An ordering recommendation needs to account for products sold by both the bottle and the case. If that information is fragmented or outdated, an AI-generated recommendation may simply help a retailer make the wrong decision faster. Santé says its invoice tools scan distributor invoices and automatically update inventory quantities and unit costs within minutes. That removes a repetitive task, while also supplying information that could improve decisions elsewhere in the business. A price recommendation, for example, becomes more useful when it reflects what the store most recently paid for the product. The company’s merchandising agent builds on that foundation. It analyzes item-level sales data and suggests pricing and promotional strategies for slow-moving goods. The opportunity is to help merchants put their cash to better use. Clearing a product that has been sitting on the shelf can make room for something customers are more likely to buy. But the economics require care: a discount can accelerate sales while reducing the profit earned on each bottle. That makes the quality of the recommendation more consequential than the speed at which it is delivered. Customer marketing offers another route to growth. Santé says its marketing agent groups shoppers according to purchase history and launches email and text-message campaigns promoting products, events and discounts. The attraction is the connection between inventory and customer behavior. A store might have both an oversupply of a particular wine and a group of customers who regularly buy similar bottles. Bringing those facts together could give the owner a more focused way to move the stock. That example illustrates the intended value of the platform. The announcement does not establish how completely the process runs without merchant involvement. But it explains why owning the operational software could matter. The system already sits close to the information needed to decide what to promote and to whom. Santé is applying a similar approach to staffing. Its scheduling agent uses store-level sales patterns to help match employees across roles with expected demand. The platform also brings delivery orders from DoorDash, Uber Eats, GrubHub and Instacart into the point-of-sale system. It generates descriptions and images for online product catalogs, according to the company. Individually, these tools address familiar retail chores. Together, they support a broader ambition: making Santé a central part of how an owner manages the business throughout the day. For the lead investor FINTOP, specialized software and embedded financial services are central to the appeal. “It’s rare to find a founder and team at this stage that have both proven the solution is superior and are executing at an elite velocity in a massive, complex vertical,” said Brittani Roberts, the Director at FINTOP who leads the firm’s Vertical SaaS and Embedded Fintech thesis. “The team has built intuitive and practical AI back office workflows, with embedded fintech throughout the platform, so store owners aren’t simply getting another tool to track inventory. They’re getting an intelligent platform that directly expands their profit margins and operational scale.” The $15 million round is a bet that a specialized software provider can turn the daily records of a neighborhood business into real growth. You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition? Here’s how Gen Z is “reorganizing the American Dream” and cutting back to afford their goals.  Copied to clipboard Gen Z is cutting costs everywhere — except at the airport.  A new report from Fox Business’ The Big Money Show shows that Gen Z is abandoning everyday splurges but refuses to give up travel. According to a Future Partners study, 43.6% of Gen Z take spontaneous leisure trips very frequently or frequently compared to the 25.2% average across generations.  Gen Z is trading dining out and self-care for a passport stamp. A Skyscanner 2026 travel trends report shows that the generation consciously made financial sacrifices for their most recent vacation. More than half of the respondents (52%) said they ate out less and 40% said they cut back on haircuts.  Taylor Price, founder of Priceless Tay, a personal finance education and coaching platform, told Fox Business that Gen Z is “reorganizing the American Dream.” “We haven’t forgotten about it,” she explained. “So back in my parents’ generation, it was work, get married, have children, get a house, retire, then go and travel the world.” Price said that owning a house now feels outside of the realm of possibility and is “out of touch” with Gen Z’s reality. Instead, the generation is focused on achieving other, more immediately attainable goals.  “We’re beginning to travel a lot more now,” she said. “We’re just changing that reality for us.”  Price mentioned that Gen Z is thinking about homeownership in a “very strategic way.” Instead of buying a home, this generation is taking their savings and investing the funds, growing them over time.  “With investing apps now, we have so much accessibility in different ways to build wealth,” Price said. “Going back to homeownership, that was a principal way previous generations were able to create wealth.” She mentioned that now, Gen Z is looking at creating wealth by investing in the stock market. “It’s amazing because this is one way that we’re able to accelerate our wealth-building opportunities,” she said.  Gen Z is also focused on career growth. Those who live in rural areas can easily move to cities for work without worrying about making mortgage payments on a house.  Americans now expect to be about 40 when they purchase their first home, compared with 28 in the early 1990s, according to data cited earlier this year by Fortune.  More than half of non-homeowners said in the data that buying a house feels unattainable. Even renters under 40 earning six-figure salaries said they were less confident about becoming homeowners than they were five years ago. Some Americans are turning to travel as an alternative to a grounded, home-owning version of stability that feels out of reach. They are becoming digital nomads, traveling while earning money through remote work.  An estimated 18.5 million Americans identify as digital nomads, up from 7.3 million in 2019, according to workforce consulting firm MBO Partners. Millennials and Gen Z account for 75% of that group. Lisa Su told reporters in Taipei that AMD will substantially increase supply in 2027 and could use more, called the Trump administration's Super Intelligence Force an important step, and repeated a pledge to put more than $10B into Taiwan Lisa Su, AMD CEO AMD’s Lisa Su said chip demand is running ahead of supply and will stay very high for years, and urged the AI industry to work together as an ecosystem on safety rather than naming any regulator. The European Commission has been able to inspect models, restrict market access and fine providers 3% of global turnover since 2 August. AMD’s chief executive says demand for its chips is running ahead of supply and will stay very high for years. She also says the AI industry should work together on safety. The European Commission has been able to inspect models and fine their makers since August. Lisa Su told reporters in Taipei that AMD increased its own supply and capacity this year and demand is higher still, and that it will substantially increase supply in 2027, as Bloomberg reported. She was visiting supply chain partners including TSMC. She called AI “incredibly good for the world” and said she does not believe it will harm people, as others in the industry have suggested it might. What she proposes instead of rules is cooperation. The most important part, she said, is that “we work together as an ecosystem“, and she called the Trump administration’s Super Intelligence Force an important step forward. Four officials were named to lead it at the weekend. The body has no statutory authority, no budget and no place in government. One of the four, the Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson, runs the inquiry into OpenAI and Anthropic. Europe did not wait for an ecosystem. Since 2 August the Commission has been able to demand evaluations before a model reaches the market, restrict access to it and fine 3% of turnover or EUR 15M, whichever is higher. Providers based outside the EU have to appoint a representative inside it. Spain’s prime minister put it less diplomatically. Pedro Sanchez said in September that self-regulation does not work, and that part of the goal behind the industry’s own safety warnings may be to attract investors. The money, meanwhile, is going east. Su repeated a pledge from May to put more than $10B into Taiwan, covering packaging capacity through ASE and SPIL and supply for the Helios rack platform. She said the island remains critical to AMD and to the semiconductor supply chain. No comparable European commitment has been announced. AMD passed a trillion dollars in market value last month, and is buying Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs for $8.2B, a deal that still needs regulatory clearance. Updated:                       10/06/26       Brand marketing has always been about controlling the narrative, so that the story your company tells about itself is the one the market hears. That job has gotten harder.   Answer engines construct descriptions of your brand from what’s been written about the brand across the web. That includes reviews, comparison pages, forum discussions, and third-party editorial coverage. The result is often a version of your brand that doesn’t match what you’d choose to say. Brand teams gaining an edge are actively managing how AI describes them. The first step in brand narrative management is to know what the AI is saying. That means understanding how your brand is described across different answer engines, which competitors are cited alongside you, and whether the language in AI answers reflects your current positioning. When brand teams don’t have visibility into AI-generated descriptions, they can’t respond to inaccuracies or gaps until a stakeholder notices them in the wild. That wait-and-see approach comes at a cost, because by the time you’re correcting the record, the description has already shaped buyer perception. HubSpot AEO‘s Brand Visibility Dashboard shows how your brand is appearing in answer engines, including your AI visibility score, share of voice against competitors, and the citations driving those appearances. You can see which sources are shaping AI descriptions of your brand and identify where the narrative diverges from your messaging.  Within one month, HubSpot’s mention rate went from 0% to 33.5% in France and 17.1% in Germany, according to HubSpot’s marketing team. Knowing how your brand is being described is the foundation. The next step is creating the content that shapes those descriptions. Answer engines cite authoritative, well-structured content. When your owned content, such as positioning pages, comparison guides, and category explainers, is optimized to earn citations, it becomes part of the source material that shapes AI-generated brand descriptions. Brand content that was written for human readers and search engines may not be structured to earn AI citations. The gap between your intended narrative and the AI-generated version stays open without a process for auditing and updating that content. HubSpot AEO surfaces Recommendations for specific content changes that are likely to improve your citations and brand visibility score. You can prioritize owned content updates based on which gaps are most directly affecting how your brand is described in AI answers.  Building the content only gets you halfway. You still have to track whether it’s actually shifting how your brand shows up. Brand marketing is often measured by proxies like awareness surveys, share of voice in earned media, and branded search volume. AI visibility score adds a new signal that occurs earlier in the buyer journey: how prominently your brand appears when buyers are actively forming their category understanding. Changes in AI-driven awareness are invisible in your reporting without a consistent framework for tracking brand visibility in AI results. That makes it difficult to connect brand investment to AI presence, or to demonstrate progress to leadership. LIV Golf was founded in 2021, with its first season taking place the following year LIV Golf has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season. The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, starting a court-supervised "restructuring process" that they hope to complete in early 2027. It is unclear how much of the $300m LIV requires to start next year's schedule and which players will start the season. The competition's participants are owed at least $45m (Â£33m) and have the option to leave. However the agreement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until 25 October. BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf. League insiders see the committed investment as a "significant" step forward in the court-supervised restructuring process. "Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf's emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season," said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement. Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0 The credit firm, which provides financing to middle-market companies, said the funding would support the next phase of LIV Golf, under which players would become equity owners of both the league and its teams. The financing remains subject to bankruptcy court approval and customary conditions. "This investment is an important step forward for LIV Golf," said LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil in a statement. "We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers." Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (Â£3.7bn) has been spent by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), with major winners including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money. However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early. Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims.  Two-time major winner Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (Â£5.5m). DeChambeau ($5.7m - Â£4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - Â£4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - Â£3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - Â£2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (Â£1.25m). The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (Â£33m). A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts. Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business. PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (Â£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process. The class representative Liz Coll says a commission of up to 30% was passed into the prices about 20 million British consumers paid on the Play Store since October 2015, and Google is contesting a claim it chose to settle when app developers brought it Google is defending a £1.2B claim at London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal brought for about 20 million British consumers who say Play Store commissions of up to 30% were passed into the prices they paid since October 2015. It settled an equivalent claim from UK app developers for £260M six weeks ago without admitting wrongdoing. Google is defending a £1.2B claim in London brought for about 20 million British consumers over Play Store commissions. Six weeks ago it agreed to pay £260M to settle a claim from the developers who paid those commissions. It is contesting this one. Liz Coll is the class representative, the class covers purchases from 1 October 2015 to 31 July 2026, and the trial at the Competition Appeal Tribunal is listed for seven weeks, as Bloomberg reported. The case is that a levy of up to 30% ended up in the prices consumers paid. Google says it is not dominant in the market for facilitating digital content transactions between developers and consumers, and has asked for the claim to be dismissed. It made a similar argument to the developers and settled anyway. We reported in August that Google would pay £260M to settle a claim brought by the competition academic Barry Rodger for UK businesses that sold apps between August 2018 and July 2026. Of that, £160M went to developers and £100M to costs, with no admission of wrongdoing. The consumer claim is nearly five times that, and reaches back almost three years further. Lawyers for the class told the tribunal that Google has “exploited its market strength to extract unfair prices” and generated extraordinary returns for almost two decades. Google says Android gives people more choice than any other mobile platform, and that Play offers “some of the lowest fees in the market“. The regulator has already settled part of this argument. The Competition and Markets Authority found that Apple and Google run an effective duopoly, gave both strategic market status this year, and proposed letting developers send users to cheaper checkouts. That changes the future rather than the past. Brussels took the money route instead, fining Google €890M in July, of which €430M was for stopping Play developers pointing users towards cheaper channels elsewhere. None of that reaches the people who paid. An EU consumer cannot bring Coll’s claim, because only non-profits may file representative actions there, and in Ireland a statute from 1634 still blocks the litigation funding they would need to do it. We’ve seen the GeekMagic SmallTV line of devices before — these cheap gadgets combine a microcontroller and a display in a little plastic case that can be used to show the time or weather. Powered by either an ESP8266 or an ESP32, the things could easily pass for a hobby build if it wasn’t for their professionally produced enclosures. In fact, we wouldn’t be surprised if GeekMagic lifted the idea from an existing DIY project. As you might expect we’ve seen several hacks for these devices already, which usually involves replacing the stock firmware. But this latest approach is unique in that you don’t need to mess with the stock software, nor do you need to break out the soldering iron. By leveraging a built-in photo viewer function of the SmallTV [Yongha Kim] shows how you can get the gadget to display pretty much whatever you want. The trick here is that the image is being generated by a machine on the network, say your desktop or server, and being pushed over to the SmallTV over HTTP. In this example the image is being generated in Python with the Pillow library, and [Yongha] has it showing Claude and Codex usage data, but you could really approach this however you wish. All you need to do is create a 240×240 image and shoot it over to the device, so you’re free to come up with whatever sort of visuals you’d like. It even supports GIF if you’d like to work animation into it. The content can of course be whatever information you’re interested in showing, and it can be generated by whatever programming language or tool you’re most comfortable with. It’s a fascinating proof of concept, and now that the method has been demonstrated we’re interested to see where the community can take it. If this all sounds a little too easy for your tastes, don’t worry. There’s a plenty deep rabbit hole you can dive into should you elect to replace the device’s firmware entirely. I’d pay $20 for something like this but with e-paper and a battery/cordless mode to show my “available/in a meeting/do not disturb/not here” status on my office door. Hey that could be pretty cool. I wonder why supermarket electronic label makers haven’t branched out into applications like this Ooooh.  I’ve got one of these and think it’s really cool.  But the info as presented on the screen is just… not… quite… the way I want it.  I’m gettin’ to work to design my own screens.  [evil laugh] Ha ha ha!  Fools, I’ll destroy them all! Tech > Services & Software > Applications I tried the new Knockoff extension to filter out all the cheaply made junk I don't want to buy. October 6, 2026, 5:53 pm ET Developer Josh Pigford built the Knockoff extension to address Amazon’s growing problem with generic, mass-produced brands flooding search results. Amazon is hosting its Prime Big Deal Days, which means there’s a lot of good stuff on sale right now. It’s one of the biggest online retail shopping events of the year, and you may have to swim through a bunch of generic brands and algorithmically generated names to find what you want. It turns out that there’s an extension that can help with that.  The extension, called Knockoff, makes shopping on Amazon more bearable by graying out or blocking fake brands, increasing visibility for products from actual brands. It’s available for Firefox, Chrome and all Chromium-based web browsers such as Microsoft Edge, Opera and Brave. It’s also available as a Safari extension. Developer Josh Pigford launched the tool in early July, and it’s since gone viral, with over 100,000 downloads. A few days before the launch, Pigford posted on X, “Built a little chrome extension that lets you dim (or hide!) all the crap, mass-produced, fake brands on Amazon.” The post garnered 22,000 likes. More from CNET Knockoff is now live!Filter out the knockoff crap brands on Amazon.Sorry to brands like WNPETHOME, EHEYCIGA, YXYL, LU&MN, JOYIN, TOMY, GODONLIF, YOOJEE, LINGTENG, LANEIGE, VISCOO, BIODANCE, COOFANDY, BALENNZ, TOSY and LUENX.https://t.co/9mLk0EAsfG https://t.co/K07lMkepOW It works pretty simply. Once the extension is installed, any products from fake brands, dropshippers or otherwise suspicious vendors are marked and grayed out, highlighting the more reputable brands you might actually know. There’s also an option to automatically hide fake brands so you don’t even see them.  In an interview with 404 Media in July, Pigford said that Knockoff is built on prior extensions that aim to do this, such as AmazonBrandFilter and Amazon Brand Detector. The extension, which runs locally, doesn’t require an account, doesn’t send data to any company servers and doesn’t cost anything. It’s also open-source, and you can find the source code on GitHub. The extension’s functions are pretty simple to understand. If it’s grayed out, it’s likely a fake brand, but the extension does need some fine-tuning. Anything sounds good on paper, but the proof is in the pudding. I took Knockoff for a test drive to see how well it filtered the mass-produced junk.  My trial wasn’t terribly complicated. I searched for a variety of products across several categories using Knockoff’s stock settings to see how well the extension would filter out the knockoff brands without any additional tuning.  The short answer is that it did quite well. While searching for vacuum cleaners, it left most of the listings intact since they were from known brands, including Shark, Bissell and Dyson. Only a few listings were grayed out, mostly because no brand name was listed in the product description.  Solar lights fared much worse. Knockoff blocked dozens of listings for lack of brand names and also blocked listings from Jkimk, Technet, Tonulax and other unrecognized brands (most of which are stylized in all capital letters), while keeping listings for established brands, such as Brightown, a real company based in Raleigh, North Carolina. Some product categories did better than others. Solar lights were awash with fake brands, but vacuums had only a few. Phone cases are where things start to get trickier. The extension blocked brands such as Supfine, Dumkery, Hiearcool and several others. However, it initially also blocked Torras, a well-known case brand with in-store stock at Best Buy, which holds thousands of global patents for many of its products. It doesn’t get much more real than Torras, but the company’s products were flagged because its name is stylized in all caps, which the extension checks. Torras was added as a trusted brand in subsequent updates, so anyone trying it now won’t see this error. Knockoff listed some lesser-known but still legitimate earbuds brands, such as Tozo and Linsoul, as real companies, while it properly flagged phony hand tool brands, including Wgge and Horusdy. Brands that aren’t recognized by the extension often appear highlighted, but on the product page, the extension flags them as suspected fakes or entirely unrecognized.  It helps that Knockoff has a system for reporting brands that are incorrectly labeled as legitimate (or wrongly marked as fake). If the extension flags a product as fake when it’s legit, you can click the badge and “report as a real brand.” Likewise, if the extension flags a product as legit when it’s really fake, you can click the badge and “report as junk” when you click on a badge over a brand that the extension recognizes. You may need to enable badges for good brands in the settings to do this.  Knockoff lets you report brands that are good or bad to help make the extension more accurate over time. All reports are handled manually.  Since Knockoff’s launch, Pigford has released multiple updates that address user responses, including a method to directly send feedback if you want to report a brand, along with bug fixes. Overall, Knockoff is a useful extension in a digital marketplace dominated by AI-generated assets and unverified third-party products.  When you’re shopping, the biggest benefit is avoiding low-quality off-brands. Even if you’re not actively shopping for anything, it’s fun (and terrifying) to see how many grayed-out product listings you can find in any given product category. We recommend turning on badges for known brands, but otherwise, the stock settings performed the best. At the same time, Knockoff shows you brands likely to be fake on Amazon, but it doesn’t tell you which products are actually good or bad. Fake brands often have more fake or bot-written reviews than legitimate brands.  Still, it all depends on what you’re shopping for. If all you need is a pack of zip ties for light cable management or to attach a tomato plant to a garden trellis, the ones sold by dropshippers will work just fine and save you a couple of bucks.  And while Knockoff certainly makes it easier to shop for quality items, the extension still needs some fine-tuning and human analysis. Updates to the extension seem to be doing exactly that, so if you’re just now discovering the tool, it’s likely the extension has improved over time. Knockoff certainly makes it easier, but it’s still good to know how to spot these yourself, so when your package arrives, you’re happier. An eagle-eyed shopper can spot a knock-off brand from a mile away if they know where and how to look at product listings.  The first step, according to Russell Holly, director of commerce content at CNET, is to look for the brand outside of Amazon.com. “If it seems like a string of random characters and that brand name isn’t selling elsewhere, there’s a good chance the seller is not the manufacturer,” said Holly.  Holly also says to pay closer attention to negative reviews, since brands often fake only positive reviews. Negative reviews can be a better indicator of quality problems that may help explain why a product is cheaper than others in the same category.  Similarly, you can also look for a brand’s product support. If the only way to report a problem is directly to Amazon, Holly says you’re most likely dealing with a dropshipper that doesn’t offer product support if something breaks.  Another way to spot a fake brand is to find the same product sold under multiple brands. An example is a Broserengy alarm clock, Bluetooth speaker, phone charger combo. It is nearly identical to this product from Fansbe, including the RGB lights at the bottom, the placement (and labeling) of the buttons and the auxiliary USB port around the back for charging an accessory. These are two subtly different versions of the same product.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is suing the operators behind Chumba Casino, Global Poker and Stake.us, alleging that their sweepstakes casino platforms violate state gambling law and seeking to shut them down. The cases put more than the operators’ access to Florida at stake: the state is also seeking civil penalties and recovery of Floridians’ losses. As South Florida Reporter describes it, the lawsuits mark a shift from a proposed statewide ban to litigation targeting two major companies. One suit targets VGW, which operates Chumba Casino and Global Poker, along with payment processors. The other targets Stake and related parties. Florida is seeking to bar the sites from operating in the state and recover money lost by Florida players. The state is also seeking penalties of up to $10,000 for each willful violation, rising to $15,000 per violation when play involves a minor, senior or disabled customer. Those are requested penalties, not fines already imposed: the cases remain at an early stage, and no court has ordered the sites shut down or awarded player restitution. The payment companies named in the VGW case make the dispute relevant beyond the brands visible to players. A separate Florida gambling enforcement effort involving payment processors shows why the companies enabling transactions can become part of the state’s scrutiny, although the claims and defendants in these cases are distinct. Earlier in 2026, Florida lawmakers pursued Senate Bill 1404 and House Bill 1467, which would have banned sweepstakes casinos. Neither bill passed. Uthmeier’s lawsuits instead seek to stop two operators through court action and pursue recovery under the state’s gambling laws. Florida’s approach follows other legal pressure on the sector. New York secured an $8 million settlement with VGW after resolving allegations that the company unlawfully operated online gambling platforms through its sweepstakes brands. The agreement is a concrete example of the financial and operating consequences a state action can produce, though Florida’s cases are separate and their outcome is unresolved. South Florida Reporter also cites a Washington state jury award requiring High 5 Casino to pay $24.9 million in damages to social casino players. That case adds to the legal risks facing the category, but it does not determine whether Florida will prevail against VGW or Stake. Sweepstakes casinos commonly use two types of virtual currency: Gold Coins for free play and Sweeps Coins that can be used in games connected to prizes. Operators describe the model as distinct from conventional gambling, while states increasingly argue that redeemable play brings these platforms within gambling laws. The stakes extend to a large and still-growing market. South Florida Reporter puts the U.S. social sweepstakes casino market at $10.2 billion in 2026, forecasting $14.3 billion by 2030, and says more than 400 standalone sites are operating. Those figures underline the scale of the industry exposed to state enforcement, not a measure of Florida’s own market. The enforcement focus may also extend to advertising. In separate reporting published Sept. 29, Casino.com said Uthmeier sent letters to Google, Meta, Reddit, Snap and TikTok asking them to prevent promotions for sweepstakes casinos from reaching Floridians. The reported Oct. 23 deadline was for the platforms to respond; the letters are not court judgments against those companies. For now, Stake, Chumba Casino, Global Poker and LuckyLand Casino remain accessible to players in Florida, according to South Florida Reporter. The lawsuits seek a different operating position, but access will change only if the state secures court relief or the companies otherwise alter their service. The cases are expected to continue into 2027, according to the report. Whether Florida can obtain injunctions, penalties and repayment of player losses remains for the courts to decide. Reading a book is very different from studying a textbook. With the former, you flip through pages at whatever pace you read. With the latter, you leave the textbook open to a particular page while you take notes, transcribe, or re-read text in order for it to sink in. For this latter situation, Japanese stationery company Kokuyo detected a problem. In 2022, the company sought feedback from junior high and high school students on what their study-time paint points were. The students noted that holding a textbook open with one hand while trying to write with the other was a hassle. Some used spring-loaded clips made for the purpose, but these made turning the pages a hassle.  Others compensated by using a bunchin, a traditional calligraphy scroll weight that's essentially a piece of bar stock, square in cross section. But the flat bunchin didn't hold the books open well, as the flat shape only contacted the curved surface of the open pages in two places.  Kokuyo then devised this object, made out of brass. The designers arrived at the precise curvature after measuring several dozen representative books.   Hedging their bets, the company only produced a small batch of 300 units. They sold out immediately. Concept proven, Kokuyo then put the objects—called "book-hugging paperweights"—into production in early 2024. The brass units hit the market first, followed by lower-cost steel versions in black and grey. The same year they won a stationery award.      Demand emerged for an even larger model, for thicker art books and coffee table books, and that model hit the market last month.   It's fair to say Kokuyo wouldn't have thought of this product without that crucial feedback-seeking initiative. October 6, 2026 10:00am by 			        Barry Ritholtz       The biggest question confronting investors today isn’t about AI, market concentration, or technology. Instead, it’s about the bond market. Like nearly everything in investing, it’s rarely about any one thing; instead, a mix of factors drives interest rates. Some matter more than others, but together, they can create a perfect storm of elements that have driven yields appreciably higher. Let’s run through a dozen of these to see what’s driving bond prices lower, the investment opportunity this creates, and the risks that keep investors up at night (but perhaps shouldn’t). My list, from most to least significant: What Is Driving Rates Higher and Bonds Lower 1. Oil and the Iran war premium. Brent is over $100; the Iran conflict remains unresolved –and worse, is unlikely to end until 2027 (if we are lucky). Energy is +16% y/y. THIS IS THE BIGGEST FACTOR impacting CPI inflation. Oil drives transportation costs for goods (diesel for ships, trucks, and rail) and home heating/cooling, travel, and commuting. Goods inflation affects Shelter prices. Oil also impacts fertilizer costs, raising food prices. Note: Core CPI is nonsense – it’s “inflation ex-inflation” — ignore it, and watch Energy if you want to know where inflation is going. 2. Reaccelerating growth, driven by CapEx in the Artificial Intelligence sector, including the data center buildout. September PMIs showed output growing at the fastest pace in over five years. Although we won’t see the first Q3 GDP numbers until October 29th, the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow is at 3.7%. Remember, a hot economy does not need cheap money; the market is repricing expectations accordingly. 3. Long-term rate normalization. I discussed this extensively last week (“The Aberrational Century”). It is an uncomfortable possibility that perhaps 2001–2021 was an anomaly, and what we are seeing is a reminder of what normal yields look like historically. From 1960 to 2007, the 10-year average was 6–7% nominal, tracking GDP growth; today, nominal GDP is running 5–6% (with CPI inflation a major factor). At 5%, the 10-year Treasury is not an outlier. Real 10-year yields near 2% are back to their pre-GFC range. A zero-rate decade(s) was a product of temporary conditions: throw in a Fed balance sheet at 35% of GDP – and that is before we discuss the deficit…  4. COVID fiscal stimulus and the CARES Acts. The numbers are shocking: CARES Act 1 ($2.2 trillion, March 2020), CARES Act 2 December 2020 package (~$900 billion), both under Trump; the American Rescue Plan aka CARES Act 3, under Biden ($1.9 trillion, March 2021). All three were $5 trillion in fiscal stimulus in one year. That was the largest fiscal stimulus as a percentage of GDP since World War Two. That regime change was from monetary to fiscal stimulus. It permanently reset the deficit baseline: spending never returned to pre-2020 levels, while interest costs compounded; it added trillions to the debt that now has to be rolled at 5% instead of 1%; and it destroyed the market’s assumption that inflation was structurally dead. 5.  Trade and tariff policy. Tariffs feed directly into goods inflation (and into the Fed’s reaction function). Alienating foreign creditors while needing them to buy our Treasuries is an avoiable, self-inflicted wound. Speaking of which: 6. Hawkish Fed’s hiking cycle. Warsh delivered the first hike since 2023 in September (Fed funds 3.75–4.00%); that level comes from a secondary source and should be checked against the Fed statement), said summer inflation readings “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved,” and the dot plot has 16 of 19 members projecting more. Futures price 70%+ odds of another hike in October and better than even odds for December. The front end is repricing the entire path. 7.  Japan leading global yields higher. JGB 10-year at ~3.08%, up 143 bp y/y, with the BOJ at 1.25% and likely hiking again in October. Japan’s 30-year is now above 4%. Higher domestic yields reduce the incentive for Japanese institutions, historically the largest foreign holders, to buy U.S. Treasuries. Foreigners hold ~30% of US Treasury stock — slipping marginal demand matters. 8. Corporate supply competing with Treasury. Data-center/AI capex is being financed in the bond market, with estimates of $250B this year and up to $400B next. Yields are attractive (at the expense of credit quality and too many unknowns to ignore). But those bonds are competing head-on with the Treasury for the same investor dollars, and IG spreads have widened ~35 bp since August as refinancing costs rise. 9. Sticky inflation. August CPI ran +0.4% m/m, 3.4% y/y headline, with core at +0.3% m/m. Gasoline alone was a third of the monthly gain; airfares +23% y/y. The PMIs showed input costs rising at the steepest rate in 4 years, with pricing power improving — and that points to higher prices in the pipeline. 10. Weak natural demand for long-dated paper (and Bessent knows it). 10-year auction in August was highest-yielding since 2007; the 2-year cleared at 4.79%. Treasury doubled its long-end buybacks to $4B per operation explicitly to “provide liquidity support.” Beat the House: Buying back $6B when you owe $40T is LOL foolish. 11. Deficits and the term premium. Deficits running ~6% of GDP at full employment, with interest costs consuming roughly 30% of federal revenue. Investors are demanding more compensation to hold duration against fiscal uncertainty. 12. The Fed is reducing duration. Aggregate QT ended December 1, 2025, after taking the balance sheet down $2.2 trillion from its $8.5–9 trillion peak, and since then the Fed has actually re-expanded Treasury holdings by ~$364 billion through short-dated “reserve management purchases.” The Fed balance sheet is NOT shrinking in total; what is shrinking is the Fed’s long-duration holdings: MBS continue to run off (down ~$794 billion from the 2022 peak to $1.91 trillion). Expect more Fed balance sheet runoff in 2027. ~~~ Note: I suspect many investors are still anchored in lower 21st-century rates and the painful 2022 selloff, and are not taking full advantage of this…        Previously: The Aberrational Century (September 29, 2026) What’s Upsetting the Bond Market? In April, another agency launched a “Machine Relations” practice. It announced the service on a national newswire, published its pricing and called Machine Relations “the emerging discipline of AI search visibility.” It didn’t mention where the name came from. I coined the term in 2024. Plenty of founders would have spent that week fighting over credit or losing their minds. I saw it as the moment I had been building toward. A category doesn’t exist because the person who named it says so. It exists when someone else starts using the word as if it had always been there. Today, other firms publish their own guides to the discipline, and some are doing their best to claim it. But ask AI search engines who coined it, and they still point back to me nearly every time. That’s because the sources they lean on all tell the same story: the official definition, the wire coverage, the public profiles and the research built on top of them. I’m not telling you this to take a victory lap. I’m telling you because it points to the one part of AI visibility almost nobody is competing for, and most aren’t even aware of. Most companies are fighting to show up in AI search. They should be. Getting recommended when a buyer asks an AI engine for the best option in their category is worth real money. But a spot on that list is rented, and the rent resets daily. You read that right. Daily. Paralax, an AI search research publication I oversee, tracked the same questions across five engines every day for 89 days. On an average day in September, Gemini dropped 42.8% of the websites it had cited the day before. ChatGPT dropped 35.9%. That means you could win a spot on Monday and lose it by Tuesday. But here’s the kicker. Not every question is treated the same. The Machine Relations Index, which my team also runs, tracks what six major AI engines cite. Within a single category, asking whether something is worth it instead of asking for the best tools made those engines more than four times as likely to cite Wikipedia—the internet’s default explainer. Same subject, same engines, same window. Ask a machine for the best vendor, and it hands you names. Ask it whether something is worth it or how to choose, and it reaches for whoever explains the category most clearly and, more importantly, most consistently. That’s the part almost nobody understands: the company whose explanation it borrows has already framed the decision before the shortlist even forms. None of this is new. The economics of categories have always rewarded that position. A widely cited analysis by category-design firm Play Bigger found that among venture-backed tech companies, category leaders captured 76% of their category’s market value. AI doesn’t change that math. It compounds it, because the one explaining your category to your buyers is now a machine. This is where Machine Relations gets strategic. I define it as the discipline of earning AI citations and recommendations for a brand by making that brand legible, retrievable and credible inside AI-driven discovery. Most people hear that and think about rankings. The bigger prize is this: a buyer asks ChatGPT how to choose in your category and gets your criteria, in your words, before a single vendor is named. The result? Your competitors get judged by your yardstick. You may be thinking you can’t invent a new word for what you sell. You don’t need to. Every market already has contested ground: what the problem is called, what separates a good solution from a risky one and how the outcome should be measured. So whether you’re a founder, a marketer or the person running SEO and AI visibility, here’s how I’d go after it. It’s the same playbook I ran. Most markets don’t need a new category. They need someone to state plainly what a buyer should look for. A cybersecurity vendor doesn’t need to coin anything. It needs to be the source that tells the machine which three questions a buyer should ask before trusting anyone with their data. Start with three sentences: the problem, the standard and the measure. If your customers keep describing the same frustration in different words, the first sentence is already waiting for you. I only coined a name because the shift handed me one. Years of living and breathing earned media at my company, AuthorityTech, showed me that the first reader of a placement was no longer a person. It was a machine absorbing the placement to answer humans. Public relations was quite literally becoming Machine Relations in real time. Machines reward consistency. If your website defines the idea one way, your executives describe it another and your press materials use a third phrasing, you’ve handed the machine three weak signals instead of one that compounds.  Write the definition once, date it, give it a permanent home and use the same words everywhere: your site, your bylines, your interviews, your public profiles. It’s boring, but it works. Simple scales. This column is a live example. The definition I gave earlier matches my dated public record and the official glossary word for word. That’s the point. Your own site can define a term. It can’t make the market adopt it. A definition becomes the category’s when it shows up in coverage, interviews and analysis written by people with no reason to promote you. That’s the job earned media has always done for reputation, and now it does the same job for the machines. Pitch the shift, not your company. Editors will cover a change their readers are living through long before they’ll cover your product. Every credible outlet that uses your language the way you defined it is one more source telling the machine whose idea it is. When a competitor adopts your language, the instinct is to fight. Don’t. It is spending its own budget to distribute your category. That April newswire release carried Machine Relations to an audience I never paid to reach. If you’ve done the work, your energy already went into the record. That’s why it matters so much to date your definition, make its origin easy to verify and keep every public profile saying the same thing. When the record is that consistent, any machine asked about the category finds the origin fast. Then every new adopter makes the category bigger, and the record keeps pointing back to you. When it happened to me, I didn’t post a rebuttal. I simply reinforced the record by doing more of what I had already done right. Every month, ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google’s AI Mode three questions about your category: what it is, how a buyer should evaluate it and who defined it. Don’t stop at whether you’re mentioned. Check whose language the answer uses and whose sources it cites. How often those sources are yours is what I track as share of citation. If the machine explains your market with a competitor’s framework, you’re competing inside its frame, no matter how many “best of” lists you show up in. Rankings get reshuffled every time someone presses enter. Definitions get inherited. And once yours is, every ranking you win works harder. The companies that own their markets in AI search won’t be the ones that show up in the most lists. They’ll be the ones whose frame the machine reaches for when a buyer asks what matters. Japanese watches have earned a solid reputation thanks to their combination of technology, durability and designs that have attracted generations of users. Casio, Citizen and Seiko became famous for classic analog designs but also experimented with digital devices. Today, these manufacturers continue to expand smartwatch features and make cool watches. Japanese manufacturers also offer interesting options, though Chinese smartwatches have also established themselves in the market, often as an alternative to the Apple Watch. Casio, for example, marries the durability of its watches with smart features. Other companies also make hybrids, often keeping the look of traditional watches. Beyond the famous brands, companies like Sharp and Omron have also made Japanese devices with smart features, especially for anyone interested in health monitoring. That's why we've selected some of the coolest Japanese smartwatches you'll want to wear. Whether it's for their appearance, the features they come with, or the blend of modern technology and these brands' traditional designs, they have something for everyone. Casio fans will find plenty to love about the G-SHOCK GM-H5600-1, since the smartwatch keeps the iconic square shape that made the line famous. However, it also adds a stainless steel bezel for a more modern look. It still offers the durability that G-SHOCK watches are known for, making it a solid choice for anyone who wants a familiar design with a more contemporary feel. The biggest difference from regular G-SHOCK watches is the addition of sensors to track heart rate, steps and performance during exercise. It also offers sleep analysis, call and message notifications and Bluetooth connectivity with your phone. Another advantage of this Casio model is its good battery life. The manufacturer says it can last up to a month in watch mode with heart rate monitoring turned off. If you use it continuously during physical activity, battery life drops to about 35 hours, but it still supports solar charging. Sharp doesn't have the same long history in the Japanese watch market as Casio or Citizen, but the manufacturer entered this segment anyway. So in 2026, it introduced its first smartwatch, the Karada Mate Watch MH-W01, which has a different take on the common designs available in the country. Its main highlight is its capacity to estimate how many calories the user consumes during the day without them having to manually log each meal. It does this through sensors that detect changes in bodily fluids and glucose metabolism, allowing users to monitor these changes. In addition, the Karada Mate Watch monitors the body's hydration balance and alerts the wearer if it detects signs of dehydration. It also offers heart rate monitoring, integrated GPS, physical activity tracking and sleep monitoring. It also comes in a more minimalist design with a 1.32-inch OLED display and a steel case in two colors, and the battery autonomy is two and a half days. Unlike the GM-H5600-1, which combines a more classic watch design with some smart features, this Casio model takes a much sportier approach. Casio designed it for people who exercise frequently and need a durable smartwatch with more features than basic monitoring. It delivers this with a rugged appearance and a build that can withstand these activities. The GBD-H2000-1A also features built-in GPS and six sensors that let users measure heart rate, altitude, atmospheric pressure and temperature. It also logs running, cycling and swimming data and analyzes performance and physical recovery after sleep with Polar technology. For athletes, this Casio model is a good option. Its battery life also deserves attention. The battery can last up to two months in watch mode with heart rate monitoring turned off. During extended activities, GPS use can reduce battery life, but the watch includes solar charging to keep its basic functions running. Although this Omron model doesn't offer the same level of connectivity we expect from modern smartwatches, the company focused on building a watch for health monitoring. This model even includes a small inflatable cuff built into the strap, letting you measure blood pressure directly from your wrist. The watch also tracks step count, physical activity, and sleep duration, and lets you view all this information on your phone. Unlike other health-monitoring features we see in smartwatches, this Omron model requires you to take your blood pressure manually. So, during the measurement, you need to be in the correct posture for the best results. Omron has discontinued this model in the American market, but the Japanese store still sells it. But the manufacturer says this product is only available in Japan, and it is for wrists with a circumference between 16 and 19 centimeters. For anyone looking for a watch that is a little different from the traditional analog design, the Citizen CZ Smart PQ2 delivers. Instead of preserving that more classic look, it uses a 1.28-inch AMOLED display and supports Wear OS, giving users an experience closer to what they expect from a traditional smartwatch. The 44mm case is also made of stainless steel, and it also offers GPS, NFC, and Wi-Fi for connectivity. Among its main features is YouQ, a platform created by Citizen with artificial intelligence models developed in IBM Watson Studio and research from the NASA Ames Research Center. The system analyzes sleep, activities, and other moments throughout the day to suggest habits to the user. In addition, the watch can monitor heart rate, and Wear OS compatibility lets you install other features commonly found in smartwatches. YouQ, however, will end its services in December 2026. So, features connected to the platform may stop working starting next year. Even so, it remains a good-looking watch, and for anyone who wants to try the best Wear OS features, it can be an interesting model. To select these Japanese smartwatches for this list, we considered models from different manufacturers, aiming to present options that combine watch designs with smart features. Beyond established brands like Casio, we also looked at other companies that took different approaches, especially for anyone looking for health monitoring features. For these watches' smart features, we considered connectivity, durability, sensors, and functions that distinguish these models from traditional watches. Japanese brands also generally haven't tried to compete directly in the smartwatch and ecosystem market the way companies like Samsung and Apple have. Instead, many have preferred to add smart functions to their existing watches while maintaining more traditional designs, with features such as activity and health monitoring. We also looked at devices with unique features, and some of the most original options we found were designed specifically for the Japanese market. As a result, not every model on this list is sold worldwide, and some are officially available only in Japan.

Finn Gomez/Getty Images                                       hide caption  President Trump was elected in 2024, in large measure, with a mandate to bring down prices. But that hasn't happened. Instead, Trump is facing record-low approval ratings, and voters are blaming him for costs that have continued to rise since he took office this second time around. As a result, Republicans are likely to pay the price at the ballot box next month. One month out from Election Day, the electoral landscape has shifted even more so in Democrats' direction. They are favored to win the House, albeit with a fairly narrow majority. The Cook Political Report forecasts a five-to-15-seat net gain for Democrats at this point. That would give them in the range of 220 to 230 seats come January. (218 is needed for a majority.) The Senate has shifted more dramatically over the last several months. Six seats have moved more in Democrats' direction since June in comparing Cook's ratings from then to now. When the cycle first started, the Senate was a long shot for Democrats. Now, it's within reach. And that's largely because of the national mood, which is usually the case in midterms. Trump has just a 37% approval rating, according to an average of the polls. That's tied for the lowest pre-midterm approval in the last half century. The only other president to be that low in that time was George W. Bush in 2006. Back then, Iraq was spiraling into civil war, and Republicans lost both the House and Senate. Trump is also facing a historic intensity of opposition; 53% in the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll said they strongly disapprove of the job the president is doing, the highest ever recorded in the survey. That's not a great sign for Republicans with Trump insisting that the midterm elections be about him. As it is, history is unkind to the president's party in midterm elections. They usually lose about two dozen seats in the House and four in the Senate. It's even worse for the party in power when the president's approval rating is below 50%, as Trump's is now. Loading... There are multiple reasons Democratic gains might be limited, including mid-decade redistricting helping to insulate Republicans, fewer competitive-to-potentially competitive House seats, with most in districts Trump won in 2024, Republicans' campaign spending edge and the unpopularity of the Democratic Party. That said, the headwinds the GOP is facing are very real. Economic issues continue to rate as the top problem and most important issue facing the country. Most presidents get more blame and credit than they deserve for the economy, but the war with Iran and Trump's tariffs were choices that have directly led to increased costs on many goods and energy. The economy is increasingly bifurcated with the wealthy doing well and regular people struggling. Wealthy Americans are seeing increases in their wealth and stock portfolios, which are dominated by AI companies. It's a different story for many others. Inflation is outpacing wages, meaning people's paychecks aren't taking them as far. There isn't a lot of turnover in the labor market, so if someone doesn't have a job or is looking to change, it's not an easy thing to do. Plus, many are turning against AI. In many places, it's driving up utility costs and, along with the rising national debt, is making borrowing more difficult. All of that is coming at a time when gas prices have skyrocketed because of the Iran war, and interest rates are creeping higher. In trying to tame inflation, the Federal Reserve hiked rates this fall. That makes it more expensive to borrow money and harder to pay for things like houses and cars. The blame for that sort of thing often gets pointed directly at the White House and the party in power, and right now, that's Trump and Republicans. An AP/NORC poll released last week, for example, found that 65% said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump's policies than factors outside of his control. Just 26% said they approved of the job he's doing on the economy. An NBC News poll from September found that for only the second time in the Trump era, respondents said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans on the economy. (Though it was within the margin of error, the movement in the survey was clear.) The only other time Democrats led on that question was in 2018 – the last midterm year when Trump was president. Democrats won 42 seats and control of the House then. Add the widely negative views of the economy to the administration's immigration enforcement tactics, discretionary domestic cuts, the slashing of regulations and the government workforce, and it's all firing up Democrats. An opposition party enthusiastic to vote is a major warning sign for the president's party, especially in a midterm year. In 18 of the 20 midterms since World War II, the president's party has lost House seats. On average, it's 26 seats, and it's nine more than that when a president's approval rating is below 50%. The last three midterm elections have seen fewer lost House seats, despite unpopular presidents, in large measure because the universe of competitive districts is smaller. The president, himself, though, has acknowledged multiple times the political headwinds his party faces in midterms. "Whether you have a great president or not, Republican or Democrat, they don't do well in midterms," Trump said Friday at a campaign rally in Alabama. "I don't know why. Nobody's explained it." There are reasons, however. First, turnout in midterms is historically about 30% lower than in presidential years. So, the voters most fired up to vote show up in outsized numbers. Anger is a great motivator, and often the voters more aligned with the opposition party most want to register their frustration. And, as noted earlier, the intensity of opposition to Trump is at historic levels. A CBS poll out Sunday found Democrats with the enthusiasm edge – 84% of Democrats and 82% of independents surveyed said they are "definitely" going to vote compared to 77% of Republicans. What's more, a key indicator of which party does well in midterms is pointing in the Democrats' direction. Surveys, including the NPR/PBS News/Marist poll, ask a version of: "If November's election for Congress were held today, which party's candidate are you more likely to vote for in your district?" In an average of the 2026 polls, Democrats have a nine-point advantage on this question, known as the congressional ballot test. Democrats tend to need a larger lead on the question historically than Republicans, given how districts have been drawn. But +9 is in the range of what Democrats need. To put a finer point on it: in each of the past seven midterm elections, the party with the advantage on the congressional ballot has made gains. Loading... With independents and Latinos, two swing groups, souring on Trump during this second term, that's an added problem for Republicans in competitive districts. Their jobs are made even tougher when Trump says things like "pretend" he's on the ballot and makes the election a "referendum" on him. The White House's theory of the case is that Trump has had success turning conservatives out when he's on the ballot, and Republican candidates need them to show up in big numbers. But whether that's enough is going to be tested. In swing districts and some key Senate races, candidates also usually need voters in the middle to win. The bottom line is with less than a month to go until all the votes are in, the political compass is pointed in Democrats' direction. For multiple reasons, Democrats' gains might not be as big as similar numbers might indicate in past elections, but there is no doubt that, right now, they have the wind at their backs.
