When you start looking for a new camera, whether you want film or digital, affordable or high-end, Canon is going to be a recommended brand. After all, it has had the number one share of the global interchangeable-lens digital camera market for over 20 years. While it may not be the first brand to make cameras for consumers, Canon does have a history in the United States dating back to 1955. The brand is now over 70 years old, yet its name is still widely recommended. With so many other options, it's reasonable to wonder why it's still the most popular camera brand. Ultimately, Canon's variety of cameras at different price points is a large part of it, and the brand's reputation for reliability fills out the rest of the puzzle. Its affordable, beginner-friendly cameras that anyone can buy and successfully use eventually translate to people buying more expensive, more technical cameras for even better results. From the best Canon digital cameras for everyday use to professional photographer quality, the wide range of cameras gives the brand a large market. Plus, once people do get a Canon camera, they typically experience the photo quality and reliability that keeps consumers loyal to the brand. Add the reputation for reliability and the long brand history together, and you're left with a strong used camera market as well, adding another affordable entry point to the brand. Finally, Canon has made significant innovations in the field, pioneering features like built-in CPUs and autofocus, keeping the brand associated with improvement rather than stagnation. Canon's major United States introduction was in the 1950s, but it originated in Japan. The first Canon camera was created in the 1930s, and even then, the priority was a combination of impressive technology and accessibility. Canon's relatively early expansion to the U.S. gave it a global market. Early Canon cameras were noted for their reliability as well. Consumers saw a company that was innovative, consistent in quality, easy to find, and often fairly affordable. It has a good market for beginners, which everyone is at some point, and the cameras are high-quality enough to get people to stay loyal to the brand and recommend it to others. When beginners do want to upgrade to a nicer camera, they can stay with the brand they trust. They might not even have to switch all of their equipment, as many Canon lenses are compatible with multiple Canon cameras, letting you save thousands of dollars by upgrading one piece at a time. Canon is also special for continuing to make technological strides. Just look at one of Canon's seriously impressive ultra-wide hybrid lenses. In the 2010s, Canon introduced the EOS M and EOS R series. These cameras are more compact and lightweight than traditional DSLRs, making them more portable and easier to use. Now, Canon cameras can shoot 8K video and have in-body image stabilization, animal eye detection autofocus, focus bracketing, weather seals, and built-in WiFi, depending on the model. Canon's autofocus advancements and lens compatibility within the brand, in particular, keep many photographers loyal. You can really see Canon shine when you look at other popular camera brands, like Nikon and Sony, and their comparable models. Canon is so significantly more widely used, though, that it is worth examining some differences. The Sony brand started not too long after Canon, but Sony didn't enter the camera world until the 1980s. These decades gave Canon and Nikon far more time to gain notoriety. However, while Canon made its cameras accessible to the masses, Nikon's history shows more tailoring to professional uses. By the time Nikon and Sony became focused on selling cameras to both beginners and professionals alike, Canon already had the market. In fact, Canon's global sales percentage has continued to increase over Nikon and Sony for the past few years. Photographers may have different opinions when it comes to which camera is actually best, but there is no denying that Canon dominates the popularity contest (45.7% market share) so much that it must be doing something right. From its early rise to its targeting of both amateur and professional photographers to its reliability, Canon's popularity is indisputable.

You drive by Costco and see the parking lot teeming with cars. The left-hand turn lane to enter is backed up 50 yards. The gas station is packed with people planning to head inside after they fill up. It's the busiest intersection in town. But then you pull up a stock chart. Shares are down 16% since a peak in May. You're confused. Didn't you just read that earnings were strong this past quarter? The stock underperformance isn't just a Costco issue. Walmart — another retailer that shoppers have historically traded down to when trying to spend less — has an eerily similar recent stock chart despite continuing to add customers. What gives? Aren't these supposed to be all-weather winners of a consumer pullback? In an ironic way, the reputation of Costco and Walmart as defensive plays may have worked against them. As worries about the consumer grew, investors built a premium into their stocks. That, in turn, gave them less room for error, and made them more sensitive to further signs of weaker spending. The chart below shows just how badly both stocks have underperformed the market — and the broader consumer staples sector — since they closed at record highs on May 19. The following day was when President Trump said Iran-war negotiations were in the "final stages," sending oil sharply lower and taking some of the shine off the defensive trade in Costco and Walmart. Then, on May 21, Walmart forecast second-quarter profit below analyst expectations, triggering a sector-wide sell-off. Neither stock has been able to claw those losses back. Costco gave investors plenty to like in its quarterly report last month. Both overall and comparable sales were up from a year earlier, and the company said it plans to open 33 additional warehouses over the next fiscal year. But the resulting 3% post-earnings gain was a drop in the bucket compared to how much ground the stock has to make up. But US comparable-sales growth also slowed to its weakest pace in six years. And that, of course, is what investors focused on. The reason is familiar: Even though the company is gaining market share and adding customers, they still aren't growing fast enough for investors. The ultimate tension with Costco and Walmart is that the more their stocks get priced up as defensive plays, the more investors care about their growth — and the higher the stakes get when they report. Ultimately, the story of Costco and Walmart in the stock market isn't a tale of empty parking lots and aisles. It's quite the opposite. The more people flock there for deals, the higher the bar gets. Torrendell says her 20-year career, which included stints at Apple and Meta, taught her to recognize signals about the next big thing before they became obvious to everyone else. Copied to clipboard When Sarina Virk Torrendell decided to leave Amazon in September 2025, she knew that the safer choice was to stay put.  Torrendell had spent two decades building a consumer technology career. Her compensation at Amazon was in the high six figures, enough to support a family in New York City. At the time, Torrendell had two children and had just learned that she was pregnant with her third child.  Then she quit to start YouPop, an AI startup for content creators and founders that combines all of their different ventures onto one platform. YouPop arose out of Torrendell’s conversations with content creators. She noticed a pattern. People were no longer simply posting videos or building an audience online. They were instead creating multi-platform businesses by launching courses, writing books, hosting podcasts, selling products, taking speaking engagements and landing brand deals.  Torrendell believed that the problem was that the tools supporting those businesses were fragmented. Creators had analytics in one place, sponsorship work in another, storefronts somewhere else. That insight became YouPop, the startup Torrendell describes as an “intelligence layer” for modern content creators. The company aims to help creators make more informed decisions about what to build, sell and prioritize to make more money. “There is just a massive opportunity ahead of us,” Torrendell tells Entrepreneur in a new interview. “We’re really setting out to build the next unicorn in this space.” She notes that the venture “was certainly risky.” But she believed the time was right to start YouPop and that the timing mattered more than the comfort of a corporate job.  Torrendell faced well-meaning advice from her family and friends about her decision to leave Amazon. They pointed out that a high-paying job with paid maternity leave and stability had its appeal — especially for a mother who was five months pregnant in an expensive city.  Even Torrendell’s husband, whom she calls her biggest supporter, initially questioned if the timing made sense.  “He was like, ‘I don’t think this is the moment to do this. Why don’t you wait until you have the baby?’” she says. But Torrendell believed waiting could mean missing the market entirely. Torrendell did not approach the decision to leave Amazon impulsively. She gave herself 90 days to raise the money needed to begin building YouPop. If she could not do that, she had a backup plan: return to the job market. “I had all the scenarios mapped out,” Torrendell says. “And I also just had high conviction in myself.” That confidence was grounded in both her experience and her network.  Torrendell’s career has put her at the center of shifts in how people buy and sell. She joined Apple in 2018, leading global App Store partner marketing before moving to Apple Pay to help expand contactless payments.  At Meta, she helped small businesses move online as the pandemic upended physical retail. She then spent about three years at Amazon working on creator partnerships and live shopping. Those roles taught her to spot changes in consumer behavior before they became mainstream, she says. With YouPop, she is betting on the rise of creators who turn professional knowledge and audiences into multiple income streams. Torrendell deliberately limited the fundraising process, targeting investors who understood consumer technology and the creator economy. Rather than taking every possible meeting, she estimates that she spoke with about 20 investors. From those meetings, Torrendell raised about $1 million, enough to finance a technically ambitious first build. After raising the funds, Torrendell moved fast. YouPop built its beta product in roughly five and a half months. To build the product, Torrendell hired employees, including a chief of staff and principal AI engineer. She created it with a trusted team of engineers and a product designer.  Torrendell describes YouPop as an “agentic operating system” for creators. The AI-powered platform combines a creator’s online presence in one dashboard, then provides insights to help them grow their businesses and identify new income streams. Torrendell gave the example of a content creator who is thinking about writing a book. If they want to decide what kind of book to write, they can go on YouPop and ask the engine. YouPop then goes into the creator’s proprietary data set from their various platforms and will say something like, “Your audience is really interested in your fundraising journey,” and mention three topics that the book could cover.  The tool doesn’t stop there. After identifying topics, it might offer to draft or outline a book proposal. “We’re really creating data that’s an insight layer that understands you specifically and then helps you understand what new revenue opportunities you can get as a content creator,” Torrendell says.  The venture is still in an early stage. YouPop launched its beta in August and has not yet begun reporting revenue. YouPop plans to charge creators a fee to use the platform. Its initial growth has been heavily relationship-driven. Torrendell began with her own network of creators, then benefited from public support from investors, advisors and creators already using the platform.  Torrendell says the result is a waitlist approaching 1,000 people. The company’s biggest challenge is the technical complexity of what it is building. It isn’t easy to create a platform that can pull the most important parts of a creator’s online presence and translate them into reliable recommendations and tools.  But Torrendell says the scale of the opportunity has surprised her, too. She knew creators were increasingly building businesses beyond social media. What has become even more apparent is how many professionals with traditional jobs are beginning to build public expertise online and have a social media presence.  For founders, Torrendell’s advice comes back to a balance of conviction and discipline. She says to know your competition, but avoid reacting to every rival’s funding announcement or product update. Pivot only when the market gives you a meaningful reason to do so. “It’s very important to trust yourself and have conviction in what you’re building,” she adds. “People are going to give you their opinions without having all the context that you do. Feedback is critical for growth, but to also just really have that conviction and confidence in yourself, I think that’s what makes a really strong founder.” When Sarina Virk Torrendell decided to leave Amazon in September 2025, she knew that the safer choice was to stay put.  Torrendell had spent two decades building a consumer technology career. Her compensation at Amazon was in the high six figures, enough to support a family in New York City. At the time, Torrendell had two children and had just learned that she was pregnant with her third child.  Then she quit to start YouPop, an AI startup for content creators and founders that combines all of their different ventures onto one platform. Asos app users in the UK got a push notification on Tuesday morning in which the senders claimed to have fully compromised the online fashion retailer’s Snowflake instance. The message, titled “ASOS HACKED”, addressed the company’s data protection officer (DPO) and IT team. “Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it,” the notification read. Dozens of people told the BBC they had received it, Joe Tidy reported. Users began reporting problems with the app just before 10am UK time, TechRadar reported, citing the outage tracker Downdetector. Asos said it was aware of the reports but did not confirm a hack or comment further, the Guardian reported. The National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, is offering Asos its help, the newspaper said. The website and app appeared to keep working on Tuesday morning, the Guardian said. The message linked to a channel on the messaging app Telegram. The channel belongs to a new group calling itself the Xuanye Group, which set it up on Tuesday, according to the BBC. When the BBC checked, the channel had three posts, the latest about Asos. The channel also carried a message saying that “payment information is not affected”, with no further details, the Guardian reported. Sophos told the Guardian that no one had mentioned the group before on hacker forums or other Telegram channels. The message refers to the cloud platform Snowflake, which companies use to store and analyse data. The BBC reported that it is not known whether Asos is a Snowflake customer, or what data, if any, it keeps there. In 2024, a data theft campaign targeted Snowflake customers including Ticketmaster, Santander and AT&T, The Register noted. “Sending a push notification to ASOS’s app users would require access to the company’s notification system, which is separate from the Snowflake data platform the attackers claim to have compromised,” Dan Bird of the cybersecurity firm Horizon3 told the BBC. Alan Snyder, chief executive of the mobile security company NowSecure, said in comments sent to TNW that a compromised app reaches both a company’s customers and its data. “Customers shouldn’t have to figure out whether their shopping app is speaking for the retailer or an attacker,” Snyder said. Asos shares fell by more than 14% on the London Stock Exchange after the notification, according to the Guardian. The Financial Times put the fall at more than 10%. It's free. seths.blog/subscribe  A very long rant, riffing on the opportunity for bootstrapped startups who seek to create value using AI. I wrote it a while ago, thought it was too long, but in arguing with an AI today (everyone needs a hobby) I realized it was worth sharing: Most AI success stories to date are about cost reduction or speed improvement. A startup offers businesses a way to get more done with fewer people, replacing customer service or programming teams with bots. The upside of cost reduction is that it’s a very easy sale—give the client a free sample, once it’s demonstrated to work, they have an instant benefit in switching. The downsides: it’s difficult to win a race to the bottom, since someone can always promise more savings than you. And it’s finite—once the savings are made, there’s no incremental value left to create. The opportunity lies in something generative. A use of AI that doesn’t reduce costs, it creates value. It opens new opportunities, leads to growth, connection, and utility. Worth paying for: Most bootstrappers target price-sensitive customers and then wonder why growth is hard. But people and organizations with expensive problems and real resources don’t just put up with paying more for things they value—they prefer it. Premium pricing signals seriousness. Look for a market where the problem is real, the budget exists, and the solution creates something they couldn’t get otherwise. What people actually pay for: At the foundation of almost every premium purchase are three drives:  status (I matter, people like me see me as significant),  affiliation (I belong, there are people like me and they accept me), and  freedom from fear (I am safe, the threat is not coming).  Freedom from fear may be the most primitive—you can’t pursue status or affiliation while in survival mode. And most premium purchases are a quest for freedom from fear pretending to be something else. Built on those roots is a middle layer of things that offer one or more: legitimacy, transformation, belonging to a narrative, control, certainty, protection, trust, health and longevity, leverage. And the outer layer that’s easier to measure—things people buy because they deliver the middle layer: access, capital, time, attention, convenience, efficiency, delight, new experiences, beauty. Commodities—food, shelter, sex, addictive substances—are often outside this hierarchy. They don’t really build toward the three roots; they allow survival or temporarily suppress the anxiety that comes from not having them. An AI business worth building delivers something from the middle layer, justified by the outer layer. Nobody goes shopping for transformation.  What businesses actually pay for: The hierarchy for individual consumers doesn’t translate directly to organizational purchases. In B2B, the customer is spending someone else’s money. That means that the dominant question they’re asking is, “what will I tell my boss?” Three desires sit at the foundation of almost every business buying decision: Avoid blame — if this goes wrong, it won’t be my fault. The IBM principle: nobody ever got fired for buying the market leader. The champion inside the organization often needs a defensible story before they’ll act. Claim credit — I brought something in that worked and people noticed. The flip side of blame avoidance, and the engine of the internal champion. If your solution lets someone look good, they’ll sell it to their peers, you won’t have to. Reduce uncertainty — we can plan around this, the chaos goes down. Organizations pay significant premiums for the ability to forecast, commit, and stop worrying. Built on those roots is a middle layer of things organizations reliably spend on: growth, efficiency, compliance, competitive advantage, talent, morale, resilience, optionality, speed, legitimacy, relationships. And an outer layer that justifies the middle: cost savings, time savings, data, access, convenience, integration, reporting, support. Mechanics without a story is the race to the bottom, and being the cheapest is not the best use of your time. New vs. repeat purchases require different approaches: Repeat purchases are won by switching costs, relationships, and relentless incrementalism—you’re replacing someone, which means you need to be cheaper, easier, or have a better story and sales force. New purchases require someone inside the organization to become a champion, which means they need a story that serves their career, not just their company’s interests. Not all problems are equally interesting: Some purchases—like gaining market share or entering a new category—are chaotic and interesting, with room for narrative and ambition. Others—like cheaper materials or faster processing—are grinding commodities where the only story is price. Commodity buyers fear paying too much. Buyers in chaotic spaces fear making a wrong choice.  The forcing function: Businesses rarely lead the way on new purchases without a crisis compelling them. Without a forcing function, even a perfect solution sits in the pipeline forever—committees form, pilots stall, and champions get reassigned. Three kinds of crises create forcing functions: Competitive crisis — a rival did something and now there’s urgency. “They have it and we don’t” is a sentence that ends a discussion and starts the buying process. Technology crisis — the old way stopped working, or a new capability made the old way look reckless. AI itself is currently creating this for many industries simultaneously. This time, the forcing function and the solution are the same thing. Public/market upheaval — regulatory change, cultural shift, a collapse in input costs, a pandemic. These are the most powerful and least predictable. They create entirely new categories of buyer. The opportunity for a bootstrapper: sell into a forcing function that already exists, don’t try to create one. Organizations already feeling the crisis don’t need convincing—they need a solution that lets their champion say “I found it.”  NOTES: Naked AI is a trap. If all you’re doing is building a gateway to Anthropic or ChatGPT, your token costs eat a significant portion of your revenue—and you have no defensible position. Hidden prompts are insufficient. Breakthrough prompting can create real value, but there’s no protectable, reliable way to sell it as a business. If one of the frontier companies made it a business model, the mechanics would work in the bootstrapper’s favor, but I haven’t seen this. The network effect matters. Selling benefits one person at a time is brutally expensive. The breakthroughs come with projects that have the network built in—where interactions work better when your colleagues are using them too. Asymmetric information is worth seeking out. Some of the most durable advantages come not from network effects but from knowing something others don’t, or from helping a cohort work together to pool what they know against a party that currently has structural information advantage over them. Let all of Walmart’s vendors see information that they currently hoard, for example. So, a theory of profit—a framework for the kind of project that becomes a business: Bonus: A note on data stack reality. A network built on user data is only as good as the willingness of users to populate it. And willingness requires two things: it has to be frictionless enough that people don’t have to think about it, and it has to feel safe enough that people don’t have to worry about it. These two conditions are almost always in tension. The more automatic the data collection, the more it feels like surveillance. The more control you give people, the more friction you add. The most promising data stacks are ones where people are already generating the data, are already comfortable with it existing somewhere, and the innovation is simply giving them better access to what’s already theirs. The forcing function for consumer data sharing may be the simplest one of all: I already feel watched. I might as well get something back. The cautionary version of this is the email surveillance tool—a business reads all internal email and gets a report on who’s helpful, who’s toxic, who’s looking for a job. The value is real and obvious. The fear is also real and obvious. And in most organizations, the fear wins. Any data stack business has to answer the question: who controls this, and what happens if it goes wrong? If the answer isn’t immediately reassuring, the business doesn’t get built. The sponsored model. Not every valuable AI business needs the end user to pay. When the problem is real but the affected population lacks resources, a foundation, brand, or institution with aligned interests can fund the miracle instead. The economics flip entirely: instead of acquiring thousands of customers one at a time, you close one relationship with one institution that already has the distribution, the mission, and the budget. The user gets the miracle for free. The sponsor gets impact, data, or loyalty.  This model works when three things are true: the population being served is large and underserved, the value created is legible to an institution that cares about it, and the data generated serves both the individual user and the sponsor’s mission.  For example, a foundation pays $2,000,000 and 40,000 families of the incarcerated have access to a tool that generates a ten-page legal document instead of a bushel of random papers—and the shared data starts identifying patterns in the system (bad actors, defective paperwork) that no single case could surface alone.  A bank funds a personal finance tool for its own customers. A health brand funds a fitness coach for an underserved population. The viral problem is much easier to solve: once it’s free, you don’t need to work hard to persuade users to recruit each other, you need one institution with existing distribution to say yes. The cheap inference model. Not every AI application needs a frontier model. The problems worth looking for here aren’t the ones that require reasoning or nuance—instead, look for structure, pattern recognition, aggregation, and organization at scale. Form filling. Document organization. Transcription plus summarization. Matching similar records across large datasets. These problems are unglamorous but enormous in volume and largely underserved. Moore’s Law is on your side. The models that feel too limited today will evolve to become adequate in eighteen months. Building on cheap open-source inference means your margins improve as the technology does, without changing your product (which is the data stack and the network). And “huge” doesn’t mean huge—a single business school graduating class is enough to populate a meaningful census of what jobs actually lead where. The data stack doesn’t need to be large. It needs to be specific, trusted, and ahead of what anyone else has assembled. This was a particularly long rant, thanks for hanging in. I started writing it for a friend six months ago (with many inputs from others), but it’s more true now than then.  October 6, 2026

Skydance CEO David Ellison welcomed Warner Bros. Discovery employees and thanked Paramount staffers for their patience at the combined company's first-ever town hall. The Ghent company maps employees' skills and tasks and will become a core part of SAP's SuccessFactors HR software. SAP Headquarters, in Walldorf, Germany SAP has agreed to buy TechWolf, a Belgian company whose AI maps the skills and daily work of a firm’s employees. The two companies announced the deal today but did not disclose its terms. The acquisition is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approval. Until then, the two companies will continue to operate separately. TechWolf, based in Ghent, builds a continuously updated model of a company’s workforce from the HR and business systems it already uses. The model covers three levels: the tasks within each job, the skills staff hold and apply, and the external labour market. Companies then compare that picture with their business strategy to decide where to hire, retrain or move staff. TechWolf’s customers include HSBC, GSK, Ericsson, AMD, PayPal and Booking.com. SAP plans to make the technology a central part of SuccessFactors, its HR software, and of Joule, its AI assistant. “TechWolf’s proprietary context graph for skills and work provides an excellent grounding layer for agent queries regarding work and skills planning and talent management,” said Manoj Swaminathan, president and chief product officer for SAP Autonomous Suite and member of the Extended Board of SAP SE. Andreas De Neve, TechWolf’s chief executive and co-founder, said companies everywhere are trying to work out how AI is changing their workforce. “Organizations everywhere are trying to figure out how AI is reshaping work, and what their workforce needs to look like because of it,” said Andreas De Neve, CEO and co-founder of TechWolf. Under SAP’s current plans, TechWolf will stay an independent unit under De Neve in Ghent, with offices in London, New York and San Francisco. Its platform will also remain open to companies that do not use SAP software. The deal extends a run of AI purchases by the German software group this year. In March, SAP agreed to buy data management company Reltio, and in May it added Dremio and Prior Labs, committing more than €1bn to Prior Labs over four years. It's just $100 short of a brand-new PS5 Pro from Best Buy.  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  GameStop has increased the price of refurbished PS Pros from $800 to $1399.99, meaning used units cost 55% more than their list price for brand-new consoles, and well over double the PS5 Pro's original MSRP. A Redditor working at the retailer has leaked a memo telling employees that the higher price of used consoles versus new ones is intentional. A r/GameStop subreddit moderator has confirmed the validity of the post, saying that the original poster has been properly vetted. The leaked prices are now showing on the GameStop website. Brand-new PS5 Pro units have an MSRP of $899.00, which has already increased from $749.99 earlier this year because of chip shortages. It’s unclear whether Sony requires retailers to sell brand-new PS5 units at or close to the MSRP, but they generally have more freedom in setting the prices of pre-owned devices. Unfortunately, it seems that there’s a shortage of new PS5 Pros across several retailers. Sony, GameStop, and Target, which list the consoles at $899.99, are out of stock. While new consoles are available on Best Buy and Walmart, they’re priced at $1,496.01 and $1,554.99, respectively. Gamers who find these prices too rich might want to take their chances on eBay or Facebook Marketplace, but the situation there isn’t any better. New sealed PS5 Pros are going for more around $1,300 or more on these platforms. While they might be cheaper, you’ll miss out on some of the protections and peace of mind that retailers with brick-and-mortar stores provide. Many people blame the AI-driven memory chip crisis for the PS5 Pro shortage. AI data centers’ appetite for HBM and willingness to pay top dollar for these chips meant that DRAM manufacturers have pivoted most of their capacity towards this more lucrative market, with manufacturers of consumer goods fighting over a smaller pie of DRAM production. The situation has led to a 500% increase in RAM prices in the past 12 months, with the shortage now starting to spill over into other industries like smartphones and automotive manufacturing. The situation is likely compounded by the anticipated launch of GTA VI this coming November, which started pre-selling in June 2026. While Rockstar isn’t targeting 60 FPS for the game at launch, it seems that gamers are willing to pay top dollar just to ensure that they can get the best possible performance when the game finally arrives after years of waiting. It seems that buyers who have saved just enough cash to buy a PS5 Pro are out of luck as retailers are taking advantage of the shortage and jacking up prices, even for used models. The basic PS5 Digital (Slim) and Disc (Slim) editions are still priced at or close to the MSRP, though, so those who want to get their hands on a PlayStation right now without overpaying scalpers would have to settle for these instead. Gamers who are specifically buying a console just to play GTA VI at launch could also settle for an Xbox Series X instead, which is a bit cheaper than the PS5 Pro at MSRP while offering more performance than the base PS5, or they could experiment with the open-source AnyPS5, which runs PS5 console games natively on PC. Duncan Batty came from M&G Investments in January 2025 to build the division, his exit surfaced in Companies House filings, and it lands as Revolut adds businesses at a pace the European Central Bank has already told it to slow down Duncan Batty, hired from M&G Investments in January 2025 to build Revolut’s commercial real estate lending business, has left the company, with his departure appearing in Companies House filings and confirmed by a spokesperson. Neither a reason nor a successor has been given, and it comes as Revolut expands across banking, wealth and payments ahead of a listing it says is about two years away. The executive Revolut hired to build its commercial property lending business has left, less than two years after joining. The company confirmed it. Nobody has said why. Duncan Batty was co-head of the real estate finance platform at M&G Investments before Revolut recruited him in January 2025, and his departure surfaced in Companies House filings, as Bloomberg reported. A spokesperson confirmed the exit. No successor has been named. Revolut was not a fully licensed British bank when he arrived. It won the licence with restrictions in July 2024 and spent twenty months in the mobilisation stage, with capped deposits, before completing it in March 2026. Francesca Carlesi, who runs the UK bank, said then that it laid the foundation for a broader range of products, including credit. The pace of that expansion is already a regulatory question. The European Central Bank paused new product launches in the European Economic Area in July 2025 and ordered an independent review of Revolut’s risk, compliance and legal functions, with in-house sign-off and a board assessment required before future launches. Revolut’s European business is supervised from Frankfurt and Vilnius. It was valued at $115B in July, up from $75B in November, on 2025 revenue of about £4.5B. Management has projected $9B of revenue and $3.5B of net profit for this year. Property lending is a small part of that, and Revolut has never published a figure for it. The company has been adding businesses quickly. A private bank opened in Britain and parts of Europe this summer with a £500,000 threshold, alongside an Australian banking licence, a United States bank charter application and a euro stablecoin. All of it points at a listing. Nik Storonsky told Les Echos in September that Revolut is planning a dual listing in London and on Nasdaq, after two years of calling a London listing irrational. British commercial property is the one market on that list that is not growing. Hopes of a rebound in UK dealmaking have faded as the conflict in the Middle East kept inflation concerns alive and interest rates high, and lenders competing for a shrinking number of deals are squeezing their own margins, according to Bloomberg. The Boston software company, relaunched last year, will use IBM's quantum computers to develop practical applications. Zapata Quantum, a Boston quantum software company, has joined the IBM Quantum Network, it said on Tuesday. It will use IBM’s machines to build software for its clients. Zapata does not make quantum hardware. Instead, it helps organisations figure out which problems quantum computers can solve, then creates the software to do that. It says hardware is improving faster than the software that uses it. “The rapid progress IBM is making on the path to fault-tolerant quantum computing brings the quantum application gap into sharper focus,” said Sumit Kapur, Zapata’s chief executive. IBM aims to deliver its first fault-tolerant quantum computer, one that can correct its own errors, by 2029. Jonny Olson, Zapata’s co-founder and vice-president of strategy, said IBM’s superconducting machines appeal to customers because they run fast. “Joining the IBM Quantum Network lets us better identify valuable opportunities for organizations that need the fastest systems, and then prepare those organizations for the precise moment that quantum gives them real ROI,” said Jonny Olson. The two companies have worked together before. In a 2025 Nature Biotechnology study, Zapata ran part of its work on IBM hardware and found possible drug candidates aimed at KRAS, a protein linked to several cancers. Scientists from both firms also co-wrote a paper on using a quantum chip to factor numbers. What Zapata learns will feed into Quantum Pilot, a tool that helps firms pick and build the right projects. It is built to run on any maker’s hardware. The deal comes a year after Zapata’s comeback. The firm, which spun out of Harvard in 2017, re-emerged in September 2025 after a bankruptcy restructuring and now trades on the OTCQB market in the US. Ray Dalio says the US is careening toward a debt crisis before the end of this decade. The billionaire investor said in a Bloomberg Television interview on Tuesday that he anticipates a debt crisis "within the next three years," or by the fall of 2029. The author of "How Countries Go Broke" and founder of hedge-fund behemoth Bridgewater Associates said the scale of the national debt and the rate at which it's growing mean we're "approaching our limits." US debt breached the $40 trillion mark in August, representing an inflation-adjusted increase of more than $10 trillion, or over 33%, since 2019. Dalio said that this trajectory is unsustainable because of the soaring cost of servicing the debt. Those interest payments exceed $1 trillion a year or almost one-fifth of the federal budget, leaving less money for Social Security, healthcare, defense, education, and other priorities. "When debts accumulate faster than they're paid back, then debt service costs grow," he said. "That becomes a higher and higher percentage of one's cash flow. And when that happens, it starts to squeeze out spending. And so then you have a problem." Dalio also underscored that geopolitical tensions have tempered other countries' demand for US debt. Moreover, the AI boom has become "heavily debt-financed," which threatens to tighten credit in riskier categories such as auto loans, he said. The Wall Street veteran warned that trend could feed tensions over the wealth gap, as "the people who have less get squeezed the most in that part of the cycle." Dalio said he's seeing even AI hyperscalers "begin to encounter issues" with accessing credit, and he's "starting to see those limits being hit." Hollywood has spent a couple of years trying to figure out Skydance CEO David Ellison, who now runs the companies formerly known as Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. Now they have a new character to get to know: Ynon Kreiz, Ellison's newly appointed co-CEO. Kreiz, who is expected to co-host a press event with Ellison on Tuesday night, comes to Skydance from Mattel, where he is best-known for two things: engineering a deal with Warner Bros. and actress Margot Robbie to produce the colossally successful "Barbie" movie — and taking an ax to the toymaker's payroll, by laying off 22% of its workforce in one fell swoop. At Skydance, no one expects him to be making deals with studios and talent — that will be Ellison's purview. Instead, Kreiz will be expected to take on the grim task of finding $6 billion in savings over 3 years — a job that will likely involve meaningful layoffs. It's a job that has drawn repeated comparisons to Gunnar Wiedenfels, the former CFO at WBD, who repeatedly hacked at that company's P&L via layoffs and other cost-saving measures, like mothballing TV shows and movies. "He's Gunnar," one of Kreiz's friends told me this week. But few people outside the company knew who Wiedenfels was. Instead, people in and out of Hollywood focused their attention and ire on David Zaslav, the spotlight-loving WBD CEO. This time around, it seems clear that Ellison will be the public face of Skydance, and the one who gets to do fun stuff like schmoozing with stars. Kreiz will be the one getting his hands very dirty. People who've worked with him in the past say he's cut out for the role. "He's very serious," says Candle Media co-CEO Kevin Mayer, who negotiated with Kreiz when Mayer was a top executive at Disney, and Kreiz was CEO of Maker Studios, a web video startup Disney ended up buying in 2014. "He's unflappable, and is willing to take on the heaviest of heavy lifts." Kreiz, who declined to comment for this story, arrives at Skydance with a résumé stocked with media bona fides: He ran Endemol, the Dutch TV production company, back when it was a powerhouse; he helped Maker, founded by a group of young YouTubers-makers, scale up into something Disney was willing to buy for $500 million; and he led Mattel's move into IP licensing, which also gave us this year's "Masters of the Universe" movie. People who've worked with him describe him as an exceptionally high-energy executive. "Ynon will get on an airplane and fly across the country for a meeting if it's critical, and fly back the next morning," says Upfront Ventures' Mark Suster, whose VC firm was the primary investor in Maker. Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl, who has known Kreiz for decades, says Kreiz has a tough demeanor that's a little misleading. "Ynon's not a teddy bear. But he's a warm person," he says. Kyncl says Kreiz and his wife are the first people in Kyncl's emergency file — the people his kids are supposed to ask for help if anything happens to Kyncl and his wife. Kreiz has demerits on his record: Disney never figured out what to do with Maker, and Kreiz left Disney a couple of years after selling to them. And while Kreiz cut Mattel's costs, he struggled to grow the company — while Barbie sales shot up after the movie's blockbuster success in 2023, they fell again over the next two years, and eventually returned to pre-movie levels. Mattel's stock has been listing for some time. And while Kreiz is a veteran executive, he's never been in a position like this: While he's co-CEO of the giant media conglomerate, he's definitely not running the place. That person is David Ellison, who engineered acquisitions of Paramount and then WBD, backed by his father Larry Ellison's fortune. Tellingly, Ellison's title remains CEO, not co-CEO. And while Skydance won't have the same kind of pressure from shareholders that troubled Zaslav at WBD — the two Ellisons have effective control of the whole company — Kreiz will have to contend with the people who own the company's staggering $80 billion in debt. With the release of the M6 Mac mini and its more powerful M5 Pro counterpart, Apple quietly killed off one of the machine’s most compelling features. While both new Mac mini models look like their predecessors from the outside, Apple nixed the hidden feature that made the previous-generation Mac mini an incredible value.  					Jeff Benjamin's favorite wireless earbuds; they just keep getting better.				 When it first launched, the M4 Mac mini provided a huge bang for the buck. Not only did it feature Apple’s M4 SoC, but it also came with a healthy 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI, and Ethernet. At just $599 or $499 at the student discount price, the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac in Apple’s lineup but also, pound for pound, the best Mac in the lineup.  Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos But Apple’s smallest Mac had a secret up its sleeve that made it an even more valuable machine: a slot for upgradable storage. Users could literally pry open the machine’s back cover, unscrew a few screws, and access a removable NAND module that could be easily replaced with a third-party SSD up to 2TB. The benefits were multifaceted. Not only could you upgrade the SSD or easily fix a drive that failed, but you could also save some serious coin by forgoing Apple’s build-to-order upgrade option and do it yourself with a much cheaper third-party SSD.   					Jeff's favorite screen cleaning cloth that polishes to a shine.				 At the time, Apple charged $800 for the 2TB upgrade, transforming the “budget” computer into a $1400 computer with the click of an option. By upgrading after purchase with a third-party SSD, users could save nearly $500. Of course, as someone who likes to tinker, I was extremely excited about this and ended up posting a full video tutorial showing, step by step, how to upgrade the stock SSD with a third-party drive. It proved to be quite popular, amassing half a million views.  It was nice while it lasted. With the launch of this latest generation of Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly to the logic board, effectively eliminating the ability to upgrade it post-purchase with a third-party NAND module.  					Apple's budget MacBook, the cheapest way to experience macOS on the go.				 The Mac mini has gone from what was hands-down the best bang-for-your-buck Mac to a significantly more expensive product, not just for the base model, which goes from $600 to $900, but also for the 2TB upgrade, which goes from $800 to $1000.  Today if you want an M6 Mac mini with a 2TB SSD, you’ll need to pay Apple $1900. The equivalent M4 Mac mini, with a 2TB aftermarket upgrade, would have set you back roughly $920 when you factor in the $320 aftermarket upgrade price being charged at the time. Obviously, things have gotten more expensive, so it’s not exactly Apple’s to Apple’s (see what I did there), but that’s a $1000 increase in price, not only because Apple is charging significantly more, but also because Apple eliminated the ability for customers to upgrade the machines themselves. I have a good idea as to why Apple opted to increase the price of the base Mac mini by $300, and I can even understand why its SSD prices have increased so much. Because of AI and other factors, component, SSD, and memory prices have all skyrocketed. But that doesn’t explain why Apple opted to solder the SSDs to the logic board instead of keeping them user-replaceable like before. They are certainly capable of doing it; they simply choose not to. Major markets and blocs—such as the European Union, China, and India—need to enforce strict guidelines requiring phone manufacturers, including Apple, to adopt modular designs. This should extend to companies like Sony and Microsoft as well. Consumer protection is currently non-existent. We can speculate, but we may never know the real answer for Apple’s decision to revert back to soldered SSDs. What we do know, however, is that these machines are significantly more expensive, and even that sounds like an understatement. In the case of the M4 Mac mini with a 2TB aftermarket upgrade vs the M6 Mac mini with a 2TB build-to-order upgrade, it’s roughly a 106% price increase.  					Jeff Benjamin's favorite screen cleaner for Apple products.				 It can be difficult to find a base model M4 Mac mini on the used market at a reasonable price, but if you can manage to do so, it remains an excellent machine for its baseline performance, features, and upgradable SSD. The good news in all of this is that all of Apple’s Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, so you can easily add high-bandwidth external storage via a USB or Thunderbolt SSD. I’m personally a big fan of the Samsung T9, which offers a relatively affordable way to add extra storage.  What do you think Apple’s reasoning is for getting rid of user-replaceable SSDs in the Mac mini? Do you have any particular theories? Sound off in the comments with your thoughts. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Every company has a story. In many small businesses, however, that story can be told only by the owner. The owner knows why money was borrowed, why equipment was purchased, why a key employee was hired and why the company changed direction. But what happens when the owner is not in the room? What happens when the owner must defend a past decision and has only memories and recollections to offer? A company should not depend upon its owner to explain every important action. Its records should be capable of telling the story. Three components build that narrative: the business plan, the bookkeeping and the corporate records. Together, they explain where the company intended to go, what actually happened and who authorized the important decisions along the way. The business plan should not be a ceremonial document written once for the purpose of landing a bank loan. It should be a periodically updated record of management’s thinking. A useful plan explains the market the company serves, its competitive position, growth priorities, staffing and capital requirements, major risks, marketing efforts and the expected purpose of significant investments. The plan provides context that financial statements cannot supply on their own. Suppose recent statements show weaker earnings because the company hired additional staff, opened another location or invested in infrastructure. The numbers reveal the decline in current profit, but the plan explains whether management expected it and what the investment was intended to accomplish. Without that explanation, a deliberate investment in future capacity may simply look like deteriorating performance. A useful business plan also creates a benchmark. Management can compare what it expected with what later occurred. Were the projected sales realistic? Did the new employee produce the expected capacity? Did the marketing campaign reach the intended customers? The differences between the plan and the results are often where the most valuable lessons are found. The plan therefore serves as both a statement of intent and a record against which management’s judgment can be evaluated. Good bookkeeping is the hub of a company’s financial operating system. It establishes what the company earned and spent, what it owns and owes, where its cash came from and where it went. It allows the owner to see whether performance is improving or deteriorating, and it supplies the foundation for tax reporting that can be supported after the fact. Timely bookkeeping is especially important because it preserves details while they are still available. A transaction downloaded from a bank or credit card account, properly categorized and supported by an invoice or receipt, creates a better record than a year-end reconstruction based on memory. When the work is kept current, the financial statements can also guide decisions during the year instead of merely reporting history after the opportunities to act have passed. Bookkeeping alone, however, has limits. A ledger may show that the company spent $75,000 on equipment, borrowed money or made a large payment to an owner. It may not explain the purpose of the equipment, the reasoning behind the loan or whether the payment was compensation, a reimbursement, a distribution or repayment of a shareholder loan. The books record the transaction. The business plan and supporting documents help explain it. Corporate documents are the most overlooked part of the story I encounter in my work with business owners. They can also become vital when a transaction is questioned. A tax position may be weakened even when the underlying expense or strategy is otherwise permissible because the business never created the records needed to establish its purpose, terms or authorization. Minutes, resolutions and written consents provide evidence that the owners or managers considered and approved important actions. Depending on the company, those actions might include officer appointments and compensation, major purchases, loans, retirement plan adoption, related-party leases, shareholder loans, distributions, acquisitions, changes in ownership and significant contracts. These records also help demonstrate that the company was operated as a separate enterprise rather than as the owner’s personal checkbook. Consider a building owned personally by the business owner and leased to the operating company. The bookkeeping may show the rent payments, but it does not establish the terms of the arrangement. A written lease, appropriate approval and consistent payment history tell a much more complete story. The same principle applies to money advanced by an owner. Without a note, repayment terms and proper records, an intended loan may later be difficult to distinguish from a capital contribution or distribution. The required documents and formalities vary according to the entity type and the law of the state in which it was formed. A corporation and a limited liability company may not have identical requirements. This is where a good business attorney earns a place on the company’s advisory team. The goal is not to manufacture paperwork after a question arises. It is to document important decisions when they are made. The eventual reader of this story may be a lender evaluating risk, an IRS examiner reviewing a tax return or a prospective buyer conducting due diligence. It may be a key employee assuming more responsibility, an executor settling an estate or a spouse forced to step into the business unexpectedly. Each will approach the company with different questions, but none should have to depend entirely upon the owner’s memory. The quality of the record matters because unexplained activity invites assumptions. A buyer may discount the value of a company whose decisions and financial results cannot be reconstructed. A lender may view an undocumented obligation as added risk. A successor may repeat an old mistake because the reasoning behind an earlier decision disappeared with the person who made it. Clear records reduce that uncertainty. A business that cannot explain itself without its owner remains dependent upon its owner. That dependence creates risk and limits transferability. Good bookkeeping, a living business plan and disciplined corporate records allow the company to speak with its own voice. They preserve its financial history, management’s reasoning and the authority behind major decisions. The objective is not paperwork for its own sake. It is to build an enterprise whose story remains coherent even when the founder is no longer in the room. Every company has a story. In many small businesses, however, that story can be told only by the owner. The government has issued a public interest notice, with a CMA report due by 19 October. BT told Ofcom TalkTalk still runs Huawei kit in parts of its network. BT Group has acquired TalkTalk’s consumer and wholesale businesses out of administration. They have 1.5 million retail customers and 1 million wholesale customers. BT announced the deal on Monday. It said a prolonged sale process for those operations had been unsuccessful. BT bought TalkTalk Telecommunications Limited and PlatformX Communications Limited, the wholesale business, on a debt-free basis. It estimates the total cash impact in its 2027 financial year at about £400M. That figure covers the consideration, transaction and administration costs, and working capital impacts. It also includes a trading loss of about £60M. Another £100M or so would otherwise have been due to BT’s Openreach. TalkTalk reported revenue of about £1.2bn over the last 12 months and was loss-making, BT said. TalkTalk and BT will operate separately and continue to compete while a regulatory review takes place. “This is a genuinely unprecedented situation, where millions of citizens and businesses were at risk if TalkTalk had collapsed,” said Allison Kirkby, BT Group’s chief executive. Lisa Nandy is the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. On Monday she issued a Public Interest Intervention Notice under the Enterprise Act 2002, the government said. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) will report on competition concerns. The notice then lets her consider the wider public interest. The CMA must report to her by 19 October. TalkTalk’s networks support calls to emergency services, ambulance and hospital communications and medical alarms, the government said. A number of potential buyers had been unable to agree a sale of the whole business. “Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure. If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services,” Nandy said. BT made a non-binding offer on 2 October. That day, Kirkby wrote to Melanie Dawes, chief executive of the regulator Ofcom. In the letter, which Ofcom has published, she wrote that TalkTalk still operated Huawei kit in some parts of its network. BT’s due diligence indicated this. BT would keep the TalkTalk legacy network entirely separate from its own network, including its core, she wrote. No Huawei equipment would move into any of BT’s networks. She asked Ofcom to confirm this in writing: that it would treat TalkTalk’s past non-compliance pragmatically and collaboratively, not punitively. BT has about 31% of the UK retail broadband market, CCS Insight analyst Kester Mann said, according to Bloomberg. “This has all the characteristics of a stitch up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” a Virgin Media spokesperson said. In the same statement, Virgin Media O2 pointed to the CMA’s plan to potentially block nexfibre’s deal with Netomnia. Virgin Media O2’s owners, Liberty Global and Telefónica, co-own nexfibre with InfraVia. Services A website allows New Yorkers to submit complaints about hard-to-cancel subscriptions. October 6, 2026, 5:35 pm ET A year after an appeals court effectively canceled a nationwide regulation requiring companies to make it easier to get out of subscriptions, New York City has revived it for those who live there. Announced last week by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, alongside the city’s top tech officer and consumer protection commissioner, the rule says companies must make it as easy to cancel a subscription as it is to sign up. That applies to gym memberships, a cellphone contract or apps that charge a monthly fee. It’s similar in principle to the “click-to-cancel” rules that were proposed in 2024 during the Biden administration but never fully rolled out. NYC’s law was set by an executive order in January and went into effect on Oct. 1. “No one should need 45 minutes of hold music to stop paying for something they never wanted,” Mamdani said in the announcement. “If a company can take your money with one click, you should be able to get your money back with one click. And now, if they won’t let you cancel, the city is coming for them.” More from CNET Part of “coming for them” is a web page where New Yorkers can file a complaint. The site allows a visitor to search for or add a business, even if it’s not based in New York City, and select from a list of issues, such as, “The business delayed canceling your subscription,” or, “You were not informed of auto-renewal.” A text box and an option to upload documents, such as screenshots, allow for elaboration on what happened. Those filing complaints can also choose the type of outcome they’d like to see, including “refund and cancel subscription.” According to Samuel Levine, commissioner of New York City’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, full-time staffers will field those web-submitted complaints. “They’re not going to be diverted into a chatbot doom loop,” Levine told The Verge. “We’re going to have actual people whose full-time job is to help them.” Businesses that are the subject of a complaint will be investigated, and if they’re found to be in violation of the city rules, they could be fined up to $525 per violation. What will happen in the rest of the country, where, according to a CNET survey, Americans spend on average more than $1,300 a year on subscriptions, some of them unused or subscribed to by accident? Emily Peterson-Cassin, director of competition and market fairness at the Consumer Federation of America, said New York City’s click-to-cancel law shows how local governments can create new ways to protect consumers. “This innovative move highlights yet again that local and state consumer protection agencies are stepping up to protect consumers even while federal agencies aren’t and provides a roadmap for other regulators to do the same.” California, for instance, has a rule that requires businesses to get a customer’s explicit consent before they are charged for a subscription renewal. That law was beefed up last year to include protections like offering cancellation on the same medium the subscription originated; a business can’t, for instance, make you go to a physical location to cancel something you signed up for online. It also requires companies to notify customers before an upcoming renewal charge and to give annual reminders about auto-renewals using the same method of communication used to enroll. A Maryland law that went into effect in June also requires companies to give customers a “cost-effective, timely and easy-to-use” way to cancel auto-renewals of subscriptions. The law falls under Maryland’s Service Contracts and Consumer Products Guaranty Act and can result in fines (PDF) of up to $10,000 per violation or $25,000 for repeat violations. Colorado’s equivalent law, the Online Cancellation Act, went into effect in 2025 and mandated that merchants provide a one-step cancellation link. Earlier this year, the act was expanded to include transactions between two businesses or entities. The “patchwork” approach, as some describe these disparate regional laws, is in lieu of the national rule that was stalled because of a procedural error. When the Eighth District Court of Appeals struck it down, the court said it was because the proper regulatory analysis hadn’t been done, not because the court disagreed with its intent or approach. There are signs that the Federal Trade Commission could be taking the initiative to revive a national click-to-cancel policy, or at least parts of it, but it’s hard to tell from its language. In a January press release, the FTC said it was submitting a draft proposal related to “Negative Option Plans,” another way of saying auto-renewals, in which businesses don’t give customers notice or the option to cancel for ongoing subscription charges. In March, the FTC opened up the floor for public comment after it said it received 100,000 complaints in five years over businesses making cancellations difficult or impossible. A representative for the FTC told CNET in an email, “We don’t have an update related to this issue” regarding click-to-cancel or the New York City law. Peterson-Cassin of the CFA said that so far the FTC has mostly focused on disclosing fees rather than banning auto-renewals, “so it’s hard for us to believe they would come up with something as strong as the New York rule.” However, she said, “Given how much attention there is on this issue and New York’s good example, there is still time for them to do the right thing, and protect all Americans from these predatory subscription traps.” Have a story tip you want to share with CNET? Growing up in Tampa, I learned early that getting to my area's most famous beaches isn't always as easy as it looks. Clearwater and St. Pete Beach are undeniably gorgeous, but by mid-morning on a weekend, the parking lots are full, and the sand is packed with umbrellas — and then, the traffic getting home takes hours. So these days, when I want salt air and sunshine without the shoulder-to-shoulder crowds, I drive my car to a place that feels like a well-kept secret hiding in plain sight. Known as the "sponge capital of the world," Tarpon Springs sits about 30 minutes north of Clearwater on Florida's Gulf Coast, or 20 minutes from my family's home in northern Tampa. The beach is special, but so are the layers of history and culture wrapped around it. In the early 1900s, Greek immigrants arrived to work in the sponge-diving industry, and their legacy still shapes the town's food, architecture, and rhythm today. Walking around feels less like you're in Florida, and more like you're stepping into a little corner of the Mediterranean. I always start at the sponge docks. The working waterfront is lined with boats, and vendors still sell natural sponges pulled straight from the Gulf. It's part market, part living museum. From there, I wander into the Greektown Historic District, filled with delicious food options. This is where I've eaten some of the most authentic Greek cooking I've found anywhere in the state: flaky spanakopita, thick Greek coffee, and fresh, crunchy Greek salad. When I'm ready to jump in some cool water, I head to Fred Howard Park. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    This is my favorite part of visiting. The park connects the mainland to a small barrier island, and the water here is calm, clear, and blissfully uncrowded compared to the bigger-name beaches down the coast. I like to rent a kayak or paddleboard to explore the inlet coves, drifting past mangroves and spotting the occasional dolphin or heron in the water. Whenever I'm paddling, it's easy to forget how close I am to a major metro area. On the island, I love the scenic, mile-long Fred Howard Causeway, which links the mainland to the beach. You can walk it, bike it, or drive it slowly with the windows down, and the water stretches out on both sides the entire way. Fred Howard Park is family-friendly and the perfect place to spend some quality time with loved ones. On the mainland side, kids can play at the two playgrounds or spread out on the open softball and ball field. When I go with my family, we usually claim a shady picnic spot, unpack a spread of food, and settle in for the afternoon. My favorite tradition is staying late enough to watch the sunset. There's a stretch where the sky turns orange and pink over the Gulf, the temperature gets a little cooler, and the whole place feels like it belongs to just us. Tampa's headline beaches will always draw in crowds, and I understand the appeal. But when I want beauty, history, great food, and room to breathe all in one trip, Tarpon Springs wins every time. I've been to Italy 16 times, and if you give me an opening, I can work it into just about any conversation. But surprisingly, it wasn't Venice, Rome, or the Amalfi Coast that made me fall head over heels for the country. It was Bologna, the capital of northern Italy's Emilia-Romagna region. Bologna has it all — food, wine, art, history, architecture, and the kind of energy that makes you seriously consider missing your flight home. Sure, seeing the Colosseum is cool, but I prefer eating perfectly made tortellini with a glass of pignoletto in Bologna. Here's why I always recommend tourists add Bologna to their itinerary, even if they can only spare one glorious, carb-loaded night. Every Italian I know tells me their region's cuisine is the best, but I'm here to tell you that Bologna is home to the best food I've had. I fell hard for the mortadella, the tortellini, and the Bolognese, and I've spent practically every trip to Italy since chasing those foods. One of my favorite things I did in the city was wander through the Quadrilatero, the city's historic market district, where butcher shops, cheese merchants, and specialty food stores practically demand that you stop every few feet. When I was there, I grabbed a mortadella sandwich and a glass of Lambrusco, then sat in one of the stunning cobblestone alleyways to people-watch. The region is also well known for producing Parmigiano Reggiano, which always seems to taste freshest here. For a traditional Emilian dinner, I always recommend A Balùs. The Bolognese was the best pasta dish I've ever had in all of Italy, and the sardines served on bread with butter literally melted in my mouth. Bologna isn't just a city where you eat extraordinarily well. It's also a place where visitors can stumble into hundreds of years of history while walking off lunch. One place that particularly moved me was the Archiginnasio Municipal Library, which houses rare books, centuries-old manuscripts, and other special collections. Although, in my opinion, it might not be as visually impressive as the Trinity Library in Dublin, knowing that some of these manuscripts date back more than a thousand years made this place feel pretty extraordinary to me. One of the city's highlights is the University of Bologna, which dates back to 1088 and is widely recognized as the oldest university in the Western world. But Bologna isn't a typical college town where the bars are packed with rowdy students and every night feels like a fraternity party. Instead, the city has a much more sophisticated energy. I saw students mingling with professors, artists, young professionals, and longtime residents, creating this incredible mix of old-world Italy and youthful enthusiasm. I also loved visiting the Piazza Verdi, a square filled with students catching up with friends after class. One of the unique things about Bologna's design is its porticoes. I love these eye-catching archways that line the streets, many of which date back to the 12th century. In fact, Bologna has about 38 miles of porticoes, with the most famous being the Portico di San Luca, a pathway that extends for about 2 miles and has more than 600 arches. I always recommend Bologna to travelers because they don't have to sacrifice seeing other parts of Italy to go there, since the city is one of the country's main railway hubs. By train, Florence is only 30 minutes away, Milan is about an hour away, and Venice is just about 90 minutes away. Overall, I think Bologna is one of Italy's greatest culinary and cultural destinations, and I couldn't recommend it enough. No comments right now, check back later.
