Since being founded by two friends just four years ago, Omhu has sold more than 40,000 sofas. In this interview, CEO Simon Salomonsson explains how the Danish company is disrupting the furniture industry. If you're an Instagram or TikTok user, you've probably seen it before: a modular corduroy sofa with fat, L-shaped back cushions and an external chrome frame that allows for easy transformation into a bed or conversation pit. Sometimes referred to as "the viral sofa", the Teddy has achieved a level of cut-through that few, if any, furniture designs of recent years can match. And yet, it was not created by a furniture designer or an established furniture company, but by two childhood friends with an Instagram-based vintage furniture business. Having had some joy selling second-hand, mid-century pieces during the pandemic, graphic designer Jonas Larsen and creative marketer Frederik Frøsig decided to develop a product of their own. Taking inspiration from their own stock, in 2022 they manufactured a batch of Teddies, sold them, and built from there. "I could see this was really taking off" By summer 2024, with the Teddy and the company they established to sell it, Omhu, gaining significant traction, Larsen and Frøsig contacted Salomonsson. The three had met studying in Peru in 2009, after which Salomonsson had gone on to success as a digital marketing entrepreneur. "It wasn't really on my bingo card for 2024 that I should be a board member of a sleeping-couch company," Salomonsson told Dezeen. "But I could see this was really taking off." "A lot of the different angles they had to the furniture industry was super interesting, super disruptive. And I figured if I could professionalise that and build an operation around it together with them, then we could make something really big out of it." Salomonsson joined Omhu as CEO two years ago, becoming its fifth employee. There are now nearly 60, while Larsen and Frøsig are no longer actively involved. Omhu now ships to 26 different countries, has 80 showrooms and is working on setting up a factory in the US to add to its existing production facility in Poland. The company keeps quiet about how much money it has made, though Salomonsson confirms it has been profitable and self-funded from day one. It's the kind of commercial success that young furniture brands dream of, and in testament to the Teddy's instant-classic status, the internet is littered with knock-off copycat versions. How has all this been achieved in just a few years? "When people ask me what is the kind of secret of the success, I tend to say the multifunctional part of it; the design, which is playful, warm, you can customise it," said Salomonsson. "And then the affordability. It depends on the region, but I would say mid-pricing, like a little bit more expensive than IKEA, but not where you see Hay and Muuto." "Omhu is hellbent on being at that price point" This affordability, according to Salomonsson, is a result of Omhu doing things differently to other furniture brands. While most focus heavily on business-to-business sales, including selling to retailers, from the beginning Omhu has concentrated solely on selling directly to consumers from its own website. "For us to charge 1,500, 1,600 euros for a sofa, if we had to go through a retail store it will be a lot more expensive because there's a middleman taking a cut," said Salomonsson. "So I think that's what has really enabled us to keep that price point." "Omhu is hellbent on being at that price point going forward," he added. "We cannot go down on IKEA level, but I think there is a sweet spot where we want to be like a global furniture brand, but not be in the Hay or Muuto or Vitra area of expensiveness and keep a lower margin, lower price compared to the market, and be affordable, where you get quality for what you are paying." To get the word out about its product, Omhu has focused almost entirely on social-media marketing, sending Teddy sofas to influencers and paying for Instagram ads. Early on in the brand's operations, a video of the Teddy by Danish influencer Astrid Olsen blew up over a single weekend in 2023, and led to a surge in orders across Europe and from the US. It doesn't hurt that the sofa's straightforward adaptability lends itself perfectly to a quick social media reel – with clips of people converting it from a couch to a conversation pit to a bed filling potential buyers' feeds. Again, Salomonsson says, this approach represents a divergence from the policies of most established furniture brands, which carefully manage their product imagery. "We just put it out to cool influencers and see what they can do with it, and don't try to control too much, and I think that has been a big part of our success," he said. "It's always been hard in the furniture industry to sell sofas online. For many of our customers, it is the biggest purchase they'll make that year." "They need to trust us, they need to trust the sofa. So the more we can show the different angles of how it can be used, how the colours look, how it fades over time, how a customer views it, the more trust we can build." The same philosophy has been applied to establishing spaces where potential customers can see the sofa in real life – for instance, through the Friends of Omhu initiative, where trendy stores and cafes can be sent a Teddy for free. Omhu has invested in having lots of showrooms but the spaces tend to be basic – providing a space to test out the product though without the feel of a flagship store. "That's also different from what you normally see from furniture people, where they're very much around brand experience," said Salomonsson. "We want to be eye-level with our customers and not be, like, too aspirational in our look either. We want them to be able to relate to us." "We have a lot on our plate" Despite being native to Copenhagen, Omhu has been conspicuous by its absence at the Danish capital's vast annual design festival, 3 Days of Design. "It takes a lot of time and costs a lot of money to be part of 3 Days of Design," said Salomonsson. "And we have a lot on our plate." "At some point we're gonna be at one of these events – if it's Milan or 3 Days of Design or New York, we have not decided yet. But it will be different things we are doing, because we are different." For now, Omhu is preoccupied with its ambition of becoming, in Salomonsson's words, a "big global furniture design company". As well as the US factory and trying to open up more markets in Asia, the company is actively working on expanding its product range beyond the Teddy and variants thereof. Working with both in-house and external designers and also seeking to license existing designs, it is aiming to make new releases within the next year. The new product categories will be partly based on what people are searching for on the Omhu website, while the company plans to continue to prioritise multi-functional, modular designs. "It's hard to say what is Omhu design, right, because we just have the Teddy," said Salomonsson. "But I think when you see it, you'll see the playfulness, the multi-functionality, that is liveable, is warm, and it'll be at a fair price, it won't be like art pieces." Not that the Teddy is perfect, as Omhu itself acknowledges. Reviewers online often complain that the chrome bars that serve as the sofa's frame move around, and so need to be pushed back into place regularly. "The gliding bars has been a real headache for us that we're trying to solve, and we're still working on improving the product in that sense," said Salomonsson. Rubber grips that slide over the bars are now provided as standard with every purchase. Sustainability is also an issue. The absence of an internal frame – what has sometimes been described as a "boneless" design – helps to keep the Teddy's price-tag down, but it also means the product uses a lot of polyurethane foam. "It's a sensitive question, but I would like to be straight here," said Salomonsson. "Our product – Teddy – it's foam. That'll never be the most sustainable thing in the world." "We can't hide from that, but what we have done is we have an interchangeable product where we change the covers, it evolves with you, it's multifunctional, it's really high quality what we make; it lasts very long." For now the Teddy is also made-to-order, though as Omhu's product range expands, the company will transition to holding stock in warehouses. Looking ahead, Salomonsson is convinced Omhu can become a household name through its unconventional approach – a furniture company better-suited to current times. "We're a bold company, we do things differently, we have another point of view on marketing, on culture," he said. "I really believe there's a huge opportunity for Omhu here, and I'm really determined to go at it, and that's also why we want to come out with new stuff." The photography is courtesy of Omhu. In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month. In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites. With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead. Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati. The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave.  "I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says. He has little doubt they are dead.  But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years. The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month. Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance. Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (Â£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (Â£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (Â£491; $651) for each additional death. But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare. "In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari. He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues. For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate. When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us. Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods  Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them. Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed. Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data. The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol. The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over. Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality. Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue. "Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC. He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to. For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses. More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at Â£123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households. This implies losses of about Â£14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family. The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster. Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied. "We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities." The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution. In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required. The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to Â£3.6bn ($4.8bn). Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy.  Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects. Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming. "When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders. This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster. For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar. He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati. But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village. Once again, he is without a home. "I have lost everything," he said. So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal. Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies. He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home. It’s a deadline for decisions about who matters most, what the business is really selling and what no longer deserves space. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Website redesigns often begin with familiar complaints: The site looks dated, navigation has become difficult, conversion is underperforming, or the business has outgrown what was built years ago. Those are valid reasons to start. But they are rarely the reason a redesign becomes difficult. The difficult part is that a website forces a company to make choices it may have postponed everywhere else. Growth can support several audiences at once. Acquisitions can add capabilities without requiring the company to explain how they fit together. New services can be layered onto old ones. A homepage is less forgiving. Something has to come first, something has to be explained clearly, and something may no longer deserve the space it once had. That is why a redesign can be useful well beyond marketing. It creates a decision deadline. Look at the sitemap of a company that has been operating for a decade or more, and you can often reconstruct its history. A service launched, so it received a page. An acquisition brought in a new capability, so it received a section. A division wanted more visibility, so it was added to the navigation. An old offering stayed because a few clients still buy it. A campaign page became permanent because nobody had a reason to remove it. None of those choices is necessarily wrong. The problem is accumulation. Over time, the website can become a record of everything the business has been rather than a clear expression of what it is now. What looks like a navigation problem is often a prioritization problem. The menu is crowded because the business has not decided what can move down, merge or disappear. Companies often respond to internal disagreement by giving everyone space. If two groups use different language, both terms appear. If leadership wants a new audience but does not want to alienate the old one, the homepage tries to speak equally to both. If several offerings are politically important inside the company, they receive equal weight whether or not customers see them that way. Internally, that can feel fair. Externally, it creates work. The organization avoids making a difficult choice, and the user inherits the ambiguity through longer menus, repetitive pages, competing calls to action and broad messaging that tries to include everyone without being especially useful to anyone. This is where strong web design becomes less about decoration and more about hierarchy. The interface can make priorities visible, but it cannot invent those priorities on behalf of leadership. The most useful conversations often begin with three uncomfortable questions. Who actually pays? A business may serve many audiences, but they rarely have equal commercial importance. One group may generate most of today’s revenue while another represents the market the company wants to grow into. That distinction should influence what appears first and which paths receive the most attention. Prioritizing an audience does not mean ignoring everyone else. It means being honest about who should understand the business first. Which offer is actually strategic? Companies accumulate services for all kinds of reasons. Some are highly profitable. Some help win larger engagements. Some still exist because longtime clients request them. Others represent where leadership wants the company to go next. Presenting all of them with the same weight may be accurate as an inventory, but it is not necessarily useful as a strategy. A redesign should force a clearer answer about which parts of the business deserve to grow. Which page should die? Organizations are much better at adding than subtracting. Every new initiative gives the website another reason to expand, while almost nothing creates a natural moment to remove an old page. A redesign should. If a page no longer reflects how the company sells, operates or wants to be understood, keeping it is not neutral. It continues to consume attention and shape perception. Many business disagreements remain manageable until someone has to write the homepage. Sales may describe the company differently from leadership. One business unit may think in products while another thinks in industries. Marketing may be pursuing a new customer while much of the existing site still speaks to the old one. These differences can coexist internally for years because each group operates in its own context. A website removes some of that separation. One navigation has to organize the business. One headline has to introduce it. One page has to explain why a customer should care. When a redesign stalls on language or hierarchy, the answer is not always another round of copy edits. Sometimes the project has found a disagreement that belongs with the people responsible for the business decision. That is not a failure of the redesign. It may be one of its most valuable outcomes. A successful redesign should produce a site that is clearer, easier to navigate and more effective at supporting the business. But some of the most important improvements happen before the new experience is visible. Leadership decides which audience matters most, which offers are central to future growth, where old language no longer fits and which pages have survived mostly because nobody wanted to make the call. Once those choices are made, downstream decisions get easier. A homepage does not need to carry six competing messages when the business has agreed on two priorities. Navigation does not have to preserve every historical distinction when leadership has decided which ones customers actually need. Reviews become less about personal preference because there is a clearer reason for what is being emphasized and what is not. Growth gives companies room to carry multiple versions of themselves for a while. A website eventually asks for a hierarchy. The businesses that treat a redesign as a decision deadline, rather than merely a visual refresh, can end up with something more valuable than a better site: a clearer understanding of what deserves to come first. David Ellison is taking a victory lap after completing Paramount's merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, a $110 billion deal that formed the new-look Skydance and will transform Hollywood. "It has taken hard work, perseverance and commitment with many challenges along the way — but we did it!" Ellison said in a memo to employees on Tuesday morning, which was obtained by Business Insider. Ellison expressed thanks to staffers across Paramount and WBD for "your patience, your resilience and, above all, your belief in what we could accomplish together." Skydance will be "powered by creativity and technology," Ellison said, adding that the company has four top priorities: Skydance is now a Hollywood behemoth that owns assets including Paramount Pictures, the Warner Bros. studio, Paramount+, HBO Max, Pluto TV, Discovery+, HBO, CBS, CNN, TruTV, TLC, and Comedy Central. However, the combined company faces fierce competition from Hollywood rivals like Disney and tech giants, including Google's YouTube. Paramount and WBD's streaming viewership share on US TVs was 3.6% in July, according to Nielsen — lower than Disney's 4.7%, Netflix's 7.8%, and YouTube's 14.2%. "Audiences have more choices than ever, technology is reshaping how stories are created, distributed and experienced, and competition for people's time and attention has never been greater," Ellison said in his memo. "We don't just want to succeed in this environment — we want to win and help shape the future of the industry." The Skydance CEO also had a section on "financial strength," which he said will give the company "the freedom to take creative risks, invest in our people and our technology, and pursue the kind of opportunities that set us apart." Ellison said the combined company will generate close to $70 billion in revenue and will save $6 billion from this merger. It will also have about $80 billion in debt. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    Ellison has brought in Ynon Kreiz as Skydance's co-CEO to oversee the merger integration and run day-to-day operations. The former Mattel top exec is known for cutting costs, as Business Insider's Peter Kafka noted. The Paramount-WBD merger followed a monthslong saga in which Ellison's company started a hostile bid for WBD, outbid Netflix, faced lawsuits from 12 states and the Writers Guild of America, and settled those suits by agreeing to concessions. Hate the company or love it, it's undeniable that where Apple treads, others often follow. There is no shortage of examples. The company didn't invent smartphones, but the iPhone basically changed the course of the entire mobile industry, seemingly overnight. Tablets? The iPad wasn't the first tablet on the market, either. Yet, in true Apple fashion, it popularized the tech. It's not just massive shifts either. Think about how almost all phones started packing in fingerprint sensors after the iPhone 5S made Touch ID cool. Seems like the next big thing will have to do with batteries. More precisely, Android phones may start copying Apple's method of packing batteries inside the device, which could lead to massive jumps in overall capacity. According to reputable leaks, at least one of the major Chinese manufacturers is working on copying Apple's steel-encased battery design that graces the new iPhone 18 Pro Max. Why is this a big deal? Well, the company is combining the steel shell with stacked cells, which may allow it to deliver batteries with capacities as large as 10,000 mAh. Apple's approach solves a major problem with standard soft-pouch battery packs that require extra space for thermal dissipation and to minimize damage in case of cell swelling. Because of its rigid design, Apple was able to pack cells tightly without worrying as much about thermals in an enclosure that's significantly thinner. This is likely the reason why the iPhone 18 Pro Max, with its 5,391 mAh battery, delivers approximately 21.06 Wh (watt-hours) and can truck on for over 19 hours. For comparison, the Galaxy S26 Ultra (5000 mAh battery with 19.4Wh) tops out at a little over 16. It remains to be seen whether the next generation of these supercharged devices will be available in the United States. Sure, the Android phone with the best battery life, the OnePlus 15 with its 7,300 mAh battery, was initially available in the States, but OnePlus has since withdrawn from the North American market. Elsewhere, the Xiaomi 17 Max that sports an 8,000 mAh battery was never officially released in the United States. The main problem on this front is that phone manufacturers have to meet strict criteria under federal regulations for transporting lithium cells and batteries. The current limit is 20 Wh, which doesn't leave much leeway, and is the reason why most companies selling in the U.S. limit their batteries to around 5,000mAh. Wait a minute — doesn't the OnePlus 15 technically exceed this limit? After all, isn't 7,300 mAh way over the 20 Wh cap? That's correct. However, OnePlus found a nifty workaround: it switched to a dual-cell battery, and neither of the two exceeds the mandated figures. There's another way to stay legal with batteries, which is what Apple did with the iPhone 18 Max. New iPhones come with firmware that bumps down the capacity below its full watt-hours during transport. The moment users activate the phone, the maximum capacity is unlocked, which technically helps the company stay under the limit. As long as manufacturers implement something similar, Android phones with massive batteries may grace the U.S. market — let's cross our fingers they do.

Learn how strategic “no’s” can accelerate execution, strengthen decision-making, and create the clarity needed to build a faster-growing company. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Early in building my company, I believed momentum came from saying yes: yes to partnerships, yes to investor conversations, yes to every opportunity that looked like scale. It felt productive and ambitious. In reality, it slowed execution and scattered our focus at the exact moment clarity mattered most. One example stands out. While we were still refining product-market fit for our savings and investment app for young families, I spent time pursuing partnerships with large financial institutions. On paper, they looked transformative. In practice, they moved at a completely different pace than we did. Months of meetings, compliance reviews and internal approvals pulled attention away from customers who were already raising their hands. We were chasing future potential while neglecting the traction we already had. That experience reshaped how I think about growth. Momentum comes from disciplined focus, and focus requires saying no far more often than yes. Here’s how to put that into practice. Early on, everything feels urgent, and founders often assume the biggest risk is doing too little. In my experience, the bigger risk is doing too much with limited resources. Every new initiative adds complexity. Every partnership adds coordination. Every feature adds maintenance. Those hidden costs compound, and when everything moves forward at once, nothing moves forward fast. I learned this the hard way. In the early days, I tried to build, hire, partner and fundraise all at once. It felt like progress, but it was really fragmentation. Execution improved only after I started removing distractions. I still use a simple framework at my current company, Mostt. Before committing to anything, I ask three questions: To make the filter stick, score each opportunity from 1 to 3 on each question and write down what you’d have to stop or delay to take it on. If it doesn’t score high on the first two questions, or if you can’t name the trade-off, the answer is no for now. Saying no is easier when it isn’t permanent. Keep a running list of opportunities you’ve turned down, with a note on why and what would need to change for you to revisit them, such as a revenue milestone, a new hire or a later stage. Review it once a quarter. Most items will stay there, but the few worth revisiting will come back at a time when you can actually execute on them. While fundraising, I heard “no” from plenty of potential investors, and almost every no came with advice. Early on, I tried to adjust to every piece of feedback, and it nearly pulled us in too many directions. I had to learn to filter input without losing conviction. My approach was straightforward: look for patterns across multiple investors, consider each person’s expertise and separate feedback about execution from feedback about the core problem. A practical way to do this is to log every piece of investor feedback in one place, tag it by theme and act only on themes that come up from several investors with relevant experience. One-off opinions get noted, not acted on. Saying no applies to capital, too. At one point, an investor offered funding with terms that would have limited our flexibility as operators. We needed the money, and accepting would have relieved short-term pressure. But it would have created long-term constraints. I walked away. That decision meant we had to keep pitching and extend the process, but it protected our ability to grow on our own terms. The wrong capital can slow a company more than delayed capital. Before you take a term sheet, ask: Which terms would limit our decisions as operators, and would we still accept them if we didn’t need the money right now? If the answer is no, treat it as a warning sign. Big-name partnerships create excitement and credibility, but they can also introduce risk if the boundaries are unclear. Looking back, I’d set three rules earlier: Before committing, ask a potential partner how long their approval process typically takes and who makes the final decision. Then compare that timeline to your runway. In my experience, large institutions operate on different timelines and incentives. Optimism helps open doors; realism protects your company once they’re open. Teams move faster when they focus on one or two critical goals instead of juggling 10 competing ones. Some of our strongest growth periods came when we narrowed our focus to one channel, one customer segment and one core problem. That clarity created speed and alignment across the team. Saying no also improves morale. Teams gain confidence when they see progress, while endless pivots, shifting priorities and stretched timelines create confusion and fatigue. To put this into practice, limit your team to no more than three priorities per quarter, write them down where everyone can see them and test every new request against that list. If something new gets added, something else has to come off. Many founders hesitate to say no because they worry about damaging relationships. In practice, clear communication builds more trust than vague commitments. When I decline an opportunity, I follow four steps: Here’s how that can look in practice: “Thank you for thinking of us. We really appreciate the time you put into this. Right now, we’re focused on [your current priority], so we can’t give this the attention it deserves. That’s about our timing, not the opportunity. If it makes sense, I’d love to reconnect in [timeframe] once we’ve hit [milestone].” This approach preserves relationships while protecting your focus, and it signals discipline, which builds credibility over time. Founders often look for an edge in strategy, funding or product. One of the most overlooked advantages is disciplined decision-making. In my experience, the companies that move fastest aren’t the ones doing the most. They’re the ones doing the right things consistently and not letting distractions pull them off course. By Dade Hayes  Business Editor  	The long-gestating merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed Tuesday, yielding a new major player in media.  	Shares in the combined company, Skydance, will start trading later in the day on the New York Stock Exchange. Shares of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery have been discontinued on the Nasdaq.  	The closing brings to an end a year-long saga over who would control two century-old movie studios along with a pedigreed stable of TV studios, streaming services and networks including HBO and CNN. Now, attention will turn to the difficult economics faced by the new company. It starts off with some $80 billion in debt and an ambitious plan to convert a traditional media company into a tech-oriented operation capable of measuring up to Netflix, Amazon and Disney.  	           RELATED: A List Of Major Warner Bros. & Paramount Franchises, Film & TV Titles Coming Together At New Skydance   			Watch on Deadline		       	Larry Ellison, the billionaire co-founder of Oracle, is a key backer of Skydance. His son, David Ellison, an actor-turned-producer who has made a dramatic entrance to the Hollywood corporate scene at just 43 years old, is running the company as chairman and CEO.   	“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” David Ellison said in a statement. “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality. We’re grateful to everyone who made this possible – the employees, creative talent, and production teams of both companies, who worked tirelessly to get us here and inspire audiences around the world every day, as well as the advisors and partners who guided this transaction to completion. Our focus now turns to the future: building a company that empowers creatives, entertains audiences and rewards shareholders. We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.”  	           RELATED: Skydance Bumps Pay, Extends Contracts For Top Execs; New Bonuses For WBD Brass  	Gerry Cardinale, a Skydance board member and key financier via his firm, RedBird Capital, called the merger close “a defining moment for the industry. By applying our owner-operator model to Paramount and WBD’s unmatched portfolio of iconic franchises, premium original programming, and live sports rights, we can protect that legacy while building for a media landscape that’s undergoing transformational change.”  	The merger was set in motion about a year ago when Paramount, soon after combining with the previous incarnation of Skydance, made an unsolicited offer to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. The overture was rebuffed multiple times, and it took more than a dozen attempts for the board of WBD to finally warm up to the deal. Along the way, a bid was accepted from Netflix to acquire just the streaming and studio side of the company. Ultimately, that proposal fell by the wayside when Paramount made its sweetened pitch to buy all of WBD.  	The transaction sailed through regulatory approval, only to hit a major road block in July when the attorneys general of 12 states filed a lawsuit seeking to block the deal on antitrust grounds. The Writers Guild of America filed a similar suit. Thousands of actors, writers, producers and others in the creative community signed a petition opposing the deal. It will likely remain a talking point, especially for high-profile opponents like Mark Ruffalo, who stars in HBO series Task.  	Initially, it appeared that legal and industry objections could have a chance to derail the combination, or at least result in a shrinking of its scale. In the end, though, the AGs agreed to settle the lawsuit with only so-called “behavioral remedies” required under a 5-year consent decree. Skydance agreed to negotiate pay-TV deals for Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery as though they were still separate companies as well as supplying a minimum number of theatrical movie releases, among other concessions.  	Ties between the Ellisons and President Donald Trump have long been scrutinized over the course of the year-long quest for WBD by Paramount, as well as Skydance’s $8.4 billion purchase of Paramount in 2025.   	While Skydance has steadfastly denied it has gone out of its way to appease Trump, critics have questioned the motives behind a series of moves by David Ellison and his senior leadership team. The company, which acquired rights to the UFC mixed-martial-arts circuit last year, broadcast a live match from the White House lawn over the summer. It also acquired the Free Press, a right-leaning digital news outlet, and installed its co-founder, Bari Weiss, as editor-in-chief of CBS News despite her lack of TV experience. Paramount, during the lead-up to the deal, hosted Trump during the White House Correspondents Dinner, and Ellison also paid a visit to his compound in Mar-a-Lago.  	Democratic members of Congress have voiced concerns about the future of CNN, though the consent decree agreed to with the state AGs calls for an editorial oversight board to be installed. RESEARCH STARTER The mathematics of geothermal energy involves the application of various mathematical methods to explore and optimize how geothermal heat from the Earth's interior can be harnessed for energy production and heating. Geothermal energy is derived from the heat generated by the Earth's formation and ongoing radioactive decay, with the temperature increasing significantly with depth, a concept known as the geothermal gradient. High-gradient areas, particularly along tectonic plate boundaries like the Ring of Fire, are prime locations for geothermal energy projects. Mathematicians and engineers utilize models such as LagrangianâEulerian flow models to understand fluid movement and its implications for geothermal reservoirs, while stochastic and geometric models help in optimizing energy extraction processes. Additionally, geothermal heat pump systems have been developed to transfer heat for building heating and cooling, though large-scale water movement can lead to geological concerns such as subsidence. Electricity can also be generated from geothermal resources, with power plants utilizing steam to drive turbines. Despite the advantages of geothermal energy, including its low greenhouse gas emissions and reliability compared to other renewable sources, its adoption has been slow due to perceived limitations in quality sites and the high initial capital costs. Nonetheless, renewed interest in geothermal energy is evident, especially amid global concerns about climate change. Authored by: Churchill, Jason L. 1 of 4 Published in: 2022 2 of 4 3 of 4 4 of 4 SUMMARY: Geothermal energy can be harnessed for domestic heating or to produce electricity via steam turbine. âGeothermalâ refers to heat from the interior of Earth generated from the forces that led to the planetâs creation and the ongoing slow radioactive decay that continues to generate thermal activity. While Earthâs surface is relatively cool, temperatures increase dramatically with depth, which is known as a regionâs âgeothermal gradient.â The interiors of continents tend to have lower gradients than âspreading centerâ regions, where continental tectonic plates are slowly separating. A prime geothermal area is along the Ring of Fire rimming the Pacific Oceanâs eastern, northern, and western coasts. High geothermal gradients make prime candidates for geothermal energy projects. However, the average gradient is approximately 2.5â3 degrees Celsius per 100 meters. Approximately 6000 kilometers beneath the surface, molten rock reaches temperatures of approximately 5000 degrees Celsius. A small portion of this extreme heat makes its way to the surface as steam through cracks and fissures. Geothermal leakage to the surface leads to dramatic volcanic eruptions as well as to the formation of hot springs and geysers. Geothermal-warmed, mineral-rich waters have long been considered to be sacred or to have healing properties by many people. Geysers such as Old Faithful in Yellowstone continue to attract visitors from around the world. Mathematicians, geothermal engineers, geologists, and other scientists use mathematical methods to research various aspects of geothermal processes, such as the deformable, porous properties of soil and rock that allow geothermal heat to make its way to the surface. These studies have broad applications in many scientific areas, including the way brains deform during neurosurgery and in industrial injection molding. In other cases, LagrangianâEulerian flow models, named for Joseph Lagrange and Leonhard Euler, are used to model characteristics such as precipitation and transport, which have applications for engineering geothermal reservoirs and isolating radioactive waste. Stochastic models for system optimization and control as well as geometric models also help mathematicians understand geothermal heat. Many are working on computer models to update, integrate, and expand the U.S. Geological Surveyâs MODFLOW, a three-dimensional finite-difference groundwater flow model first published in 1984 and widely used for research and industrial applications. As long ago as the nineteenth century, scientists and engineers began to develop geothermal-based applications for chemistry and heating, though there is evidence that even prehistoric people built dwellings around naturally occurring geothermal heat sources. With abundant geothermal resources, Iceland began to emerge by the late 1920s as a world leader in the use of geothermal energy for domestic heating and cooling. Advances since that time have led to the development of geothermal heat pump systems. During cold periods, heat pumps transfer to buildings heat from either the ground (beneath the frost line) or from the bottom of ponds. During warm periods, the process is reversed and heat is taken from buildings and put into the ground or ponds. However, purposeful movement of water on a large scale can have geological consequences. For example, in Venice, the removal of subsurface water resulted in subsidence (settling of loose, porous soil), which lowered some buildings. Adding or subtracting water from one part of a geothermal field can affect all aspects of the field, including system pressure and surface vents. Seismologists use mathematical models describing the behavior of deformable porous rock and soil to predict where events like earthquakes might occur as a result of water-pumping activities. Geothermal resources can also be used to produce electricity. The first geothermal electric power plant was built in Larderello, Italy, in 1904. Japan and the United States followed suit in 1910 and 1921, respectively. The spread of geothermal energy has been slow in the decades since. However, because of concerns regarding global warming and a quest to develop nongreenhouse gas (GHG)âemitting energy technologies, geothermal power generation has received more attention. There are two types of geothermal power plants, both of which rely upon the production of steam to drive the conventional turbines that create electricity. Electricity can be produced directly from steam if the temperatures are at a minimum of 95 degrees Celsius (200 degrees Fahrenheit), and higher outputs are possible after temperatures crest at 175 degrees Celsius (350 degrees Fahrenheit). At the Geysers geothermal power plant in California, steam at a temperature of approximately 235 degrees Celsius (455 degrees Fahrenheit) is used to directly drive turbines. At lower temperatures, geothermal heat can still be used, but it relies upon specialized fluids that have a low boiling point capable of producing high pressures, rather than natural steam. While the capital costs are high for both types of geothermal electricity, once in production it has several advantages over other forms of electricity generation. Like wind, its fuel costs are negligible. Similar to wind and nuclear power, once constructed, geothermal plants produce far fewer GHG emissions than traditional fossil fuel plants. Geothermal also has advantages over other alternative energy producers. Unlike wind, which is intermittent because of its dependency on weather conditions, geothermal electricity can be relied upon to produce consistent baseload power. Geothermal plants are also less intrusive visually than large wind farms and tend to draw less public attention. Geothermal also has two key advantages over nuclear generation. Nuclear power plants are dependent upon a finite resource (uranium), and nuclear waste disposal is both controversial and costly. In contrast, geothermal generation depends on a virtually infinite source (heat generated in Earthâs interior), and there are no long-term waste issues. Popular and government interest in geothermal energy and its advantages over both traditional and alternative electricity generating options led to a 20% increase in global geothermal electricity production between 2005 and 2010. In addition, there has been a 52% increase from 2007 to 2010 in the number of countries developing geothermal resources. Despite the increasing numbers, geothermal energy production continues to significantly lag behind other electricity sources at the start of the twenty-first century. In part, this lag is the result of a perception that there are a limited number of high-quality geothermal sites that would enable geothermal energy to become a major producer. In addition, there are technical, permitting, and electric transmission issues that drive up capital costs and inhibit substantial expansion. Bundschuh, Jochen, and Mario SuÃ¡rez. It's no secret that the last 12 months have been terrible for buying PC hardware. From RAM and SSDs to graphics cards, everything has reached record prices, thanks to the global silicon shortage. CPUs, however, haven't seen major price hikes, which remains a silver lining for those looking for an upgrade. However, the total platform cost that comes with it has spoiled the party for DDR5 enthusiasts. Those of you already using a previous-gen, DDR4-based system can instead look toward AM4 and LGA 1700 processors. These CPUs are compatible with the DDR4 RAM you already have in your rig, and they aren't bad buys by any definition. At the right price, whether brand-new or pre-owned, these "old" CPUs can be great drop-in upgrades for both modern gaming and productivity. CXMT is playing by the same rules as Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron The recently relaunched Ryzen 7 5800X3D remains both iconic and powerful even in 2026. The first chip to truly show the potential of AMD's 3D V-Cache, the Ryzen 7 5800X3D still trades blows with modern 6-core chips from Team Red. Despite chips like the Ryzen 7 7800X3D and 9800X3D handily beating it in gaming performance, the Ryzen 7 5800X3D is still a decent pick for AM4 users. If you're switching from any Ryzen 1000, 2000, or 3000 CPU, then the Ryzen 7 5800X3D will deliver a massive boost to your framerates. Most AM4 motherboards can support this chip with a BIOS update, allowing you to upgrade your PC without paying for a new motherboard and RAM kit. The only caveat is the price. The Ryzen 7 5800X3D has shot up on the used market with listings exceeding $400. Instead, a brand-new 10th-anniversary edition of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D can be bought for around $350 on multiple ecommerce platforms (at the time of writing). It's not a small investment, especially on a dead platform, but it's certainly cheaper than a full platform upgrade, which probably won't outperform the Ryzen 7 5800X3D anyway. AMD's Ryzen 7 5800X3D is the company's first gaming CPU with 3D V-Cache, which adds a ton of L3 cache for even better gaming performance. It's on the older AM4 platform, but is still a potent gaming chip. Outside of edge cases, it didn't make a noticeable difference. This 12-core, 24-thread processor is 6 years old at this point, but that doesn't mean it's automatically outdated. If gaming isn't your primary concern, the Ryzen 9 5900X should be on your radar, especially if you want to save a few bucks. This workstation chip still packs a punch in productivity workloads, and is obviously no slouch in gaming either. While it launched at $550 in 2020, you can find it on eBay for around $250 today. That's a steal for a CPU of this caliber, and it can last you for a while. The upgraded model, i.e., the 16-core, 32-thread Ryzen 9 5900XT, is regularly available for around $300 if you want something even more powerful.  These CPUs are still worth buying today. For those of you who want an affordable upgrade over your existing AM4 chip, the Ryzen 7 5700X is undoubtedly one of the best options. I've been using this chip for over four years now, and it hasn't let me down. I've paired it with the RTX 3080, and it has allowed me to enjoy the latest AAA games at smooth framerates at 1440p. This 8-core, 16-thread CPU has a meager 65W TDP despite being a decent productivity chip. Using PBO, you can extract the most out of it, and I've been able to overclock it for some extra juice, too. Its gaming performance is almost identical to that of the Ryzen 5 5600X, but it's possible to buy it at the same price, too. If the difference is significant, then I'd advise going for the 6-core chip. Used models are currently a no-go for the Ryzen 7 5700X, since they cost as much as buying it new on Amazon. The AMD Ryzen 7 5700X is an excellent processor with 8 Cores and 16 processing threads that provide plenty of power and speed.  Modern 6-core CPUs have everything I'll ever need from my PC You don't need the Ryzen 7 5800X3D to enjoy AMD's 3D V-Cache in your games. The significantly cheaper Ryzen 5 5600X3D provides virtually the same performance as the Ryzen 7 5700X3D, and sits just below the Ryzen 7 5800X3D. If you want a gaming-focused chip without spending over $300, the Ryzen 5 5600X3D can be had for just $220 (at the time of writing). It's relatively harder to find, but you can try your luck on Micro Center and Amazon. The Ryzen X3D magic fails to impress with budget and mid-range GPUs Intel's 13th and 14th Gen processors were mired in controversy due to an infamous bug causing high voltages, which dealt lasting damage to the silicon. The older 12th Gen chips, however, were Intel's comeback as Alder Lake showed what a hybrid core architecture could do. The Core i5-12400F was one of the best gaming CPUs when it launched, and 4 years later, it's certainly not old.  The 6-core, 12-thread CPU (no E-cores) is as fast as the Ryzen 5 5600X in gaming, and costs the same on the used market ($125–$150). It's a starter 12th Gen chip, so it only makes sense for those building a budget PC from scratch. This means buying a cheap LGA 1700 DDR4 motherboard and 16GB/32GB of RAM, but at least you won't have to shell out a small fortune for DDR5 memory. And you have the option of swapping your motherboard for a DDR5 model while retaining the CPU.  The upcoming Nova Lake CPUs are set to launch on a long-lasting LGA 1954 socket The Core i7-12700KF is a 12-core workhorse on the same LGA 1700 platform, providing capable multithread performance while slightly beating chips like the Ryzen 9 5900X. Whether it's gaming or productivity you want on an Intel system, the Core i7-12700KF won't disappoint. At the time of writing, it's still available brand-new for around $220 on sites like Amazon.  This 8 P-core, 4 E-core chip is powerful enough to last you a few more years while you wait for the market to settle down. When it does, you can consider buying a DDR5 motherboard and RAM kit for a sweet performance boost. LGA 1700 is a dead platform, just like AM4, but that doesn't mean it's useless in 2026.  The Intel Core i7-12700KF is one of the best processors for this job. It's a step above the 12600K and even matches the general performance of 12900K CPU at a relatively affordable price. Your 5-year-old CPU isn't "old" for gaming It's not the right time to shop for new CPUs that require selling your kidney to afford a DDR5 memory kit. Instead, upgrading to a capable AM4 CPU or building around an LGA 1700 chip can save you money without a massive drop in performance. There's no lack of options on either platform, and those with an already compatible PC need only a good deal on an older CPU to avoid the inflated PC hardware market. We want to hear from you. Luke Hartley realized how important Elon Musk's Starlink was to him when it fell overboard. Two weeks into his voyage across the Pacific in October 2023, Hartley's sailboat, Songbird, was hit by an intense squall that knocked the Starlink dish balanced on the front of the boat over the side. It was a major blow for the music teacher turned sailing influencer, who tells me he made far more money posting about his three-year voyage around the world on TikTok via Starlink than he ever had in the US education system. Without satellite internet, he had no way to upload the videos that were funding his voyage, check weather forecasts, or call his family. From the remote Pacific to the front lines of Ukraine, Starlink's network of orbital internet satellites has become indispensable to 13 million people in more than 167 countries. Starlink accounted for more than 60% of the $18.6 billion in revenue SpaceX generated last year, and was the only part of the business to turn a profit. Musk has grander ambitions for the flying crown jewels in his empire. The company plans to launch tens of thousands more satellites in the coming years as it targets new markets, in a push to transform Starlink from a boutique service for rugged survivalists into the world's premier wireless carrier and broadband provider. Many users who like it love it, and have flooded social media with praise for Musk and his creation. Beyond the profits, Starlink has also provided Musk a vital source of influence and soft power that stretches the globe. The world's richest man's attempt to gut government bureaucracy with DOGE, his massive political donations, and his erratic and incendiary posting habits on X have cost him Tesla customers and inspired boycotts and protests against his other companies. But Starlink is so useful in far-flung and war-torn places — and has so few alternatives — that it has granted Musk a rare level of immunity to political gravity. It's also left governments, adventurers, and digital nomads struggling to reconcile their reliance on the technology with the controversies that swirl around Musk. "We can criticize Musk till the cows come home, but it's an incredible product," says Hartley, who has mixed feelings about depending so heavily on Starlink. "It has a very controversial name behind it, but it is also a way for me to talk to my mom and inspire folks. Both things can be true." Nowhere is this dance between reluctance and reliance more delicately choreographed than in Ukraine, where Starlink has been essential in the war against Russia. Starlink satellites have been widely adopted across the Ukrainian military as a comms system that cannot be hacked or jammed by Russian radio warfare. The service has allowed ground teams to adapt their targets mid-mission and remotely control drones with flawless video almost to the moment of impact, with no need for giant antennas that could reveal their position. The technological advantage has come at the price of giving a mercurial CEO the power to tilt the balance of the war. In 2023, Musk sparked global headlines when he revealed he refused a request to activate Starlink to assist a Ukrainian assault on Crimea because he was concerned that "SpaceX would be explicitly complicit in a major act of war." The billionaire also threatened to stop supplying Ukraine with Starlink terminals the year prior over a funding dispute, and Reuters reported last July that he jeopardized a 2022 Ukrainian counteroffensive by cutting Starlink access to frontline troops. Musk did not respond to the report, but he previously said in a March 2025 X post that he would never turn off Ukrainian terminals or use the threat of doing so as a bargaining chip, no matter how much he disagreed with the country's government. More recently, Musk has given Ukraine an edge. In February of this year, SpaceX clamped down on Russian forces' illicit use of Starlink terminals after Ukraine's then-defense minister made a personal appeal to Musk. The cutoff severely disrupted Russia's military and allowed Ukraine to retake valuable territory. Some servicemembers and researchers say Ukraine's dependent yet unstable relationship with Starlink leaves them uneasy. "If you are military and you're operating a drone, you cannot rely on something unpredictable. All the systems should be under control," says one drone pilot and sergeant in Ukraine's unmanned brigades. "But we have no alternative right now," he adds. Alessio Terzi, an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge's Bennett School of Public Policy, tells me that governments risk entering a "Faustian pact" with Musk that would see the billionaire decide how, when, and where its citizens and militaries access the internet. He said that the closest analogy for this level of geopolitical power is not pre-war titans of industry like Henry Ford and Thomas Edison but the East India Company, the British trading conglomerate that ruled over much of the Indian subcontinent. The company was granted exclusive rights to operate the trade routes between Asia and Britain in 1600. It leveraged that monopoly to grow into a quasi-empire with its own system of taxation and standing army that ruled over millions for nearly three centuries. Terzi says that SpaceX's market share of everything sent into space — close to 80% in 2025 — outstrips the East India Company's share of global shipping at its peak. He adds that Musk and SpaceX are leveraging their own monopoly over satellite communication to act more like a sovereign state than a private company. "This is a mega-company that is chipping away at some roles that would normally fall on the government," says Terzi. When Musk first announced plans for Starlink in 2015, launching internet satellites was an ambitious side quest. At the time, SpaceX's main mission was to lower the cost of launching cargo into space by perfecting its Falcon rocket, which could be partially reused over multiple flights rather than self-destructing on impact. One former SpaceX employee said that SpaceX initially based its Starlink division in Redmond, Washington, in part to avoid distracting employees working on Falcon at the company's main facilities in Texas and California. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. By 2020, however, Starlink was at the center of SpaceX's plans. That year, Musk suggested the satellite internet service could become a $30 billion-a-year cash cow. The company spun up a production line for Starlink user terminals in a corner of its Hawthorne, California, facility that was so far away from the main campus that early employees bought bikes to travel from one side to the other. The bikes were regularly stolen, another former employee said. In typical SpaceX fashion, the production line quickly expanded, the former employee said, so much so that it spilled out into unfinished buildings with compacted dirt floors. Musk took a hands-on approach to the project, the person added, including telling employees to contact him if they encountered any roadblocks and providing technical feedback on new versions of the terminal. "If his internet was down, then we were in trouble," the former employee said. In Starlink's early days, Musk framed it as an effort to "rebuild the internet" into a space-based network that would eliminate lag while reaching the estimated 42 million Americans with no access to broadband internet. It had the added bonus, Musk said, of providing a steady stream of revenue to pay for SpaceX's Mars colonization efforts. Musk's rivals are also chasing this vision. Jeff Bezos' Amazon and Paris-based Eutelsat OneWeb have attempted to build their own satellite constellations, but the dominance of SpaceX's rocket business — the company launched its Falcon 9 rocket 165 times last year, more rockets than the rest of the world combined — gives it a steep advantage. When Amazon put 24 of its Project Kuiper (now Leo) satellites into orbit last October, they traveled on a SpaceX rocket. Recently, Musk has gone from describing Starlink as cheap internet for rural communities to something more fundamental: an oxygen source for an AI-saturated world. In SpaceX's August 2026 earnings call, Musk speculated that demand for Starlink would skyrocket as it became the connectivity network for fleets of robotaxis and armies of humanoid robots. (Tesla has already begun outfitting its Cybercab robotaxis with Starlink dishes.) Beyond the financial success Starlink has afforded Musk, it has also become a useful tool for him and SpaceX to help people in need, which can also generate positive headlines. The company regularly offers Starlink for free in countries hit by natural disasters and it waived fees for Starlink access in Iran during a government crackdown on protests. SpaceX has also used Starlink discounts to defuse the data center backlash that has spread across the US. The rocket giant's Colossus data centers in Memphis and nearby Southaven, Mississippi, have attracted opposition and lawsuits from local residents complaining about noise and pollution from the gas generators powering the sites. SpaceX responded in June by offering residents in Memphis 50% off Starlink for their "partnership and support." SpaceX extended the same offer to residents of rural Vermilion Parish in Louisiana, where it is building a $100 billion spaceport that will eventually support thousands of Starship flights a year. Musk's ambitions for the service are growing more galactic. In SpaceX's August earnings call, he predicted that Starlink could provide the majority of the world's internet within the next 10 years. One area where Starlink has already become a must-have is in the air. Executives said on the call that in-flight WiFi powered by Starlink, which has been adopted by more than 40 airlines, has become so popular that some passengers — including YouTube influencer Mr Beast — are booking short-haul flights instead of going direct because they have Starlink. The satellite internet service has become a major selling point for airlines that offer it and a headache for those who don't. United Airlines has used its Starlink in-flight WiFi to try and woo Delta loyalty flyers, after Delta picked Amazon's Leo for its fleet. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell signaled on the call that the company plans to turn its mobile service into a full-fledged mobile carrier that will aggressively target AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. "I anticipate us to be able to acquire quite a few of their customers because I think our service will be better," she said. To take on the telecoms, SpaceX is planning to fill the heavens with a lot more Starlink satellites. The company has submitted proposals to regulators to launch 100,000 of its V3 Starlink satellites, which are larger units that can only be launched on SpaceX's massive Starship rocket. Analysts say that this proliferation won't be enough to take on the likes of AT&T. Tim Farrar, president at technology consultancy TMF Associates, tells me that while low-earth orbit satellites are great at providing coverage to remote and rural areas, they struggle to provide service in densely populated cities. As they whiz around the planet at 17,000 miles an hour, Starlink's satellites spend a small fraction of their time in orbit over these areas, and far more time crossing large uninhabited expanses of ocean and wilderness. Pierre Lionnet, a space economist, says that as the company launches more satellites to try to meet rising demand in urban areas, the amount of capacity being wasted will increase, shrinking SpaceX's margins. "The problem of growing this capacity is that it means that the same satellite will spend a larger amount of time circling the earth in areas where there is no additional demand," he says. Lionnet estimates that the company would be unlikely to turn a profit on a 100,000-strong network of Starlink satellites at the current cost of launching cargo into orbit. SpaceX is working hard to bring that cost down with Starship, its most advanced rocket, which executives estimate will reduce launch costs by 10 times compared to the Falcon 9. In September, SpaceX hit a major milestone for Starship when it deployed working Starlink V3 satellites into orbit for the first time. Until Starship can ramp up to full commercial operation, SpaceX will face pressure to maximize revenue from the satellite capacity they do have, Lionnet says. That means adding new enterprise customers, such as governments and airlines, and launching Starlink in new countries. Global expansion gives Musk new soft power opportunities, but also risks entangling other parts of his business empire in geopolitics. Following the example of Ukraine and the US government — for which SpaceX has built Starshield, a secure military version of Starlink — other nations are looking closely at Starlink for military purposes. In July, Taiwan changed foreign ownership rules that previously collapsed negotiations with SpaceX to bring Starlink to the island nation. Phoebe Pham, a researcher at Taiwan's state-backed Institute for National Defense and Security Research, says that low-earth orbit satellite internet networks like Starlink would be critical for the country in the event of a conflict with China, which views Taiwan as a breakaway province. Some military analysts have predicted that in an assault on Taiwan, China would likely cut the undersea cables that provide internet to the island and launch a barrage of cyberattacks against the island's communications infrastructure. For the Taiwanese government, Starlink would provide a backup network for military and civilian comms that would be exceptionally hard for China to jam. "It would be wrong to say they're not looking at lessons learned from Ukraine," Pham says. In Taiwan, government approval or adoption of Starlink could be complicated by Musk's business interests in China and his previous comments about Taiwanese independence. He suggested in 2022 that the island become a "special administrative zone" similar to Hong Kong and described Taiwan as an "integral part" of China in 2023. Tesla has operated a giant EV factory in Shanghai since 2019, and around a fifth of the automaker's revenue last year came from the Chinese market. Pham says that if Starlink applied to operate in Taiwan, the government would have to weigh the risk that Musk's business interests in China could be used as "potential leverage." It could seek to avoid giving Musk the kind of unilateral decision-making power he has enjoyed in Ukraine, she added. "The question is, who makes these decisions about the activation and coverage?" she says. Starlink has also run into geopolitical roadblocks in India. In June, Bloomberg reported that officials hit the brakes on the service's long-awaited launch after raising concerns over reports from local Iranian media that Starlink kits were being used in Iran, despite a state-mandated block on internet access during the conflict with the US and Israel. SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer said in response to Bloomberg's report that the company remained in "active and productive discussions" about bringing Starlink to India, adding that SpaceX had set up a bespoke deployment model for operating Starlink in the country. Ukraine is now exploring alternative methods for frontline communications. A senior figure at a company manufacturing drones for the country's military says Ukraine is planning for the day Starlink goes offline, whether because Musk has pulled the plug or as a result of direct Russian attacks on Starlink's satellites. "Hopefully, it will not happen tomorrow. But if it happens in a year, Ukraine will be ready," the person says. "Every army should prepare for this scenario because it's not just a question if Elon Musk will shut it down. In the military, you always need to have backup options for connectivity. Otherwise, you may lose everything." Are you using Starlink? Twenty-four feet sounds like a constraint until Dragon Tiny Homes shows you what fits inside. Dragon Tiny Homes has built its reputation on that idea, and its updated Vista 24′ makes the strongest case yet that compact living doesn’t have to mean compromising on the essentials. Sitting on a double-axle trailer and stretching 24 ft (7.3 m) in length, the Vista 24′ occupies a sweet spot between the nimble European models gaining traction globally and the larger builds that dominate the North American market. Hitch it to a Ford F-350 and the home becomes genuinely mobile — a place that follows you rather than roots you. The exterior sets the tone immediately: green and white-painted timber cladding, a metal roof, and generous glazing that keeps the structure feeling open rather than boxy. Designer: Dragon Tiny Homes        Step inside and the 204 sq ft (19 sq m) interior greets you with shiplap walls and vinyl flooring — materials that read warm without demanding fuss. The living room is anchored by a sofa, a projector, and a pull-down screen, turning what could have been dead wall space into something genuinely functional. A staircase nearby pulls double duty, housing storage within its structure, while an electric fireplace and a mini-split unit handle climate year-round. The kitchen is where Dragon Tiny Homes has made the clearest argument for full-time livability. It’s generous by tiny home standards — a sink, an oven, an induction cooktop, a fridge/freezer, a washer/dryer, a pantry, and upper cabinetry all find a place here. It’s the kind of kitchen that invites actual cooking rather than survival-mode meal prep. The bathroom, compact and straightforward, covers the necessities: a walk-in shower, a sink, and a flushing toilet.        Two lofts define the sleeping arrangement. The main bedroom sits above the living room, accessed via the storage staircase, and fits a double bed with safety railings along its edge. The secondary loft, reached by a removable ladder, is smaller but thoughtfully finished — a storage area and what appears to be a Kallax-style unit serve as a natural room divider, offering privacy without construction. At $66,750, the Vista 24′ is priced within reach for buyers serious about the lifestyle shift. Dragon Tiny Homes offers delivery across the continental United States, with rates depending on location. It won’t suit everyone — no tiny home does — but for those ready to trade square footage for freedom, this updated Vista makes a compelling, well-considered case.
