Stocks Skipped the Midterm Blues. Will the Post-Election Rally Be Smaller? Stocks rose on Tuesday, pushing the S&P 500 to an all-time high. And many investors seem to expect even better days ahead, especially once the midterms are in the review mirror. But those of you counting on next year’s stock market to deliver the usual post-midterm bounty may discover that Wall Street has already helped itself to part of the feast. It’s easy to see why many investors expect good times ahead. The historical record of the stock market’s performance following midterm elections is impressive. Every midterm election since 1946 has been followed by a positive one-year return for the S&P 500. The average gain was 14.4 percent. With November 3 approaching, that is an inviting number to pencil into expectations for the next twelve months. The trouble is that the usual weakness preceding those gains has been conspicuously absent. Midterm years generally have been the disappointing stretch of the presidential cycle. BlackRock puts their average annual stock market return at 7.5 percent, against 12.4 percent in other years. Election anxiety has often accompanied a difficult summer, followed by a rally beginning roughly a month before the vote. U.S. Bank’s study of 31 midterm cycles from 1900 to 2025 puts the average return in the 12 months before a midterm at 2.9 percent, against 8.9 percent for all years in that sample and 12.4 percent in the 12 months after. Since 1980, the performance has been stronger on both sides of the election, about 8.7 percent before and 17.5 percent after, but the gap remains. Fidelity’s analysts looked at the period following the Second World War and found a roughly five percent gain in the year ahead of the midterm versus about 14.5 percent after. Those pre-election gains mask what tends to be a rough summer. Longview Economics finds an average peak-to-trough drawdown of about 19 percent in the year before the election, across 25 cycles since 1926. Even setting aside elections close to a recession, most still had a stock market correction of more than 10 percent, and several exceeded 20 percent. And usually, the sell-off occurs in the summer months prior to the election. This year we seemed to have skipped the summertime blues. The S&P 500 returned 12.7 percent, including dividends, through September. The comparable midterm-year average since 1950 was just 0.9 percent. BlackRock also documents unusually quiet trading: only four daily moves of at least two percent in either direction through August, compared with 20 during 2018 and 46 during 2022. A relief rally presumably works best when investors first experience something requiring relief. That matters because the explanations for post-midterm strength often depend on the unpleasantness that comes before it. The leading theory is that uncertainty about congressional control makes investors demand extra compensation for holding stocks. That depresses prices. As polls clarify the likely outcome and voting settles the question, the uncertainty discount shrinks and share prices rise. A 2021 paper in the Journal of Financial Economics found evidence consistent with this mechanism. The election helps by resolving uncertainty, whatever the partisan outcome. But a strong, comparatively calm market gives us less reason to expect a large release of pent-up anxiety this time. An election surprise could still move stock prices. The historical sequence, however, has already missed an important step. Another explanation is simpler: some of the celebrated post-midterm rally is a rebound. Stocks entering autumn after a punishing decline have more ground to recover. The subsequent gains get counted as election-cycle returns even when falling inflation, improving earnings, or the end of a bear market deserves much of the credit. Since 1950, when stocks were already higher through September of a midterm year, the following fifteen months — October of the election year through December of the next — delivered an average total return of 25.4 percent. Following losing starts, the average was 37.7 percent. Both were substantial gains, but the weaker entries produced considerably larger recoveries. That is a longer window than the 14.4 percent figure, and it shows why a single average can obscure the difference between buying after losses and buying after gains. The third explanation concerns political incentives. Presidents supposedly get painful decisions out of the way early and favor economic support as the next presidential election approaches. That could help stocks in year three, although it depends on actual policy and economic conditions. In theory, none of this should happen at all. The midterms, after all, always resolve pre-election uncertainty. So investors should anticipate that and price it in without waiting for the election to occur. Similarly, investors anticipating a post-election rebound should price that in pre-election. At the very least, the recurrence of the pattern of a post-election boost should eventually make the pattern so well-expected that it doesn’t happen at all. And there’s a hint that reality may finally be catching up to theory. We did have a sell-off this year; but it came early, running from January 27 to March 30. The S&P fell by around nine percent. This might have been investors selling in anticipation of the summertime blues. If that’s right, the recent strength of the stock market could be the typical post-election rally pulled forward. The lack of volatility could be a sign that investors have been correctly pricing the usual seasonality — which ironically eliminates it. None of this requires the post-midterm winning streak to end. After strong entries, the next year has still finished higher. It does suggest that investors should distinguish a history of positive returns from an expectation of unusually large ones. This year’s strength has reduced the room for a recovery, while its calm raises questions about the size of any election relief. Stocks can keep climbing on stronger profits and economic growth. But investors awaiting the customary electoral exhale should consider how little breath the market appears to be holding. The LG CNS partnership gives Securitize a foothold as the Seoul prepares new rules for tokenized stocks, bonds and funds beginning in February 2027. Shares of tokenization platform Securitize rallied sharply on Tuesday after the company announced a partnership with South Korean technology company LG CNS as the country prepares to introduce a new framework for tokenized securities. Securitize (SECZ) rose nearly 8% in early Tuesday trading to around $12.60, outperforming most major crypto-linked stocks, before pulling back later in the morning. The company began trading on the New York Stock Exchange in July after completing its merger with special purpose acquisition company Cantor Equity Partners II. Securitize Corp (SECZ) stock. Source: Yahoo Finance Securitize and LG CNS signed a memorandum of understanding to develop tokenized assets and digital asset infrastructure for South Korean financial institutions. The companies said the partnership will explore tokenized funds, stocks and stablecoins, while also identifying opportunities across the broader Asia-Pacific market. The agreement comes as South Korea prepares to implement a new framework for tokenized securities. Last week, the country’s Financial Services Commission proposed rules governing the issuance and circulation of tokenized stocks, bonds, funds and other securities, with the framework set to take effect in February 2027. The partnership potentially gives Securitize an early foothold in South Korea as financial institutions prepare for the new regime. LG CNS also launched a blockchain infrastructure platform on Tuesday designed to help banks and other financial companies support stablecoins and tokenized securities. Related: Securitize, Cantor target tokenized IPOs for public markets Securitize has become a major player in the tokenized real-world asset market, which has grown to roughly $40 billion. Much of the early growth centered on US Treasurys, private credit and other yield-bearing assets, but tokenized stocks are beginning to gain ground. The market for tokenized stocks has repeatedly hit record highs as exchanges and financial institutions explore bringing traditional equities onchain. Tokenized equities were valued at roughly $3.2 billion, up 10.6% over the past 30 days, according to RWA.xyz data. Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo has argued that even modest adoption could have a much larger impact on crypto markets. Speaking at ETHConf in July, Domingo said tokenized stocks could help push the overall crypto market to a $5 trillion valuation. The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE carves out a niche with its 6.7-inch display and $700 price point, but it's not the best value. With drawbacks limiting the screen and camera system, you might be better off choosing a cheaper midranger or seeking out a discounted flagship instead. However, with a flagship chip and One UI 9 out of the box, the Galaxy S26 FE certainly has its perks.  Samsung's Exynos 2500 chipset is decent 6.7-inch display is larger than most midrangers One UI 9 and Android 17, plus seven years of OS upgrades Relatively thin and light Screen lacks uniform bezels and high peak brightness levels Rear camera system is weak outside of the 50MP primary shooter Slow 15W wireless charging; no Qi2 magnets Starts at 128GB storage  Why you can trust Android Central     Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.  To get the cheapest Samsung or Google flagship in 2026, you'll need to choose a smaller phone. The Samsung Galaxy S26, for instance, is a 6.3-inch smartphone. If you want to splurge for a 6.7-inch display, you'll need to pay $1,200 for the Galaxy S26 Plus. That's $200 more than than the Galaxy S25 Plus went for, and $100 more than the Galaxy S26 Plus originally cost when it launched in March. Phones with large screens are expensive, in other words — but the Samsung Galaxy S26 FE is an outlier. It offers the same 6.7-inch screen size as the Galaxy S26 Plus for $500 less, and it's worth your attention for that reason alone. I've used the Galaxy S26 FE for weeks, and it's closer to flagship territory than you may think. But it also makes a handful of cost-cutting measures to hit that attractive $700 price point, and other phones provide a better value.      Samsung's "Fan Edition" phones have always been in a tough spot in terms your wallet will understand. They're typically priced well above Google's midrange A-series models, as well as Samsung's own A-series phones. They're cheaper than Galaxy S series phones, but not by a whole lot. Further complicating matters is that the Galaxy FE phones have a screen size matching the Plus model of the Galaxy S lineup, making them attractive to people who want a larger display. This year, the Galaxy S26 FE ships with a $50 price hike. That might not raise alarm bells considering the rising prices around the industry, but it should. The Google Pixel 11 and Samsung Galaxy S26 each saw a $100 price increase this year, and buyers get double the base storage in exchange. The Galaxy S26 FE, by comparison, still comes with the same 128GB of storage as standard. If you want to match the 256GB storage of the rest of the Galaxy S26 series, get ready to pay $100 more for a Galaxy S26 FE. The 128GB model costs $699.99 and the 256GB version costs $799.99. This creates a puzzling lineup where the midrange Galaxy S26 FE and the flagship Galaxy S26 both launched at the exact same price, provided you got 256GB of storage for both. Samsung retroactively raised Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Plus prices, and the base model now costs $999.99. That does give the Galaxy S26 FE a better value proposition, but only slightly. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android I'm starting off with pricing because it's the most important thing about the Galaxy S26 FE. As you'll learn throughout this review, Samsung's new midranger is as solid as ever, and it beats the Galaxy S25 FE in performance. However, it has the base Galaxy S26 and cheaper Android midrangers like the Google Pixel 10a and the OnePlus 13R breathing down its neck. Category Galaxy S26 FE Processor Samsung Exynos 2500 Memory 8GB RAM Operating System One UI 9, Android 17 Display 6.7-inch AMOLED, 120Hz, 1,900 nits peak brightness Battery 4,900mAh Charging 45W wired, 15W wireless Dimensions 161.6 x 76.9 x 7.4 mm Weight 193g  Rear cameras 50MP wide, 8MP telephoto, 12MP ultrawide Front camera 12MP wide View Original View Original View Original From a design perspective, the Galaxy S26 FE shares a few similarities with the Galaxy S26 Plus; it's only a millimeter thicker and three grams heavier. Due to the larger bezels, the Galaxy S26 FE has a bigger overall footprint. Reachability is a bit of an issue due to the form factor, as it's both wider and taller than the Galaxy S26 Plus. On the back, the key difference is the glossy Gorilla Glass Victus Plus. I prefer the matte look and feel of the Galaxy S26 Plus back, and that phone has newer Gorilla Glass Victus 2. But the colors for the Galaxy S26 FE are gorgeous. I reviewed the subtle Pistachio model, but you can also get the phone in Blueberry or Graphite colorways. The Galaxy S26 FE uses a mix of glass and aluminum for materials, and it's IP68 certified against dust and water ingress. I had no problems with durability, and you shouldn't either. The device feels more premium compared to midrange phones with plastic backs, like the Pixel 10a.      The Galaxy S26 FE finds a niche thanks to its 6.7-inch display. It's the same size as the one on the Galaxy S26 Plus, albeit with a lower 1080p resolution. The screen isn't perfect — it has larger bezels, and more importantly, they aren't uniform. The Galaxy S26 FE has a "chin," and the lack of a consistent bezel size is unsightly to my eyes. The chin has long been a sign you're looking at a Samsung budget or midrange phone compared to a flagship, and I think Samsung could've changed this by now. Google's midrange phone, the Pixel 10a, is cheaper and has uniform bezels.      Bezel talk aside, the Galaxy S26 FE isn't nearly as bright as its flagship counterparts. The phone has a peak brightness of 1,900 nits, whereas the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Plus top out at 2,600 nits. In practice, this means the Galaxy S26 FE won't be as easy to see outdoors. Without an anti-reflective coating, something becoming more popular on flagships, this phone is tricky to view in direct sunlight. Otherwise, the display feels responsive with a 120Hz refresh rate. It's a fine panel for the price, even if there is clear room for improvement here. This is the exact same display we saw on the Galaxy S25 FE, and the Galaxy S24 FE for that matter. If you have one of these older phones, the Galaxy S26 FE's screen isn't a reason to upgrade.      Samsung's midrange phones have come a long way in a few short years in terms of performance. As a refresher, the Galaxy S24 FE had an Exynos 2400e chip and the Galaxy S25 FE got the boost to the regular Exynos 2400 chip. This year, the Galaxy S26 FE runs on the Exynos 2500. It's a mobile processor built on a 3nm process (a major improvement over the 4nm Exynos 2400) that recently powered flagships like the Galaxy Z Flip 7 worldwide. I tested the Galaxy Z Flip 7 firsthand, so I expected the Galaxy S26 FE to be a strong performer. I didn't expect for Samsung to pull so much extra power out of the Exynos 2500 for the Galaxy S26 FE. In the benchmark results below, you'll see the Galaxy S26 FE not only handily beat the Galaxy Z Flip 7, but also crush Google's Tensor G4-powered Pixel 10a. Geekbench 6 (single-core / multi-core) Geekbench AI (quantized score) 3DMark Wild Life Extreme (score / fps) Samsung Galaxy S26 FE (Exynos 2500) 2,362 / 7,848 4,643 5,253 / 31.46 Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 7 (Exynos 2500) 1,849 / 6,822 3,581 4,400 / 26.35 Google Pixel 10a (Tensor G4) 1,707 / 4,512 3,109 2,667 / 15.97 I'm surprised that Samsung is doing that with only 8GB memory onboard the Galaxy S26 FE. The Galaxy S26 FE ships with Android 17 and will get seven years of full Android OS support. Despite the RAM limitations, this phone will be a strong performer for a very long time. The battery life is rock solid, too. It has the same 4,900mAh capacity as the Galaxy S26 Plus, but the Galaxy S26 FE's lower-resolution display and weaker chip combine to hep you squeeze a longer runtime out of it. The charging, unfortunately, is still too slow. The 45W wired speeds are fine, but 15W wireless charging is disappointing when the Qi2.2 25W standard exists.      It's worth revisiting the storage options. The Galaxy S26 FE ships with 128GB of storage by default, and you can upgrade it to 256GB or 512GB at the time of purchase. I think 128GB of storage is starting to stretch users thin because of growing app and operating system sizes. But if you upgrade the Galaxy S26 FE to 256GB or 512GB storage, you end up paying flagship prices for a midrange phone. It's quite the dilemma, and one Samsung could've avoided by making 256GB standard, like the Galaxy S26 series. If you're fine with a 128GB phone, the Galaxy A57 is lurking in the corner at $599.99, but it does come with additional compromises.      Samsung isn't one to upgrade its phone cameras often, and the Galaxy S26 FE is no exception. It's using the same 50MP primary shooter, 8MP telephoto, and 12MP ultrawide lens we've seen on prior generations of Galaxy FE phones. The selfie camera is a 12MP, f/2.2 lens. The telephoto only goes up to 3x optical zoom, but you may find digital zoom to produce passable results beyond that. The 50MP sensor at the heart of the Galaxy S26 FE's rear camera system packs enough detail, and low-light performance is impressive. Tech > Services & Software > AI The chatbot that launched 1,000 chatbots: We cover everything about the AI tool, from how it works and how to use it to some of its more controversial points. Contributor Contributor October 6, 2026, 8:45 am ET OpenAI is considering adding parental controls and other safety features to ChatGPT. ChatGPT is the artificial intelligence chatbot that brought generative AI into the mainstream. Launched in November 2022 by OpenAI, the company co-founded by Sam Altman, ChatGPT quickly became the most popular AI application, and the one everyone tried to emulate and one-up.  Since then, all the big tech players have joined the generative AI race. Perplexity, Meta AI, Google’s Gemini, Microsoft’s Copilot, Grok and Anthropic’s Claude can all do similar things. But ChatGPT’s popularity and early start gave it a strong lead. More from CNET ChatGPT became one of the fastest-growing apps in history, amassing over 1 billion users. It often stands out for its versatility and ease of use, but mostly for the sheer scale of its user base.   This AI assistant is now far beyond the familiar prompt-and-answer chatbot. You can ask it to generate images, write and debug code, build a website, help you understand your medical records and even plan your next Starbucks order. It can also research a topic in depth and handle multistep jobs, using apps and browsing the web to get things done. The tricky part can be figuring out which version does what — and whether you need to pay for it. Let’s see how exactly ChatGPT works, how to use it and what you get for free or with a subscription. (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) ChatGPT is built on a transformer architecture, a type of neural network that identifies relationships between words. Its name comes from GPT, short for generative pre-trained transformer. OpenAI says its models are developed and trained on massive amounts of data from publicly available internet content alongside partner licensing deals, user interactions and data generated by human trainers and researchers. ChatGPT’s large language models learn patterns from training data and use those, along with your prompt and the conversation, to generate responses. That’s one reason why it sometimes hallucinates or generates confident-sounding but incorrect information.  Sometimes it does it so convincingly and naturally that you might forget it’s not actually thinking. Afraz Jaffri, a senior director analyst at Gartner, says he thinks ChatGPT’s biggest flaw is that “They’re just unreliable. So even if I ask something and I get a response, I still want to check that that is actually true, which kind of defeats the point of us getting it in the first place.” Jaffri says those mistakes now happen less often than they did in the early days of ChatGPT, though.  “The advancements in the things put around the model that turn it into an agentic system in ChatGPT, that allow it to take actions, search, verify and try multiple approaches, mean that its utility beyond simple question answering has drastically improved,” Jaffri tells CNET. ChatGPT can search the web and cite sources, making its answers easier to fact-check. But it doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do it. You can easily access ChatGPT through a web browser or via its apps on Android and iOS devices.  It has also been integrated into Apple products via Apple Intelligence and Siri. OpenAI’s Microsoft Office add-in puts ChatGPT inside Word, Excel and PowerPoint, where it can help edit documents, explain formulas and build presentations. OpenAI also lets you interact with ChatGPT via phone calls and messages. You can call 800-CHATGPT from a US or Canadian number. WhatsApp messaging is available to users with EEA numbers through the verified contact at 800-242-8478. Access is based on your number’s country code. There are many use cases for ChatGPT. It can plan your vacations, practice job interview questions with you, help you with your budgeting and translating, write your resume, do your meal planning, draft emails, summarize long documents, develop business strategies and just have a conversation with you. It’ll learn from your inquiries and requests, and tailor itself to what it thinks you like. To stop OpenAI from using your chats to train its models, turn off Improve the model for everyone under Settings/Data controls. You can still keep those chats in your history. If you want a conversation removed from your history, start a Temporary chat (in the upper-right corner). It won’t add or change memories or be used for training, though OpenAI may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety. Temporary chats can still use what ChatGPT already knows about you. Choose Unpersonalized to stop it from using existing memories, custom instructions and plugins. If you save the chat later, your regular account settings apply. Deep research takes more time to investigate a question and put together a report with citations. You can steer its research toward particular websites, give it your own files and change its plan before it starts.  If you don’t feel like it or can’t type your prompt, you can talk to ChatGPT, too. Live voice lets you verbally interrupt ChatGPT mid-answer and ask it to use connected apps. Eligible subscribers can also share their camera or screen through the separate Advanced voice option on mobile.  On supported paid plans, the MacOS app’s Record feature can transcribe and summarize a meeting. You’ll need the participants’ consent before recording. You can also generate and edit images with ChatGPT. Image 2.5 is available across plans with different limits. You can generate pictures from descriptions or edit existing ones, like changing selected parts, removing backgrounds or even starting with a sketch. It’s a bit unusual for one of the biggest AI players, but ChatGPT can’t generate videos. OpenAI used to have the Sora video generator, but discontinued its consumer app and website in April.  OpenAI also officially shut down its Atlas AI browser in August after a very short run. ChatGPT Health is another feature that lets eligible US adults connect supported medical records or Apple Health data to help interpret lab results and prepare questions for a doctor. It isn’t intended to diagnose conditions or recommend treatment. If you’ve used custom GPTs, the tailored assistants people could build and share, another change is coming. OpenAI plans to retire them on Dec. 11, with plugins taking over that role. Plugins supply tools and reusable instructions for particular jobs. A plugin might let ChatGPT retrieve documents from Google Drive or work with your email, once you connect the account and grant permission.  Projects keep related chats, files and instructions together, saving you from explaining the same assignment every time. They’re available across plans and can be shared with others.  Library stores files you can reuse across conversations, including documents and images. Be aware that deleting a conversation doesn’t automatically delete a file saved in Library. In Tasks, you can schedule reminders or recurring requests, like a morning briefing. Eligible paid users can also trigger tasks in Work when something happens in a connected app, like a new email arriving or Slack activity. ChatGPT Work handles multistep tasks from start to finish. You might ask it to research a topic and build a presentation, then revise the slides together. It can browse websites and use connected apps as it works, then produce an editable file. You can ask for changes without starting the assignment again.  Codex handles software development with a more technical interface. Work can also generate interactive visuals, and eligible Plus, Pro and workspace users can build websites or lightweight apps through Sites, which are currently in public beta. OpenAI also just introduced dots, personal AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra. You can give one an ongoing job, like keeping tabs on a project, and it can work on its own cloud computer while you’re away. You decide which apps it can use and what actions need your approval. For now, you’ll need Pro or Business Premium in an eligible market or access to the beta through an Enterprise, Edu or Healthcare account. ChatGPT started with GPT-3.5, but today it has several GPT-5.6 and 6 models and GPT-6 Astra. Which one is best for you depends on what you’re asking it to do, your subscription and whether you’re using Chat, Work or Codex. In regular ChatGPT, Free and Go use GPT-5.6 Luna for everyday questions, with a Think option for harder ones. Plus uses GPT-5.6 Sol. Instant thinking level gives quicker answers, while Medium and High allow more time to reason through problems. In regular ChatGPT, Pro, Business and Enterprise add Extra High thinking level and GPT-5.6 Sol Pro for really hard tasks, along with GPT-6 Pro, powered by Astra. Usage limits apply, and workplace administrators can restrict your access. To adjust how much time a model spends on reasoning in regular chat on Plus and Pro, you need to change the thinking effort setting yourself. Work and Codex give you more models to choose from than regular Chat.  GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI’s most capable model for complex research, coding and tasks across apps. Plus subscribers can use it in Work mode with usage limits.  The newer GPT-6.1 Sol improves on GPT-6 Sol for coding and operating computers. OpenAI says it approaches Astra’s performance on those tasks and professional work. It’s rolling out in Work and Codex to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users, but isn’t available in regular Chat. Other choices include GPT-6 Luna for quicker, focused jobs such as summaries and GPT-5.6 Terra for everyday assignments. GPT-6 Luna also remains exclusive to Work and Codex. Work and Codex offer GPT-6 Sol for complex coding and tasks involving tools, GPT-5.6 Terra for everyday assignments and GPT-6 Luna for quicker tasks. GPT-6 Sol and Luna aren’t available in regular Chat. Astra’s arrival also stirred up talk of artificial general intelligence, or AGI, meaning AI with human-level abilities across intellectual tasks. OpenAI President Greg Brockman suggested it marked an “AGI era.” Whether that stands to be true remains debatable. Jaffri says Astra is one of the most capable models available, alongside Claude Opus 5.5, with its biggest gains in operating computers and coding, particularly spotting security vulnerabilities. Jaffri also points to a trade-off in its reduced use of reasoning tokens, which help trace a model’s decisions.  “Reducing the number of tokens means that the price per task of the model can be reduced, but at the cost of reduced explainability,” Jaffri tells CNET. Without understanding what models are doing, he warns, making them safe could prove to be impossible. You can do plenty without subscribing. The free plan includes everyday text chats and limited access to tools such as image generation and deep research. Free and Go users also get limited Work access on desktop. US prices start at $8 a month for Go, which increases allowances for tools and uploads. Plus costs $20 per month and adds more capable models, with Work across desktop, web and mobile. Pro now comes in $100, $200 and $500 monthly tiers. Yes, that’s $500 per month. The new Pro 500 plan gives you 25 times Plus’s Work and Codex allowance and access to Astra Ultrafast for faster responses, though that speed burns through your allowance faster, too. Work and Codex share usage limits separate from regular Chat. There’s less welcome news for $200 Pro subscribers — the price stays put, but the allowance is shrinking. The plan has reopened to new subscribers with lower limits. Eligible existing subscribers keep their old limits through Oct. 29, then their Work and Codex allowance drops from 20 times to 10 times Plus’s. Their GPT-6 Pro messages in Chat also fall from 200 to 100 per week. To soften the blow, OpenAI says affected subscribers will receive a one-time grant of 62,500 usage credits, valued at $2,500. But there’s a catch: those credits expire on Dec. 31. Business costs $25 per user per month, with a minimum of two users. Enterprise and Edu have custom pricing. Free and Go plans may show ads in supported regions. Plus and the higher tiers are ad-free. OpenAI says ads don’t influence answers and advertisers can’t read your chats. ChatGPT faces ongoing legal challenges related to industry concerns regarding the ethics and the legality of data sourcing for AI training. High-profile lawsuits against OpenAI and other technology companies include those from major publishers like The New York Times, Dow Jones and CNET’s parent company Ziff Davis (see the disclosure above), which allege unauthorized use of their content to train AI tools, as do many individual authors.  In June, Florida sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging that the company concealed serious risks, including dangers to minors. The lawsuit cited allegations that ChatGPT helped the gunman plan the 2025 Florida State University shooting.  In another lawsuit, the parents of a 19-year-old allege that ChatGPT’s advice about mixing drugs led to his fatal accidental overdose in May 2025. OpenAI says those conversations involved an older version of ChatGPT that it has since retired, and that it has strengthened its safeguards. Amid lawsuits alleging ChatGPT contributed to several deaths, OpenAI introduced Trusted Contact in May. The optional feature lets adults choose a consenting friend or family member to be notified (after human review) if their chats raise serious concerns about potential self-harm or suicide. OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT for Teens on Aug. 18, giving younger users help with studying, reminders to take breaks and added protection from potentially harmful content. Parents can also opt in to parental controls by linking accounts to manage settings and set quiet hours, though they can’t read their teen’s conversations. In June, cybersecurity firm Mindgard reported that variations of a viral “restore this photo” prompt tricked ChatGPT into generating sexually explicit and graphically violent images. OpenAI has also acknowledged breaches involving Hugging Face and Australian government systems during internal testing of experimental models. Jaffri warns that these incidents now show that “the technology itself creates a risk to society.” “The main fear is that these agents may reach a level where they can improve themselves by updating their own models, without needing human supervision or interaction, known as recursive self-improvement,” Jaffri tells CNET. That’s why AI labs have adopted “pacing,” Jaffri says. This means slowing development to give themselves more time to find reliable ways to test new models. ChatGPT is one of the default interfaces for how people interact with AI and even how they get information from the internet.  “The whole kind of technology itself is going to be transformative for a lot of different areas, which will have a direct impact on our lives,” Jaffri says. “Hopefully for the better.” If you feel like you or someone you know is in immediate danger, call 911 (or your country’s local emergency line) or go to an emergency room to get immediate help. Explain that it is a psychiatric emergency and ask for someone who is trained for these kinds of situations. If you’re struggling with negative thoughts or suicidal feelings, resources are available to help. In the US, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Bitcoin fell 1.2% to about $85,600 as of Tuesday Asian morning hours after sellers turned it back from just above $87,000 on Monday — marking the third time that level has capped a rally since Sept. 23. HYPE bucked the drop with a 3% gain to about $94. BNB was the laggard, down 2.5%, while ether, XRP, SOL and DOGE each fell between 1% and 2%. ZEC and TRX were flat, according to CoinDesk data. Outside the majors, ADA jumped 11%, GRT gained 7% and NEAR rose nearly 7%. "The price has approached the apex of the triangle formed by horizontal resistance and rising support. We should therefore be prepared for increased volatility should the price break out of this pattern," he added. The total crypto market slipped to about $2.93 trillion, just under the $2.95 trillion that FxPro marks as resistance. The selling came even as the dollar strengthened and stock indexes held steady. Login  Sagar  06 October 2026   vivo Android Hands-on Featured  vivo hosted a grand event today in Gurgaon, India, where it unveiled the V80 and S2 FE and introduced the X Fold6 to the Indian market. We used the vivo V80 for a few days, and here's how it performed. The vivo V80 is built around a 6.59" 1,260p 144Hz AMOLED display, surrounded by 1.25mm bezels. The display has a centered punch-hole for a ZEISS-tuned 50MP selfie camera. The V80's display also has a 3D ultrasonic fingerprint scanner embedded, which was fast and accurate during our use. It supports swipe-based fingerprint enrollment, and we like how it's placed far from the bottom bezel, facilitating a comfortable phone-unlocking experience. However, there were times when the phone experienced minor lag after unlocking it. It doesn't hamper the user experience, but it's still something worth mentioning. Turn the V80 around, and you see what vivo calls a "Floating Camera Module." vivo says it's a "contemporary take on the classic square camera layout, softened with rounded corners for a lighter, more balanced expression." The brand also said that the "transparent finish adds visual depth, making the design feel modern, distinctive, and effortlessly refined." This camera module features an LED flash, a circular light called Aura Light, a ZEISS logo, and three ZEISS-tuned cameras - a 50MP primary, a 50MP telephoto, and an 8MP ultrawide. The V80 wobbles when used on flat surfaces; however, the bundled transparent case does a great job of minimizing it. The V80's rear design differs from its predecessor, but it may remind some of Apple's iPhone Pro Max models, especially the Sunrise Anthem model, which is the subject of this hands-on and shows different shades depending on lighting and the angle at which it reflects light. The other two colors are Horizon Blue and Stellar Black. The V80's flat back panel and camera module are covered with a glass coating, and the finish feels identical to the vivo X300 FE. You can't tell the two phones apart without looking at them.    vivo V80's Sunrise Anthem model shows different shades depending on lighting and the angle at which it reflects light We like the vivo V80's finish. It feels premium, provides a nice in-hand experience, and keeps the back panel smudge-free. The V80's "high-strength aluminum alloy" frame has a matte finish and stays smudge-free like the phone's back panel. On the right-side frame are the volume rocker and power button - both with good feedback. At the bottom is the USB-C port, flanked by a SIM card slot, a microphone, and a speaker grille. On the top is the secondary mic with an IR blaster and another speaker outlet.     vivo V80's ports and controls The vivo V80 also has IP68 and IP69 ratings. We like its overall design. The smartphone is sturdy, feels premium in the hand, and has a nice finish. It's also not difficult to use with one hand. The vivo V80 features a 6.59" AMOLED display, surrounded by 1.25mm bezels. The display - protected by Schott Xensation Core glass - has a 2,750x1,260-pixel resolution, 459 ppi pixel density, and supports 1.07 billion colors. It also supports HDR, HDR10+, and HLG codecs, and is Widevine L1-certified, enabling 1080p video streaming on compatible apps. Our unit didn't play HDR videos on YouTube, though. The V80's display has a local peak brightness of 5,000 nits, while HBM brightness is 1,800 nits. It can also dim down to 1 nit for a comfortable low-light reading experience. The display was sufficiently bright, and we had no issues watching content even under strong sunlight. Furthermore, the V80's display supports up to 144Hz refresh rate. It can switch between 60Hz, 90Hz, 120Hz, and 144Hz, which is restricted to gaming. The display settings menu offers three refresh rate options - Smart adaptation, Standard (60Hz), and High (144Hz). When you select High, you get the "Custom app refresh rate" option in that menu, which lets you select the apps you want to run at 120Hz. Until OriginOS 6, the list also included games installed on the phone, but in OriginOS 7, you only see apps. Games are now listed in Ultra Game Mode. We find this slightly inconvenient, as having all the apps and games listed in one place is both time-saving and convenient. With Standard mode selected, everything expectedly refreshes at 60Hz. But with High mode, the refresh rate bumped from 60Hz to 120Hz when interacting with the display and remained at 60Hz the rest of the time. This behavior was consistent across most system menus and apps, including Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, Google Play Store, Google Chrome, and Google Photos. Smart adaptation mode works like High mode, but it limits the maximum refresh rate to 90Hz when using Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and Google Chrome. What about games? Well, Sky Force: Reloaded, Dead Trigger 2, and Call of Duty: Mobile - the games we usually play on most of our review devices - ran at 120Hz in High mode. In Smart adaptation mode, only Call of Duty: Mobile ran at 120Hz. In our experience, Sky Force: Reloaded, Dead Trigger 2, and Call of Duty: Mobile all ran at 60 FPS in Smart adaptation mode. In High mode, Call of Duty: Mobile and Dead Trigger 2 ran at 60 FPS, while Sky Force: Reloaded reached a maximum of 101 FPS. Hence, the High refresh rate mode is your best option if you want the smoothest experience possible on the vivo V80. The vivo V80 is powered by the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 SoC, which is the same chip that powered the vivo V70 launched earlier this year and the V60 that came last August. We would've liked a newer, more powerful chip inside the V80, but that could have raised the phone's price, which may be why vivo stuck with the same chip it used in a two-generation-old phone. That said, the vivo V80 comes with 8GB of LPDDR4X RAM and up to 512GB of UFS 3.1 storage. Our unit has 8GB of RAM and 256GB of onboard storage. On the software side, you get Android 17-based OriginOS 7, making it the first V-series smartphone to run OriginOS 7 out of the box. It comes with the promise of four Android OS upgrades and six years of security updates. vivo told us that security updates will be released every month for the first two years, quarterly for the 3rd and 4th year, and every six months for the 5th and 6th year. It's also worth noting that our review unit, an Indian model, came pre-loaded with just one third-party app - Booking.com. It didn't have any other third-party apps or games pre-installed. That's impressive for a Chinese brand! We want other brands to follow suit. OriginOS 7 doesn't come with a major design revamp, but it does bring new features, including Wiggle Theme, StickIt, and Snap Notes. We'll take a detailed look at OriginOS 7 in our full review. In terms of performance, the vivo V80 worked reliably in everyday use. It wasn't as snappy as the vivo X300 Pro or the X300 Ultra, of course, and it did stutter a few times, but overall we have no complaints. The V80's gaming performance was also good enough, and it remained reasonably cool after playing games such as Call of Duty: Mobile for over an hour. You can check the charts below to see how the vivo V80 performed in synthetic benchmarks. And now we have a couple of screenshots showing the vivo V80's sustained performance in a GPU stress test.    GPU test We also ran the CPU Throttling Test app on the V80 to see how it would perform in a 1-hour CPU stress test, but the test never completed, as the phone got very hot after a 15-minute run, prompting its system to close the app and wait for the phone to cool down to use it again. The phone prevented all apps from opening until it cooled down. The vivo V80 features four cameras - one on the front and three on the rear. All are co-developed with ZEISS and have ZEISS optics. The front camera is called "ZEISS Group Selfie Camera" by vivo. It uses a 50MP sensor and has autofocus, an f/2.0 aperture, 92° FOV, and a magnification range of 0.8x - 2x. It can also record videos in up to 4K resolution at 60 FPS. vivo hasn't revealed the sensor used for the selfie camera. The triple camera setup on the rear comprises a 50MP "ZEISS OIS Main Camera," a 50MP "ZEISS Night Telephoto Camera," and an 8MP "ZEISS Ultra Wide-Angle Camera." The primary camera uses the Sony LYTIA 700V sensor, has an f/1.88 aperture, OIS, an 84° FOV, and is capable of recording videos in 4K resolution at 60 FPS. The telephoto camera - having OIS, an f/2.65 aperture, 3x optical zoom, and 100x digital zoom - uses the Sony IMX882 sensor. The ultrawide camera has an f/2.2 aperture and 115° FOV, but vivo hasn't revealed the sensor it uses. The 8MP resolution of the ultrawide camera is the same as the previous two generations of phones, and it's about time we got upgrades in that department. That said, some noteworthy camera features the vivo V80 comes with include 4K Cinematic Video, AI Creative Camera, and AI Diwali Portrait 2.0 (India-exclusive). It also comes with ZEISS Multifocal Portrait, supporting five focal lengths - 23mm, 35mm, 50mm, 85mm, and 100mm. Berlin-based ebike startup Lemmo has been shaking up the European market with a small selection of handsome mid-range models since 2022. It's now got something in the works for families and more adventurous riders with a versatile SUV ebike that promises to take you places while delivering an exceptionally comfortable ride. The Lemmo 3 is a long-tail ebike with room for cargo in the front and rear, plus pannier bags and up to two child seats. It sports a full suspension setup, a hydraulic seatpost, and all-terrain tires to soak up bumps and make it a breeze to cover all kinds of surfaces. The brand says this model is three years in the making, and includes plenty of tech for safety, performance, and convenience that you'd expect to see on the latest ebikes. It's also capable of covering longer distances than just your usual city commutes. Let's talk suspension first. A high-load spring for the rear suspension affords 80 mm of travel to ensure your little passenger is comfortable. Up front, you've got hydraulic forks that deliver 80 mm of travel too. Meanwhile, the seatpost offers 20 mm of travel as well. Closer to the asphalt, 65 mm wide all-terrain tires offer cushioning and stability while riding with heavier cargo. Lemmo's gone with a 960-Wh semi-solid state battery, which reportedly allows for up to 110 miles (180 km) of range and won't go up in flames from punctures or thermal runaway incidents. This pairs with a rear hub Bafang H720 motor that's rated for 750 W of continuous power in the US (500 W in Canada, and 250 W in Europe), and a three-speed automatic gearbox. This setup allows for a pedal assist up to 28 mph (45 km/h). With this kind of kit, the Lemmo 3 should be up to the task of tackling steep inclines and all manner of rough terrain. The brand says its direct steering makes it easier to maneuver than conventional cargo bikes, despite its long wheelbase. Riders ranging from 5ft1 (155 cm) to 6ft5 (195 cm) can enjoy a comfy upright riding position thanks to the adjustable stem and seat. If you plan to take this out on the trail on camping trips, it'll happily handle up to 176 lb (80 kg) of gear in the rear, and an additional 44 lb (20 kg) on the front rack. There's some neat tech on here too, including GPS tracking and a motion detection alarm for security, a 3.5-inch touchscreen displaying your riding metrics, a rear-approaching radar with automatic brake lights, and keyless start. That makes this a compelling option for people looking for a more versatile ebike than the vast range available for riding only around town. Lemmo is scheduled to crowdfund this model on Kickstarter later this month, during which the Essential model will be available at about US$2,155. That's discounted down from its expected MSRP of €3,390 ($3,890) – but it requires an early reservation on Lemmo's site with a refundable $45 deposit. You can add on a belt drive for an extra $193. There are also a couple of bike bundles which include accessories like a passenger guardrail, seat pads and foot boards, pannier bags, and a front rack. With that, Lemmo's set to go up against the Amflow TL Carbon we saw earlier this year. That's another capable SUV ebike, with a powerful motor and swappable add-on battery – at a slightly higher price above the $4,000 mark. Check out the Lemmo 3 on the company's site, and head here for the Kickstarter campaign that's yet to go live at the time of writing (you can sign up to be notified when it takes off). If all goes as expected, orders are estimated to begin shipping next April in the aforementioned regions. Source: Lemmo Sign up for our FREE daily New Atlas newsletter!

Yes, you read that right. A year after hitting a record high above $126,000 on Oct. 6, 2025, bitcoin is down just 32%, at $85,453. In traditional markets, a drop that size would count as a crash. For bitcoin, that's a far gentler slide than in past bear markets. Exactly a year after the 2013 peak, bitcoin was down 69.7%. Similarly, it was down 82.3% following the December 2017 top. A year after the November 2021 high, it was down 74.6%, according to CoinDesk calculations. This shallower decline isn’t limited to the one-year anniversary. The bear market itself has been milder. At its lowest, just below $59,000 on June 30, bitcoin was down more than 53% from its peak. Past bear markets saw prices plummet 77% to 85% from record highs. Essentially, two things have changed. The bear market has been shallower, and its worst point arrived earlier. In previous cycles, the trough often came around the one-year mark or later; this time, it came after about nine months, and the subsequent recovery has been fast. “The most notable changes are the significantly shortened duration of the drawdown and the reduced time spent at the bottom," Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, told CoinDesk. The main reason previous bear markets saw prices fall much lower and for longer is who drove the preceding bull runs. Retail traders and their use of leverage often fueled those rallies, which frequently ended in crashes marked by fund blowups and exchange failures, as seen in 2022. The 2023–25 uptrend, by contrast, was driven by institutional inflows through regulated investment vehicles such as ETFs, while the subsequent downturn reflected a macro-led reversal of those flows. "While previous cycles were driven primarily by retail investors and leverage, buyers in this current cycle increasingly stem from outside the crypto market, including ETFs, asset management giants, family offices, and even corporations. This growing demand for external asset allocation is the core driving force behind these shifts," Sun said. The recent downturn was not entirely driven by "black swan" events, according to Sun; rather, it was largely caused by capital outflows resulting from changes in the external macroeconomic environment and asset allocation landscape. "Consequently, despite undergoing significant adjustments, the market did not trigger the persistent negative feedback loops seen in the past," he noted. That kind of institutional money behaves differently than retail speculative flows, Griffin Ardern, co-founder and vol desk PM at Primal Fund, said. "ETF allocation money rebalances to target weights — it buys weakness by construction.” Leverage was cleared out right at the top and never properly came back, Ardern said. "Hence nine months to grind out a 53% decline, rather than a few months of cascading liquidations taking it down 80%," he said. Most of the leverage was unwound on Oct. 10 last year, when a macro-driven sell-off triggered more than $19 billion in liquidations across crypto derivatives markets. Temporary pricing deviations on Binance for tokens including USDe, wBETH and BNSOL added to the stress, while auto-deleveraging mechanisms on several exchanges forcibly closed profitable positions to cover losses. Calmer crashes come with a cost. Calmer rallies. "As bitcoin evolves and more participants come to market, the realized volatility of the asset will decrease. This means shallower drawdowns and lower peaks and is likely a contributing factor to the more muted sell-off we saw in the last cycle," Jeff Anderson, head of U.S. at market-making firm STS Digital, said. Bitcoin’s volatility has steadily declined since U.S. spot ETFs debuted in early 2024, tempering the “Wild West” reputation the asset once carried, as CoinDesk noted last year. Sun pointed to the numbers. "Bitcoin's current annualized volatility hovers around 40%, which is noticeably lower than its long-term historical levels exceeding 80%," he said. Ardern sees the same in the options market, where bitcoin's annualized implied or expected volatility index, DVOL, has been pinned around 35 points. "The shape going forward is probably a staircase — grind up, air pocket, fast repair — rather than a parabola," he said. Sun still isn't ruling out big rallies and the reason lies in bitcoin's tokenomics. Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million, and long-term holders own a high share of it. Add to that large ETF inflows over a short period, a rapid improvement in macro liquidity, or concentrated short covering, and prices could still see sharp bullish moves, he explained.  In those cases, "marginal demand can still exert a powerful upward push on prices, potentially triggering non-linear surges." Ardern's bigger warning is about positioning. Implied volatility is near its lowest percentile on record, and one-year options skew is still neutral to bearish. "The derivatives market has bought 'shallow', but nobody is willing to pay for 'upside exposure' yet,” he said.  Options skew measures the difference between pricing for bullish call options and bearish put options. A neutral skew means traders aren't yet chasing calls or upside exposure. He also said that the moment the shallow-drawdown story is loudest is usually when downside protection is cheapest.  The depth of the next decline will be decided by the long end of the U.S. Treasury market, not bitcoin's chart, according to Ardern. "If the 30-year [yield] defence keeps failing, this cycle may not stay shallow either," he said. In other words, if the 30-year yield keeps rising, we might see a fresh sell-off in bitcoin. The 30-year yield recently hit a high of 5.7%, the level last seen in April 2002. It has risen by more than 80 basis points this year, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets like bitcoin and gold. The Treasury announced an increased bond buyback program in August to stem the rise in yields. BTC reacted positively, rising from roughly $64,000 to nearly $80,000 in days. But yields haven't stopped rising yet. Some analysts believe this hardening of yields is driven by fiscal concerns, not the growth story, which makes it bullish for gold and bitcoin. Ardern further likened today's market to the Nasdaq of 1994 to 1999, when "policy slows down, the cycle stretches, every interim correction is shallow." "Just remember how that story ended," he said. At first, I took the alerts seriously. When the Food and Drug Administration announced that a multistate cyclospora outbreak was linked to a certain batch of iceberg lettuce from Mexico, I dutifully tossed my wedge salad. Then the recalls grew more sweeping, eventually implicating more items in my kitchen—a popular brand of potato chips, some diced chunks of cantaloupe, and a jar of pistachio-nut butter that a male Instacart shopper had confidently substituted for a single bag of Flamin’ Hot Cheetos. My compliance began to curdle into exasperation. Still, I’m a civic-minded person, and I have no desire for my gastrointestinal tract to be transformed into the River Styx. All I could do was sigh, throw out the compromised goods, and accept that dinner would be a handful of shredded cheese, eaten directly from the bag over the kitchen sink. Lately, though, the push notifications alerting me to the recall du jour have taken on an unremitting, nagging tone. On the surface, this all looks like standard public-health advocacy. We’re now familiar with the boilerplate safety guidelines included in recall articles. But, all of a sudden, the math started to add up. I realized that I was getting reminders to properly heat raw meat with a frequency that rivalled that of Skyrizi commercials. Now I receive urgent, unsolicited dispatches about internal poultry temperatures apropos of absolutely nothing. For instance, the F.D.A. recommends bringing whole poultry, poultry breasts, and ground poultry to a safe minimum internal temperature of a hundred and sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit. You know who else recommends bringing whole poultry, poultry breasts, and ground poultry to a safe minimum internal temperature of a hundred and sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit? My mother. The messaging has gotten harder to ignore. Two days ago, I received an emergency alert regarding “all ready-to-eat, shelf-stable, ambient-temperature convenience-store items nationwide.” Surely this must be an error, I thought—a matter of haphazard syntax! I tapped the notification, expecting the usual recall details, and discovered the reason for the alert: Potential risk of not engaging in mise en place. Under “Recommended Consumer Actions,” the agency didn’t instruct me to return the offending items for a refund. Instead, they provided a hyperlinked YouTube tutorial on how to properly deglaze a pan. At this point, any pretense of subtext has been abandoned. Yesterday, a voluntary recall was issued for every major brand of frozen chicken nuggets because “they might contain small pieces of metal, or, worse, the crushing realization that you are a thirty-five-year-old adult who still eats like a kindergartner at a birthday party.” This morning, the agency urged me to immediately discard my store-bought rotisserie chicken and instead braise a lamb shank in a classic mirepoix. This just in: the very concept of a deli counter is now under active federal investigation. I tried to outsmart them. I stopped buying pre-cut fruit. I successfully ignored the siren song of the deli display that was luring me toward one of those pre-assembled charcuterie adult Lunchables. Thinking that maybe a team of professional chefs could help me evade agency scrutiny, I pivoted entirely to the hot-food bar at the gourmet market down the street. I believed that I’d finally beaten them, until I received a high-priority alert stating that any prepared mac and cheese consumed out of a cardboard container while watching “The Traitors” poses an immediate danger of “emotional rigor mortis.” So I drove three counties over to a tiny creamery and bought some artisanal, small-batch provisions, praying that a fancy goat cheese bisected by a line of vegetable ash wouldn’t trigger a warning. No sooner had I started my car than I was informed that every wedge had been recalled for “exhibiting unauthorized rustic charm.” They don’t want me to be safe; they want me to buy a Dutch oven. It's getting exhausting. I can’t even open a bag of tortilla chips anymore without being cautioned that my sodium levels are a “cry for help,” followed by the suggestion that I consider roasting my own chickpeas with a light dusting of organic cumin instead. So you know what? You win, Commissioner! I’ll get a cast-iron skillet. I’ll commit to using “roux” as a verb. I’ll finally figure out how to turn on my oven. I just have one non-negotiable, and it’s a deal-breaker: I refuse to eat the food I cook. Actually, never mind. There’s already an alert regarding my meatloaf. ♦ A word from the next President (self-declared). Coyote takes the Acme Company to court. I am a woman in my thirties, and I am thriving. (Mis)Uses of Technology			  Meta’s agentic AI product Muse has had a rocky few weeks since launch. The product, which features an animated avatar named Jolly (one presumes to make mass hyper surveillance seem adorable) is supposed to help you offload busywork like making restaurant reservations, paying bills, or ordering groceries.  Despite Meta having claimed repeatedly that Muse was built with a heavy focus on privacy and security, the AI agent launched with a nasty zero-day flaw that made it possible to spy on Mac users. When one tech YouTuber put Muse in charge of their Facebook Marketplace sales, it sold his stuff way below acceptable rates and doled out their home address (the user apparently didn’t understand the permissions he set).  Somebody else found that you could trick Muse into giving root access on the device it’s running on by simply pretending to be a Muse agent yourself. Others found that Muse software not only accesses people’s private messages without approval, it often ignores all permissions and uploads them to the cloud – even if you specifically tell it not to. That last problem was bad enough that Apple needed to change its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories: “Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully.” Meanwhile, Wired found that Muse consistently creates detailed profiles of all your friends, family, colleagues, “collaborators,” and people you “follow.” Obviously much of that information is necessary for the agent to get to “know” you, but this being Meta, people are understandably uncomfortable with this sort of massive ramp up of data collection in a country, under authoritarian control, that’s too corrupt to pass a privacy law or regulate data brokers: “These [AI assistant] tools are actively soliciting users to plug their whole lives in—their emails, calendars, financial institutions, everything in order to be helpful assistance,” Bogen says. “That’s dramatically more information than people might have otherwise given to some of these companies. The breadth of access to information that these tools have will lead to a ballooning of what they know about users.” But wait, there’s more! 404 Media found that in the weeks before launch, Meta was in a mad dash to quickly and sloppily fix multiple other vulnerabilities but refused to delay Muse’s launch to actually make sure the product was secure: “The Meta source said they felt security teams were asked to push hot fixes to these bugs as quickly as possible and in a way that wouldn’t delay Muse’s launch, leading to what they described as “half-baked protections being rushed out to enable the launch. Many senior engineers believe it’s inevitable we’re going to have a massive data breach as a result of Hatch.” Muse is called “Hatch” internally and in Meta’s codebase.” Many folks build their own agentic AI solutions with cobbled together open source hardware and software to ensure they have clear understanding of, and control over, what’s actually happening in their name. Meta, a glorified ad monopoly with a history of ethical “lapses,” not only wants to dominate the space, it will spend a lot of time in the new year lobbying against on device, open source, foreign, and/or open weighted alternatives to Meta. Despite Meta’s claims that privacy and security would be a priority for Muse that’s clearly not the case; it’s also extremely clear that Meta doesn’t fear any meaningful government accountability or oversight, or the product would have spent significantly more time in the oven. Tech giants that had already clearly abandoned quality control at impossible scale are engaged in a mad dash to the trough with new product launches before their funny math causes a market correction. Such is life in a country that has had most consumer protection regulators (and cybersecurity standards) lobotomized by corrupt authoritarians. Authoritarians guys like Mark Zuckerberg enthusiastically supported because they didn’t like paying taxes — and hated former FTC antitrust boss Lina Khan.  Muse’s early privacy and security problems are the kind of stuff anybody with a head on their shoulders could see coming miles over the horizon. And it’s all inevitably going to get more dangerous — and ridiculous — over the next year as unethical tech oligarchs fully exploit their successful lobotomization of the federal regulatory state. You know, for the love of innovation.
